Today's Yongkang people no longer need to travel far from home; modern machines and transportation tools have replaced their hands and carrying poles, sending "Yongkang-made products" to more and more distant "prefectures and counties." Now only one blacksmith remains on the old street, named Cheng Mingxing (born 1944, Sheng generation, 22nd generation of the Cheng family). The old man lives in the first house east of the old street, south of Songmen Bridge. His small workshop is the room at the northwest corner of the courtyard, facing the street. Whenever passing the old man's window, one can see him standing before the glowing red furnace, swinging his hammer. He often holds half a cigarette in his mouth, and the wisp of blue smoke dances to the rhythmic clanging sounds, set against the faint heat rising from the furnace. The old man says this house has a history of over a hundred years, built successively by his great-grandfather and grandfather. In the past, wine and porcelain were sold here, providing rest for pilgrims. During the "land reform," his family had 800 ba of land (70 ba equals one mu). This was extraordinary in Yanxia Village at that time, making them one of the top rich peasants. The rich peasant status, combined with his father—originally a teacher—losing his job in the 1958 "Anti-Rightist" movement, made the family's life even more difficult. In the early 1960s, he left home to learn blacksmithing in Xinchang, and later went successively to Jiangxi and Zhejiang. During peak seasons, Elder Cheng Maofa goes to the new street to sell local specialties such as water chestnuts, and during off-seasons helps at his son's small factory. Over forty years of leaving home and wandering from street to alley as a blacksmith left lifelong marks on him; the old man's back is twisted, and he walks with a limp.

The days of leaving home were hard, especially for young apprentices. Out of the traditional Chinese cultural spirit of respecting the master as a father, they not only vied to carry heavy burdens and do hard work, but also had to rise earlier and sleep later than the master; at meals they had to watch the master's expression, and going hungry was common. Elder Cheng Mingxing says his master treated him well and he did not suffer hardship. Even so, he had to get up at 5 a.m. every day and finish everything before the master rose. He first repaired the furnace with mud; then boiled water, prepared charcoal with mud, adjusted water, and made preparations for work; then boiled water, made tea, prepared washing water for the master; then went to carry water. Daily workload was calculated by "pieces": generally two people made 8 large pieces or 10 small pieces per day. These items were mostly farm tools, with some daily utensils. The old man especially emphasized, "Scissors are the hardest to forge, yet count as small pieces, making them the most disadvantageous to make."

There are also many rules and customs within this trade. Because there were few craftsmen on the old street and development was late, it did not, like other parts of Yongkang, venerate trade deities such as Lu Ban or the Supreme Lord Laozi. Hugong, as an omnipotent local deity, would receive the worship of these departing craftsmen during New Year, blessing them with safe travels and prosperous business in the coming year. Of course, besides seeking Hugong's protection for safety, one must also be very careful oneself. For example, craftsmen going out avoid days ending in seven, returning home avoid days ending in eight; the fifth, fourteenth, and twenty-third are days not to go out, while the third and eleventh are good days; if the first person encountered when going out is a pregnant woman, it is an auspicious sign; if it is another woman, it is inauspicious, and one should return home before leaving again. Among various craftsmen there are also hierarchical distinctions. Some say blacksmiths are the greatest, because blacksmiths not only make tools for themselves but also for all other trades; others say stonemasons are the greatest, because when building a house, stonemasons go first; still others say plasterers are great, because they climb highest when building houses; and some say blacksmiths and stonemasons are equally great, so when invited to a master's banquet, both sit at the head table.

Yongkang being a place "not where boats and carts converge, nor where merchants gather," there were necessarily few people in commerce. Even if there were, they would certainly have had a hard life. As described in the Yongkang County Gazetteer compiled in the seventeenth year of Guangxu (1891), merchants: "The large ones are salt merchants and pawnbrokers, all non-native people." The old street's location made transportation even more inconvenient, so for a long time people were content with a self-sufficient life. Those "non-native people" dealing in "beans, grain, cloth, thread, chickens, pigs, wine, and vegetables" were almost nonexistent here. But over the years, pilgrims coming and going up Fangyan provided another business opportunity: food, incense candles, and general merchandise serving pilgrims, as well as its distinctive inn industry.

Development of the Inn Industry

As Hu Ze was granted titles again and again, the fame of Heling Temple grew, and more and more pilgrims came. Hugong's sphere of influence gradually expanded from the initial surrounding areas of Yongkang, Dongyang, and Gushan within a few dozen li, to places hundreds of li away such as Hangzhou, Shaoxing, Ningbo, and even farther places like Jiangxi and Fujian. In the era without engines, it took three or four days to walk from Hangzhou to Fangyan, so these distant pilgrims needed to stay overnight at Fangyan. The monk's quarters of Guangci Temple on Fangyan Mountain were the earliest inns here. Guangci Temple's incense was most prosperous in the Ming Dynasty; according to former abbot Master Yunming, at its peak there were 801 monks. At the end of the Ming Dynasty, the temple was divided into eight quarters, taking turns managing daily temple affairs, and each quarter had its own monk's quarters. If pilgrims needed lodging, they stayed in vacant monk's quarters, paying whatever they wished. In the early Qing Dynasty, only six of the eight quarters remained, so there may have been more vacant monk's quarters to meet pilgrim accommodation needs. From another perspective, convenient lodging meant distant pilgrims no longer had worries, leading more people to come to Fangyan for sightseeing, worship, and supplication. However, on the fourth day of the ninth lunar month in the twenty-ninth year of Daoguang (1849), a great fire almost destroyed all buildings of Guangci Temple, including the monk's quarters. Although the temple was fully rebuilt a year later and pilgrims continued to come as before, there were fewer monks and monk's quarters than before. Cheng Yuebiao on the old street below saw this business opportunity and founded the first inn on the old street—Cheng Longxing Inn, smoothly bringing many guests who would have stayed in monk's quarters into his own home. Thanks to the auspicious characters "Longxing" (Prosperous Rise), Cheng Longxing later became not only one of the top famous inns here, but the inn industry on the old street also flourished from then on.

During the Guangxu period (1875-1908), "monks left one after another, and from then on pilgrims all stayed on Yanxia Street, no longer lodging in monk's quarters." The decline of Guangci Temple was the catalyst for the emergence of the inn industry on the old street, and the early development of the inn industry was mainly related to two families: Cheng Yuebiao (1821-1850) and his four sons, and the three sons of Cheng Lelai (1823-1882). For a period, they owned almost all the inns on the old street—all large or super-large luxury inns. Competition between these two families, and even between brothers, became the driving force behind the vigorous development of the inn industry on the old street. This competition also reflected and promoted innovation and change in architecture.

Cheng Yuebiao's Cheng Longxing Inn was located at the north end of the Shangkeng mouth, west of the old street, north of Zuoxun Gong Hall. Most of the buildings have collapsed over time, with only faint outlines of the courtyard visible. According to his great-grandson Cheng Lipeng's recollection, Cheng Yuebiao died young in middle age, leaving four sons—Zhaoxiang, Zhaoqing, Zhaoye, and Zhaoheng—and his wife Zhu continued to run Cheng Longxing Inn. In the early Guangxu period (before 1882), the four brothers divided the family. The eldest Zhaoxiang and third Zhaoye partnered under the name Xinlongxing; the second Zhaoqing and fourth Zhaoheng joined forces to continue running Cheng Longxing, renamed Laolongxing. This family division pattern—where the eldest son's inn uses the character "new" and the youngest inherits the original name or uses "old"—was a tradition on the old street. In other words, the eldest son would inherit the newer courtyard. Xinlongxing Inn was located at the Xiahukeng mouth, west of the old street, close to the Sutra Hall to the north. The site of this courtyard is now overgrown with weeds. It was likely built before the family division, or built specifically for it. After operating separately for some time, the eldest and third had financial disputes. To preserve brotherly affection, they decided to operate separately. The third brother, Cheng Zhaoye, chose a new site in 1882 to build another courtyard, named Cheng Renchang. This new inn was located on the west side of the old street, at the western foot of Lion Mountain, south of the Zhou Family Ancestral Hall; at that time it was a large three-story courtyard with thirteen rooms per floor. This courtyard was then located north of the "city head," outside the village entrance, surrounded by farmland. Within just five years, Cheng Zhaoye not only repaid the money borrowed for construction, but also added a four-bay, three-story small courtyard behind (west of) the inn. The ground floor rooms were used for brewing wine and making ham, while the upper floors were high-end guest rooms named Fortune, Emolument, Longevity, and Happiness. Each guest room was furnished with new-style furniture, exclusively for upper-class travelers from Shanghai, Shaoxing, and other places. As Cheng Renchang's business grew increasingly prosperous, it acquired more and more storefronts. In 1920, Cheng Zhaoye bought a small plot of land opposite the Sutra Hall and built a six-bay, two-story building. The first floor was rented to others for a southern goods store, and the second floor served as guest rooms. In the early 1930s, he built a three-bay, four-story, exquisitely carved Western-style building north of the old Cheng Renchang inn; and added a row of auxiliary rooms at the southwest corner of the old inn. By this point, Cheng Renchang Inn, with over 70 guest rooms of various types and more than 250 beds, became the largest inn on the old street at that time. During peak season, each bed averaged two people, and with floor mats laid in halls and courtyards, it was said to accommodate over 700 guests simultaneously. Among the many pilgrims who stayed here, the most famous was Mao Shi, Chiang Kai-shek's first wife. According to Elder Cheng Lipeng's recollection, on the afternoon of the twentieth day of the second lunar month in 1937, two brand-new cars stopped in front of Cheng Renchang. Mao Shi, accompanied by her entourage, came to Fangyan to fulfill a vow. In the mid-1930s, Cheng Zhaoye's two sons divided Cheng Renchang into two: the eldest son Cheng Xuanhu inherited the newly built four-story Western-style building and the small courtyard with Fortune, Emolument, Longevity, and Happiness guest rooms, renamed Xinrenchang Inn; the second son Cheng Xuanjie took charge of the old inn and some rear auxiliary rooms, under the name Cheng Renchang Longji, also known as Laorenchang Inn.

While Cheng Yuebiao and his sons began operating inns, the three sons of Cheng Lelai also opened shops one after another. In 1864, shortly after Cheng Yuebiao founded Cheng Longxing Inn, Cheng Lelai's third son Cheng Zhaofu (1857-1939) used the five hundred copper coins given by his father as capital, and with his wife began operating Cheng Zhenxing Restaurant. Sixteen years later, in 1880, he used his earnings to build a sixteen-bay, two-story courtyard house outside the "city head," at the eastern foot of Lion Mountain on the east side of the old street, and switched to the inn business. Over the next sixty years, Cheng Zhenxing Inn underwent four major expansions. In 1909, Cheng Zhaofu built a courtyard of the same style outside the north wall of the original inn. In 1924, he built an ancestral hall for himself on the west side of the old street, north of these two courtyards and south of Cheng Renchang Inn. Subsequently, he built a two-story, six-bay Western-style building south of the ancestral hall. In 1942, three years after Cheng Zhaofu's death, his sons Cheng Xuanmei and Cheng Xuanji commissioned a Hangzhou construction firm to build another seven-bay, three-story Western-style building south of the existing Western-style building. By this point, Cheng Zhenxing Inn had become a super-large luxury inn with three courtyard buildings, two independent buildings, nearly 130 guest rooms of various types, and over 350 beds. While Cheng Zhaofu's inn business grew increasingly prosperous, his two brothers also opened shops in the early twentieth century. His second brother Cheng Zhaofeng (1855-1928) built a similar-style courtyard north of Cheng Zhenxing's second courtyard, named Cheng Chengchang. His sixth brother Cheng Zhaogong operated Cheng Longchang Inn on the west side of the old street in Chenglu Village, south of Songmen Bridge. In 1943, Cheng Xuanmei died. Two years later, Cheng Xuanmei's son Cheng Chongxue and his uncle Cheng Xuanji divided the family. From then on, Cheng Zhenxing, with over eighty years of history, was split in two. Cheng Chongxue received the second courtyard and the Western-style building, renamed Xinzhenxing; Cheng Xuanji continued operating Cheng Zhenxing Inn using the first courtyard and Cheng Zhaofu's ancestral hall, also known as Laozhenxing.

Besides the inns operated by these two families, during the decades from the late nineteenth to early twentieth century, there were also several scattered inns on the old street. From south to north along the old street: Ma Dahe Inn at the old street corner north of Huilong Bridge; Cheng Meiyi at the northwest corner of Degeng Residence; Cheng Yifeng Inn Yaji and Cheng Yifeng Old Store at the western foot of Centipede Mountain between the old street and Fangyan Stream; Cheng Dachang at the Sanjiantou mountain ravine mouth; and Cheng Baochang, Cheng Qianchang, and Cheng Hongchang near Songmen Bridge.

While the inn industry on the old street flourished, small inns also began operating one after another beside the Heavenly Street on Fangyan Mountain. For historical reasons, the owners of these small inns were all Cheng descendants from Wenlou Village. According to former Guangci Temple abbot Monk Yunming, at its peak there were 10 small inns on the Heavenly Street, developed from the Guangxu period (1875-1908). According to statistics in "Famous Stores of Yongkang," these inns had only three or four guest rooms, i.e., storefronts one to two bays wide. Compared with inns on the old street, these shops almost never used the character "Cheng" in their names, nor words like "Zhenxing" or "Longchang." Instead, many of their names were related to Daoist allusions, such as Sanxing Tower, Yuhua Tower, Tianmen Store, and Gourd Signboard.

Culture in Competition

Anyone who has been to Jinhua must have had this experience: after checking into a hotel, some scholarly country gentlemen in blue cotton gowns would come to question you: "Are you going to Fangyan to burn incense? How many times have you come? Which inn did you stay at before?" If you answered it was your first time to Fangyan, they would take out a business card and ask you to stay at that inn after going up Fangyan. These are the "fangtou" of Yanxia Street—guest-receivers similar to but slightly different from inns. Hundreds of li away, these dispatched agents drummed up business; on one hand, one can imagine the prosperity of Fangyan's incense market year-round, and on the other, infer the fierce competition among the four or five hundred families on Yanxia Street. The so-called fangtou of Yanxia Street, those operating inns and relying solely on Hugong Temple for a living, numbered three to five thousand, mostly with the surnames Cheng and Ying, with a strong literary tradition and considerable property, all living in three-story houses. Generally, the ground floor was built in the valley, the middle floor faced the street, and the upper floor was loft; each family had thirty to fifty rooms, and during prosperous incense seasons, every family was reportedly overcrowded. Pilgrims came from Shaoxing, Chuzhou, Hangzhou, and nearby counties, already a considerable number, and the farthest came from Fujian.

This "Quiet Records of Fangyan," whose every line brims with bustle, was completed by Mr. Yu Dafu (1895-1945) in 1933. With a few strokes, he sketched the prosperous scene of Yanxia Street's inn industry at that time. The "fangtou" mentioned here are the people dispatched by major inns to solicit and receive guests. Although not as many as the three to five thousand mentioned in the article, three to five hundred seems likely. Elder Ying Yexiang, grandson-in-law of Cheng Longchang, says that before each year's incense season, Cheng Zhenxing would dispatch two to three hundred people to various places to receive guests. The county gazetteer also mentions that Cheng Renchang had seventy to eighty guest-receiving clerks. These fangtou were mostly locals, and when short-staffed, hired outsiders. They would set out over a month before the incense season to receive guests in Shanghai, Hangzhou, Ningbo, Wenzhou, Tiantai, Jinhua, Dongyang, Yiwu, and other places. Hard as it was, they also had to speak local dialects. Fangtou who could receive many guests were highly respected in the inn. It is said that the famous fangtou at Cheng Zhenxing Inn was Cheng Shuijing, son of the owner Cheng Zhaofu's sixth brother; he spoke many dialects and was a skilled guest-receiver, and even Cheng Zhaofu would listen to his suggestions on inn management. Corresponding to fangtou were "xiangtou," who specialized in organizing pilgrims locally. Xiangtou would generally write to the inn one or two months in advance, agreeing on lodging dates and the number of fellow travelers, usually specially noting "rain or shine" to show piety. Subsequently, the fangtou dispatched by the inn would contact them with gifts and give each pilgrim a red cloth strip with the inn's name to tie on their luggage. Small inns could not afford to dispatch people as grandly as large inns, so the inn owners had to go themselves. This custom continues today; although current owners no longer need to receive guests in person, they call old pilgrims to greet them in the seventh lunar month, and visit every few years.

Before engines were widely used for long-distance passenger transport, devout pilgrims either relied on their own two legs or took boats to nearby Yongkang, Dongyang, or Yiwu before switching to walking. It is unknown when sedan-chair agencies began appearing in Yongkang, Dongyang, Yiwu, Zhuji, and other places, specifically to transport pilgrims to and from Fangyan. The novel "Enmity Records of Kuocang Mountain," set in late Qing society after the failure of the Taiping Rebellion (1851-1864), mentions sedan-chair agencies in Yongkang city transporting pilgrims to Fangyan. "Yongcheng Mountain Songs," praising famous stores and sights of Yongkang, also mentions the famous Wang Jiankang sedan-chair agency in the county town. In January of the 23rd year of the Republic (1934), the Hangjiang Railway was fully opened, with stations at Jinhua 51, Yiwu, and Zhuji. The same year, the Fangyan Highway was completed and opened, with cars able to drive all the way to the Cheng Family Ancestral Hall entrance north of Chenglu Village. To provide thorough service and, more importantly, secure customers, inns not only had to make proper arrangements with these out-of-town sedan-chair agencies to ensure service, but also dispatched many clerks to wait at Yongkang and Fangyan stations, welcoming guests whose luggage bore their own red cloth strips. After the War of Resistance against Japan ended, the number of pilgrims and inns both increased greatly; at that time, any boy who could carry luggage would go to the station to receive guests.

In the early twentieth century, competition among inns on the street was fierce, especially between the two large inns Cheng Zhenxing and Cheng Renchang for customers. Although Cheng Renchang and Cheng Zhenxing stood almost side by side on both sides of the old street, Cheng Renchang had a slight advantage in competition because it was to the north. Since all guests originally planning to stay at Cheng Zhenxing would pass by its entrance, Cheng Renchang often stole Cheng Zhenxing's guests. Therefore, Cheng Zhenxing's dispatched fangtou, when encountering groups of wealthy people—especially Shaoxing guests—would personally bring the guests back to Fangyan. For ordinary guests, they could only hope that their clerks waiting at the station would be quick enough to grab luggage tied with "Cheng Zhenxing" red cloth strips. For those not received at the bus station—especially first-time pilgrims to Fangyan—when they passed Cheng Renchang's entrance, they might be pulled into that inn by Cheng Renchang's clerks. As this happened more often, Cheng Zhenxing's business was inevitably affected. So Cheng Zhenxing's owner Cheng Zhaofu went to his sixth brother Cheng Zhaogong to discuss a strategy. Zhaofu suggested Zhaogong buy land in Chenglu Village at the north end of the old street; Zhaofu would use wood from his own mountains as material and pay wages to help Zhaogong build an inn. Once the construction money was repaid, the inn would belong to Zhaogong. This new inn was named Cheng Longchang, and at its entrance would hang Cheng Zhenxing's sign. Cheng Zhenxing's guests passing through would be led by Cheng Longchang's clerks to Cheng Zhenxing Inn, one li away. To this day, Cheng Zhaogong's grandson-in-law Ying Yexiang still preserves these two signs.

Even this was not enough, because even inns run by brothers would compete. According to Elder Ying Yexiang, Cheng Zhenxing's skilled guest-receiver Cheng Shuijing suggested to Cheng Zhaofu that a chamber of commerce be established. Its purpose was to unite all inns, establish trade rules, ensure no one stole guests, with fines for violations. Specific clauses included: guests whose luggage bore a certain inn's red cloth strip could not be received by other inns; when a guest reached a certain inn's entrance or stepped one foot inside, other inns could not receive them; each inn's roadside guest-receivers should stand in fixed positions, etc. But due to the cruelty of competition, and because the chamber had no real power to penalize guest-stealing inns, the chamber was established several times, yet each time gradually became a mere formality.

Of course, ultimately, what truly made an inn strong in competition was its meticulous service and reasonable charges. Generally, pilgrims coming here stayed for "one night and two meals": they arrived in the afternoon of the first day, ate some snacks, then went up Fangyan, and left after breakfast the next day; some arrived the previous evening, went up Fangyan after breakfast, and left after lunch. Upon arrival, clerks immediately helped with luggage, invited guests to rest in the hall, then served sugar tea, pastries, lotus root starch, and vegetarian noodles. If guests had not yet gone up Fangyan, that evening's meal would be vegetarian to show piety; if they had already worshipped Hugong, upon returning to the inn they would see this scene: "The guest hall was already lit with two large red candles, set with many dishes of large meat and large chicken, waiting for us to eat dinner, with an abundance of vegetables." In the evening, the inn would often invite small singing troupes to entertain, and sometimes guests would call eager performers outside into their rooms to sing. They mostly sang festive and lively excerpts from Wu opera such as "Hundred Longevity Picture," "Dragon-Tiger Battle," and "Grand Tutor Zhang Returns to Court." Because guests differed in wealth and came from different places, their preferences for dish types and flavors varied, but inns would all attend to them carefully. Cheng Renchang Inn had three tiers of charging standards based on service and meals, with differences of twenty to thirty times. But even so-called "third-class" guests ate and drank as much as they wished, and were served a whole chicken. Cheng Zhenxing Inn, favored by wealthy guests from Shanghai, Suzhou, Hangzhou, and Shaoxing, was especially distinctive in this regard. The inn not only sent longan and lychee soup to these guests at night, but the chef also prepared meals according to their tastes; and when guests left, the inn gave gifts such as ham, flower umbrellas, tea, lotus root starch, "Fangyan Guide," and Fangyan maps. Besides these basic services, many inns provided many extra services. For example, they mostly sold offerings such as incense candles on commission, and some prepared three-animal sacrificial offerings for pilgrims to rent. Moreover, inn clerks would help carry offerings up the mountain, arrange them, and carry them back down; if it was a guest's first time up Fangyan, a clerk would guide them as a tour guide. For guests, receiving such good service meant they not only returned as loyal repeat customers every year, but sometimes also sent the inn local specialties. However, they occasionally also "stole." Descendants of Cheng Zhenchang Inn say that in those years Wenzhou people often stole bowls from the inn for their children to use, and when the children achieved success, they would return to Fangyan to fulfill vows and repay the inn tenfold.

Providing such perfect service required joint efforts from the owner down to the waiters. The busiest times at Fangyan Mountain were the first, second, eighth, ninth, and tenth lunar months. Needless to say, in the first month, locals and nearby people vied to go up Fangyan on New Year's Eve to burn the first incense, then draw a peace talisman for the new year. Fangyan people generally believed the twenty-fifth day of the second lunar month was Hugong's birthday; around that day, as was customary, Guangci Temple would invite people to perform temple fair operas for two days and three nights before the Hugong Main Hall. From the ninth day of the eighth lunar month to the fourteenth day of the ninth lunar month was the over-one-month Hugong Temple Fair, when all seventy-two townships in Yongkang would come to Fangyan to "perform Luohan martial arts," with two peaks on the thirteenth day of the eighth month and the Double Ninth Festival. The "Kuchuan Hu Family Genealogy" from Hu Ze's hometown records that the thirteenth day of the eighth lunar month was Hugong's birthday. People on the old street, however, believed this day was when Hugong "reviewed" the Luohan troupes, or when he was "deified." As a folk custom, people do not investigate its true origin. So during the temple fair, tens of thousands of people went up Fangyan daily with different purposes. After the temple fair, it coincided with the slack farming season, so most pilgrims were from out of town. This was also the inns' busiest time of year, with inns large and small on the old street all overcrowded. So inn owners would treat all clerks to a meal on the Mid-Autumn Festival of the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, hoping everyone would unite and work hard for over a month to run the inn well together. A folk ballad of the time sang: "Don't marry your daughter to Yanxia Street, for in the eighth and ninth months she becomes a signboard. Wipe her eyes once, and when her parents pass by she doesn't even drag them in." During this period, inn clerks were mostly temporary workers, paid by the day. Although wages were not high, there were generous tips. Total tip income was distributed among all staff according to the principle of "reward diligence and punish laziness," with the owner not participating. So although hard, it was considered a good job. Large inns like Cheng Zhenxing needed to hire thirty to forty, even seventy to eighty clerks each year, all available on call.

The most distinctive feature of inn operation was their "jargon." Many trades have their own jargon, existing to prevent outsiders from understanding, thereby protecting the trade's interests. The jargon common on the old street was also called "the speech of those who eat Hugong," so those selling general merchandise and incense candles also understood it. For those in the inn business, it was especially important because it avoided many unnecessary embarrassments. For example, inns inevitably borrowed things from each other such as tofu, eggs, even bed boards and bedding; if guests heard such talk, it would be somewhat humiliating, and might even cause guests who had just stepped through the threshold to turn and leave, so such exchanges were conducted in jargon. The jargon here was vivid and easy to remember. It mostly replaced things with their characteristics—for example, fish was called "water shuttle," noodles "long," soy sauce "red water," etc. Some involved splitting Chinese characters: thus rice became "eight wood," and fire "two dots person." Because of this, jargon is still used by some people today.

Provincial Government's Wartime Temporary Office Location

26th Year of the Republic (1937)
July 7, Marco Polo Bridge Incident!
July 29, Beijing fell! The next day, Tianjin fell!
August 13, Battle of Shanghai broke out; November 12, Shanghai fell!
November 5, Jiaxing and Huzhou lost, Hangzhou in critical danger! The Kuomintang Zhejiang Provincial Government was forced to move to Jinhua.
Early December, Zhejiang Provincial Government decided to move from Jinhua to Fangyan.
December 24, Hangzhou fell...

27th Year of the Republic (1938)
January 1, the Kuomintang Zhejiang Provincial Government began operating in Shoushan Keng north of the old street.

In those turbulent wartime years, because some major highways were occupied by the Japanese, and the Hangjiang Railway—only opened for a few years—was destroyed by Kuomintang troops due to wartime needs, the number of pilgrims coming from afar to worship Hugong at Fangyan also decreased. But the old street welcomed some refined, well-dressed city people with their families. The street's inns were transformed into government agencies such as the Procuratorate, Civil Affairs Department, and Accounting Office. During this special period, Fangyan, with its special terrain and the superior accommodation conditions on the old street, was chosen by the Kuomintang Zhejiang Provincial Government as the wartime temporary government location.

The provincial government operated in Fangyan from January 1, 1938 (27th year of the Republic), until May 1941 (30th year), when it moved to Songyang; in August it returned to Fangyan. In May 1942 (31st year), it moved again to Songyang, and in August transferred to Yunhe, remaining there until the victory of the War of Resistance against Japan. The Zhejiang Provincial Government operated in Fangyan for a total of 4 years and 5 months. During this period, two provincial administrative conferences, one provincial police conference, and one provincial land administration conference were held. Provincial government committee meetings, party-government joint meetings, capital and provincial capital fall commemorations, mobilization monthly meetings, commemoration weeks, and various national commemorations were held on schedule. Especially in early April 1939 (28th year of the Republic), Zhou Enlai, in his capacity as Vice Minister of the Political Department of the Kuomintang Government Military Committee, came to Fangyan and, together with Zhejiang Provincial Government Chairman Huang Shaohong, personally planted two plane trees in Shoushan Keng. On July 7 of the same year, the provincial government built a Monument to Martyrs Who Died in the War of Resistance before Taohua Peak, one of the Five Peaks, and held gatherings at the square before the monument every July 7 to commemorate soldiers who died on the anti-Japanese battlefield.

Accompanying the provincial government to Yongkang were some twenty to thirty provincial government parallel agencies, over twenty subsidiary institutions of various departments, and over twenty other organizations and groups. Many of these agencies were scattered on the old street or in temporarily built houses beside Wufeng Road. Moreover, accompanying government civil servants and their families, as well as some fleeing common people, would rent inns or private houses on the old street for long-term residence. According to elders, at that time almost every family had rooms for rent. If private houses, they mostly lived on the second floor originally used for storage; for inns, owners would reserve some first-floor rooms for sporadic pilgrims coming to worship Hugong at Fangyan, and rent out the upstairs guest rooms. At the north end of the old street and in Chenglu Village, due to proximity to the provincial government located in Shoushan Keng, every floor was crowded.

Perhaps because of the decades of turmoil following the founding of New China, people did not tell this history to their descendants as an honor-bringing family story. The elders still alive today were children then, and their memories are mostly vague. Only one-sentence stories remain, such as: "They were very clean and always fetched water from the well in the courtyard"; "Once my father went to collect rent and was beaten by them instead"; "There was an ophthalmologist Dr. Zhuo at the other end of the street who even treated my diphtheria"; "That bureau chief (police chief) was tall and big, a bit chubby, always smiling."

The large inns on the old street, with many rooms and corresponding service facilities, naturally became the first choice for government agencies. The Civil Affairs Department was successively located in Xinlongxing Inn and Shaochang Ancestral Hall. Descendants of Cheng Chengchang Inn say the Civil Affairs Department head lived in their home at that time; there were over thirty Civil Affairs Department civil servant households, some living upstairs and the rest nearby. Cheng Renchang Longji then provided some office space for the provincial government Finance Department and served as dormitories for its staff. The third floor of Xinrenchang Inn served as the office and dormitory of the provincial government Accounting Office. Cheng Zhenxing Inn, not yet divided at that time, on one hand provided office space for the Provincial Education Department and the National News Agency; on the other hand, it used the unique open space in the ancestral hall to provide venues for other activities. According to Cheng Zhaofu's grandson Cheng Chongxue's recollection, the inn specially invited three senior chefs from Tianxianglou Duoyichu in Hangzhou to cook Chinese and Western dishes and host banquets for provincial government meetings, weddings, and other celebrations. Elder Cheng Zhenkang, living opposite Cheng Zhaofu's ancestral hall, recalls that as a child he saw a Western-style wedding held in the hall, with the bride in a long white veil, very beautiful. Cultural activities were also held in the hall—for example, a Peking opera troupe from the province performed there several times. The square west of Cheng Zhenxing Inn was then called "People's Sports Ground" (now the Fangyan bus station parking lot), where large-scale gatherings were held.

Compared with the concentration of civil servants in the middle section of the old street, the southern section housed many "cultural people." The Zhejiang Provincial High Court and High Court Procuratorate were both located near Huilong Bridge; Court President Zheng Wenli, Chief Prosecutor Wang Bingyi (now 158 Yanshang Street), and Accounting Office Chief Chen Baolin (now 138 Yanshang Street) also lived there. Elder Cheng Shouyue, living west of Huilong Bridge, says his family had 11 rooms, and several doctors lived there at that time.

The provincial government's years in Fangyan had considerable impact on the old street's economy, culture, and other aspects. During the war, the number of pilgrims coming to Fangyan decreased significantly. Although government civil servants paid low rent for private houses—some even paid nothing—those rooms would otherwise be empty, so renting them out brought some income. In those turbulent times, having a stable income from the government could be considered a luxury. Without devout pilgrims, and without these refined city people, the old street's economy would likely have collapsed due to the war, let alone the post-war revival of the inn industry. Just as when the Southern Song Dynasty moved its capital to Hangzhou, what went south included not only civil and military officials but also large numbers of literati, bringing advanced northern culture and technology; this time, many celebrities from all walks of life also took refuge in Fangyan with the Zhejiang Provincial Government. Moreover, Yongkang—originally a place "not where boats and carts converge, nor where merchants gather"—suddenly became the center and transit hub for goods and information in Zhejiang Province. Due to the war, the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Railway and Qiantang River water routes were forced to中断, and provincial goods transport had to be rerouted through Wenzhou. The Wenzhou to Lishui section went by water, handled by transit agencies; the 75-kilometer Lishui to Yongkang section relied entirely on cart drivers from "civilian handcart teams," "refugee handcart teams," and "Yongkang Relief Committee handcart teams" traveling on foot. One person with one cart transported at most 225 kilograms each time, taking six days for a round trip. A large portion of these goods ultimately reached the small valley where the old street was located, supplying the city people living there. Undeniably, the large flow of goods also indirectly promoted the old street's development. For example, to facilitate transportation, the Nationalist government built a gravel road connecting Chenglu and Nanyan at the foot of Fangyan Mountain. This road finally replaced the old street's position nearly half a century later, with inns and restaurants lining it, becoming the main route for pilgrims going up Fangyan.

These civil servants from big cities were not easily satisfied with the simple pastoral life of rising at dawn and resting at sunset. The urban culture they brought, grafted onto the original local culture of the old street, had a unique charm. Such scenes as Peking opera in ancestral halls and Western-style weddings would be hard to see in other Jiangnan villages. Teacher Chen Zhihua, who came here with his father, says that on the open ground in front of Cheng Chengchang Inn, wandering performers often set up cloth curtains and sang "Shaoxing opera." It is said the provincial government's military band was also there, and sometimes performed in Cheng Zhaofu's ancestral hall. Elder Cheng Jufang, living at the north end of the old street, recalls that in those years, at the small square outside the Sanjiantou ravine mouth, not only were operas performed, but occasionally silent films were shown. Sometimes Chairman Huang Shaohong would come out of Shoushan Keng with a group of people, beating gongs and drums, to watch the opera; after watching, they would beat gongs and drums back.

More importantly, these outsiders gradually integrated themselves into local life. It is said that the police bureau, while protecting government officials, would also go up Fangyan Mountain to maintain order when there were many pilgrims; military doctors in the hospital also treated locals; school students included both civil servants' children and Cheng descendants. Ruan Yicheng, former head of the Civil Affairs Department, wrote this describing his residence and life in Fangyan: "Bamboo fences and thatched cottages, pine trees forming a forest. A small stream before the door, crossed by a wooden bridge—my happiest rural dwelling place in life, locals call it Back Mountain. In the seventh lunar month of 1940 (29th year of the Republic), my third son was born here, named Dafang, to record that he was born in Fangyan."

It can be said with certainty that if not for Shoushan Keng with good air-raid conditions and the Wufeng Academy and caves beyond the reach of aerial bombing, the provincial government would not have chosen Fangyan as its wartime temporary office location. If these city people had not come, the old street's economy and life would have been severely damaged by the war. Fortunately, during the eight years of Japanese aggression against China, perhaps due to the protection of Guangci Temple—a famous Tiantai sect temple—and the Great Emperor Hugong, this "feng shui treasure land" of the old street not only suffered no damage but actually developed economically through the provincial government's presence. So after the war ended, the inn industry here reached its peak. In just three years from 1944 to 1946, 11 inns including Cheng Baochang, Cheng Qianchang, Cheng Zhengchang, Cheng Zhongxing, and Cheng Zhengxing opened successively on the old street. These inns were mostly small and medium-sized husband-and-wife shops; except for a few located in large courtyards, most were two-story buildings along the street. Inn income was insufficient to cover the family's annual expenses, so in off-seasons they also farmed or did other trades to supplement household income.

Changes After Liberation

The inns on the old street, in the first thirty years after the founding of New China, as a microcosm, vividly recorded a series of major historical events.

People on the old street had no deep experience of war. In their minds, the Kuomintang government was not only those approachable and real city people who once lived upstairs in their homes, but also an honest government that built roads, installed street lamps, and moved cesspits here. So when the provincial government evacuated, many villagers were reluctant to see it go. Thus, during the transition between old and new regimes, they perhaps had the same confusion as their ancestor Cheng Quan. Cheng Quan worried that "officials at the beginning of a dynasty cannot be sure of surviving from morning to evening"; they perhaps similarly felt uncertain about future life. Coupled with the first few years after liberation, when various religious activities were suppressed, the old street's inns also temporarily closed due to the absence of pilgrims. The land here had long been insufficient to support the street's population, so people recall that life was hardest then. Many young people also had to leave home to find work at that time. This "sudden" hard life, in stark contrast to the bustling scene on the old street before liberation, inevitably made people on the old street full of doubts about the new regime.

In the early 1950s, together with tens of millions of farmers across China, people on the old street experienced the vigorous "Land Reform Movement." "Land Reform" aimed to abolish the feudal exploitative land ownership of the landlord class, confiscate this land, and redistribute it to the broad poor peasantry, thereby developing agricultural production. The "Land Law" explicitly stipulated that land and property directly used for industry and commerce could not be confiscated, and the interests of industry and commerce must not be infringed. These policies, which now seem somewhat imperfect, caused many mix-ups during implementation. Of course, these have all become part of history, imprinted on the old street's architecture and culture.

In the valley where the old street is located, farmland is very limited. Land on the old street was so scarce that it could not be measured in "mu" or even "fen," but in "ba." Seventy ba equaled one mu, meaning one ba was only about 9.5 square meters—a small plot about 3 meters square. In other words, the net area of one side room in Degeng Residence was larger than two ba. The Cheng Chongshun family living near Songmen Bridge was not wealthy at that time, especially compared to those doing business and running shops, but his family owned 800 ba of land. Because Cheng Chongshun taught away from home year-round and the children were young, 300 ba were rented out and 500 ba were farmed by hired labor, making them one of the top rich peasants on the old street—subject to both house and land division. In contrast, families operating large inns such as Cheng Longchang, Xinlongxing, and Laolongxing, because they also farmed themselves, became middle peasants instead. Except for the super-large inns Cheng Zhenxing and Cheng Renchang, the remaining inns did not operate year-round but were semi-agricultural and semi-commercial, with guest rooms used for storage or left vacant in off-seasons, so their property was not protected as "land and property directly used for industry and commerce." If a family lacked labor and hired people to farm, they were classified as landlords or rich peasants, and even guest-room property would be divided—Cheng Hongchang Inn at the north end of the old street is one example. Conversely, the operators of Xinzhenxing, Cheng Zhenxing (i.e., Laozhenxing), Xinlongxing, and Cheng Renchang (Laorenchang) had "class status" as industry-commerce plus landlord. The landlord portion was naturally divided, but their inns were all protected. They did not bear the heavy label of "landlord origin" but became protected "industrialists and businessmen." In 1951, after "land reform" ended, five inns—Xinlongxing, Cheng Renchang, Xinzhenxing, Cheng Zhenxing, and Ying Baoxing in West Village—reopened.

Starting in 1956, New China launched a socialist transformation movement of capitalist industry and commerce. At that time, the transformation of private industry and commerce adopted policies of peaceful redemption and joint state-private operation. Conditions for joint state-private operation were: private industry and commerce with capital over 3,000 yuan, employing 5 or more workers, and voluntarily applying for joint operation. For inn operators on the old street, what they could understand was that joint state-private operation seemed to be the only way out. After joint operation, all houses would be sold to the state at appraised value, and they could receive payments four times a year for subsequent years. As private-side personnel, they could choose to continue working in the inn as ordinary staff, receiving fixed wages, but no longer having decision-making power. In April 1957, five inns—Cheng Renchang, Xinzhenxing, Cheng Zhenxing, Ying Baoxing, and Guangci Temple Guesthouse—merged into the Joint State-Private Fangyan Inn. Xinlongxing Inn, which had reopened that year, had too few usable rooms to meet joint operation conditions, so it was forced to close again. To this day, on the outer walls of Cheng Zhenxing and Cheng Renchang, one can still see the four characters "Fangyan Inn," over half a meter high.

In 1958, the "Great Leap Forward" people's communization reached a climax. The village implemented a large canteen system; Cheng Zhengwei Ham Shop in the middle of the old street, with its spacious courtyard and food-processing conditions, was selected as the large canteen for the whole village. People on the old street were also busy with the backyard steelmaking campaign, taking blue bricks from their courtyard walls to fire kilns, so they had to temporarily set aside the Great Emperor Hugong who could command wind and rain. Although Fangyan Inn remained open, it no longer received devout pilgrims, but rather people on business trips, attending meetings, or "visitation groups" organized by factories and government agencies.

Following this were three consecutive years of economic difficulty. The Jiangsu-Zhejiang region, originally a land of fish and rice, also experienced a great famine unseen in a thousand years. Yongkang, supported by its handicraft industry, was relatively better off. Even so, of Yongkang's 300,000 population at that time, about 100,000 left home along the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Railway for Jiangxi, because Jiangxi was an old revolutionary base area with relatively better conditions. The Cheng descendants on the old street, originally bound by blood, also turned against each other because "your land suffered hail damage and poor harvest, I don't want to share grain with you." The old street was thus split in two at the location of Laolongxing Inn, called Yanshang Brigade and Yanxia Brigade respectively. When times were hard, people naturally thought again of the omnipotent Great Emperor Hugong sitting atop Fangyan Mountain. So figures of pilgrims from nearby villages appeared again on the old street.

The good days of 1961-1962 had barely lasted two days when, in 1963, a "Four Cleanups" movement began, aiming to "clean accounts, clean warehouses, clean work points, clean property." In those years, a work team from the county came and stayed in nearby Paixi. In the words of the Cheng descendants who for generations "ate Hugong and used Hugong," their purpose was to "discredit" Hugong. Cadres coming from near and far also held meetings in Cheng Zhaofu's ancestral hall—where operas were once performed for pilgrims—to publicize the importance of this movement and criticize the former owners of Xinrenchang and Cheng Zhongxing inns. The inns became quiet again, and private-side personnel in the shops were gradually transferred to state-owned units such as supply and marketing cooperatives.

In May 1966, the vigorous Cultural Revolution began. At the end of August that year, most buildings of Guangci Temple atop Fangyan Mountain, including Heling Temple, were demolished. Still, out of nearly a thousand years of affection for Hu Ze, the Pingfeng Pavilion—originally slated for demolition by Fangyan Commune—was preserved on a pretext, successively used as a village meeting place, then a warehouse, post and telecommunications school, and Factory 602. Over the next ten years, not only pilgrims but everything related to religion and culture was forced to stop. The remaining private-side personnel at Fangyan Inn were all replaced, and Cheng Zhaofu's ancestral hall was used as a village meeting place. Later, inn furniture was moved away or sold, and the inn was converted into an instrument factory and warehouse.

Two years after the end of the Cultural Revolution, on the first day of the eighth lunar month in 1978, two or three women on the old street secretly carried a newly molded statue of Hu Ze up the mountain and enshrined it in Pingfeng Pavilion. The following year, Guangci Temple welcomed its first abbot in over a decade, Master Yunming. People suppressed for over a decade surged again from all directions, prostrating before the Hugong statue. Although people were not wealthy then, they all gave generously. They hoped Guangci Temple could rebuild its former glory, provide Hugong with a permanent dwelling, and that this hard-won good life would last long. Unlike before, some of the long-absent pilgrims did not walk along this three-li old street. The tractors or long-distance buses they took could drive along the gravel dirt road at the foot of Fangyan Mountain all the way to the mountain pass west of Huilong Bridge. Meanwhile, new policies under Reform and Opening Up affirmed farmers' rights to private plots and private livestock, and encouraged them to develop household sideline businesses. So some Yanxia Village farmers confident in Reform and Opening Up opened small restaurants on their private plots by the road. Unexpectedly, business grew increasingly prosperous; the small restaurants evolved from temporary sheds to spacious and bright brick-tile houses, also operating inn businesses. In 1985, this gravel dirt road was transformed into a cement road over ten meters wide. Since then, more inns, restaurants, and general stores opened on both sides. By the mid-1990s, all inns had brand-new facades on the new street. These new buildings of varying heights had fully open ground floors, usable as both restaurants and parking; rooms on the second floor and above generally had half with private bathrooms, while the other half could serve as restaurant "private rooms" or budget guest rooms. It seemed everything had changed, but what remained unchanged was the culture retained in this industry. Inns still charged lodging guests by "one night and two meals," with high, medium, and low standards. Devout pilgrims need only spend one-fifth of the Fangyan mountain entrance ticket to stay one night and eat two meals at an inn, and can still hear inexplicable terms like "water shuttle" and "sharp mouth."

sections.name: 四、方岩百货
sections.content_zh:
旅游经济中必不可少的就是独具特色的旅游纪念品。据民国时期《永康县志》记载："岩下街有商店100余家，方岩山顶有商店20多家，多经营京货、杂货。"到改革开放以后，方岩镇共有售商店280多家，摊位70余个。其中大部分都是经营当地制作的传统旅游工艺品，俗称方岩货，其中包括各种儿童玩具、纸花和雨伞等。

纸花

最具特色的方岩货就属方岩纸花。纸花的制作始于何时已经无从考证，但是据1991年编纂的《永康县志》记载，它在"清代乾隆年间制作已盛"。做纸花用的纸通常有大红、浅红、粉色、黄色、蓝色等几种颜色，但是配以不同样式的剪裁，层次或套色，便可以做出茶花、牡丹花、菊花、月季花、蔷薇花、杜鹃花、芙蓉花、紫罗兰等品种，煞是艳丽。

在方岩山脚下曾被称为"花廊"的街上，现在只有一个卖纸花的摊位，摊位的主人是年近古稀的老人白玲珑。白玲珑老人并不是当地人，她在解放前随父亲从广东乐昌县迁到永康来谋生，后嫁入程家，现住在方岩山脚的岩上村。据她回忆，在她30来岁的时候，她便和村里的许多妇女们开始做纸花。制作纸花的工艺是从当时寄住在方岩山半山腰的罗汉洞里，一个自称是来自丽水缙云县，名叫"老杨"的流浪汉手上学到的。她和村里的其他妇女一样，用饭菜和"老杨"换来了学做牡丹花的方法。她们在此基础上稍作变化，便形成了今天这么多的品种。

纸花的制作分成"凿"、"染"和"制"三道工序。第一步就是用一把刀口形状近似为初月的小凿子给一打一打的彩纸勾画出花或叶的轮廓。"染"就是用和彩纸协调的颜色，在"花瓣"尖上做一点点套色和退晕。这好比是画龙点睛的一笔，如果恰到好处不但可以增加纸花的立体感，还可以使色彩更加艳丽。白玲珑老人讲"染"是最关键的环节，也最费时间的。她通常都是把一叠一叠染过色的彩纸放在鞋盒大小的盒子里，连同铁丝和糨糊一起带上山，在山上只需几分钟的时间就可以做出一朵栩栩如生的纸花。

据老人回忆，"文革"结束后，随着拜胡公的人数逐渐增加，纸花的生意也越来越好。当时在这条不足一百米的街上，有七八十个小摊位，仅卖纸花的人就有五六十人，而来拜胡公的人也干脆称它为"胡公花"。在拜胡公的淡季，她还会和其他妇女一样，带上几盒染好色的彩纸到外省去卖。她自己就去过福建、江西、湖南等地，其中以湖北和广东生意最好。每次一走就是一个月左右，等把带去的材料都用完了就回来。由于纸花当时只卖五分钱一束，所以后来火车票贵了，也就不去了。近一二十年，由于方岩山门票价格的逐渐上涨，再加上塑料替代品的盛行，卖纸花的人也就越来越少了。但是村里的妇女们，包括老人的女儿、媳妇都会做纸花，她们会在逢年过节或喜庆的日子里做上几朵以增添喜气，有人会把纸花插在龙灯上，有人也会拿出来卖。

玩具

方岩制作玩具的历史悠久，而且种类繁多、做工精巧。这其中不但有乖巧可爱的，还有能动会叫的。例如，有竹子做的竹箫、节节龙，泥塑的会啼叫的小雄鸡，木头雕的小鸡吃米、小宝剑，还有金属铸的响铃和钗钹等。而这其中最有名的就是用各种材料做的哨子。最普通的就是金属铸的白铁哨，声音嘹亮。木竹哨，又叫喇叭哨，约有拇指大小，声音粗犷。里面是一个竹子做嘴儿，外面套一个木质的、漆成大红色的小圆筒。泥哨就是用泥塑成小鱼、小鸡等小动物形状，吹的时候对准动物的嘴，靠留空的内腔震动而发出清脆的声音。最有特点的要算泥制的皮老虎。它两端各有一个泥做的圆板，外侧分别画上老虎的头和尾，中间用褶皱的纸相连，靠双手收放两边的圆板发声。如今，传统玩具却面临着塑料玩具和电动玩具的挑战。

雨伞

方岩的油纸花伞也是远近闻名。雨伞的样式主要分为三种：卖给老年人用的雨伞都比较大；卖给成年人用的多绘有图案，还有特别给女青年准备的漂亮花伞；卖给小孩子用的伞不但小，伞把儿还做成一个可以吹响的哨子。

油纸花伞的制作工序有几十道，从选料到做工都十分讲究。做伞架用的毛竹一般要去芝英买，因为那里产的毛竹竹壁较厚。毛竹先要泡，晒干后削成一段一段的，再用发线穿好做成伞骨，其边缘还要用棉纱线绕上几圈，以确保结实耐用。伞面用的棉纸则要去诸暨、义乌采购，棉纸要裁成三角形，然后放进柿子油里浆一下。柿子的选择也是有讲究的，要在五六月的时候到新楼去买没有熟的柿子，拿回来打散、取出子后再放进装满水的大缸里待用。浆好的棉纸会逐一的被裱在伞骨上，晾干后就可以在上面描绘花、鸟、山、水等图案了。程振丰（1939年生，崇字辈，程氏21代）老人讲，做伞最难的环节是"接油"，油是桐油和青油的混合，只有上了油，纸伞才可以防水。"接油"的同时要用明火烘干，所以"火候"是最重要的，油太老容易坏，太嫩则不容易打开。

在老街的南端，靠近回龙桥附近，原来有好几家自产自销的雨伞店。住在桥头的程寿月老人说他家在解放前一直是靠做雨伞、卖雨伞为生。他还得意地讲，他家做的伞在旺季时会供不应求，于是不得不从温州买一些雨伞回来，再卖给上方岩的温州人。他长大以后，钢骨布伞、塑料伞逐渐替代了纸伞，他也只好改行做漆匠。程振丰老人的祖父和父亲都在老街尽端做纸伞生意，据他说，有一年阴历九月初九一天就卖了1900多把纸伞。

金华火腿

在老街上，还有一个极负盛名的特产，那就是金华火腿。在历史上，现在的永康、义乌、东阳、浦江、金华等地都属金华府管辖，所以在这些地区内生产的火腿统称为"金华火腿"，而永康则是金华火腿的主要产地之一。金华地区，民间腌制火腿始于唐代。在唐开元年间（713—742年），陈藏器撰写的《本草拾遗》中就提道，"火腿，产金华者佳"。到南宋，金华火腿已经被列为贡品。

以前岩下老街家家都养猪，出笼的猪会在腊月十五后被宰掉。一般人家都会把猪腿卖给村里做火腿生意的人家，自己只留下猪头和内脏过年。只有有钱的人家才会把猪腿腌起来留着自己吃，把猪肠拿来做香肠。这种冬天腌制的火腿叫"冬腿"，和春腿相比，冬腿味道更为鲜美，而且可以储藏较长的时间。老街上做的火腿基本上都是以后腿为原料的"冬腿"，前腿由于肥肉太多而味道欠佳，所以并不是首选。做火腿的第一步是先要把猪腿用盐炒一下，然后放进大缸里腌，每次腌十几天，前后腌三次。腌好后先要蒸一个晚上，随后拿到太阳下晒三天，最后在走廊下挂上半个多月。这样做好的火腿可以保证两年不会坏。

在岩下老街上有几家专做火腿生意的店铺，其中以位于上胡坑坑口的程正伟火腿店最为著名。年已七十多岁的程圣言（1935年生，圣字辈，程氏22代）老人是这家的后人。据他讲，太公程正伟经营火腿生意起家，并在十九世纪中叶，盖了紧邻老街西侧的一幢东西向两进院落，前院地面还用卵石铺八卦图案。后来，生意由爷爷程宣尧接任并不断扩大，又贴着老屋的西墙盖了一幢南北向的两进院落。老屋因雕饰精美，还曾是文保单位，但是不幸毁于火灾。解放前，火腿店因程宣尧的去世而随之关门，但是这座建筑却成了当年那红红火火生意的见证。这座建筑走廊和厅堂屋面下的梁枋，不但格外粗壮，而且还比通常做法更密。梁枋的侧面，每隔四寸左右还会伸出一个木楔子。程圣言老人讲这是挂火腿用的，以前走廊下、厅堂里，前院、后院都挂满了火腿，足有上千只。

因为火腿生意和旅店生意一样，都是季节性的。所以老街上有几家大的旅店，在住宿的淡季也兼做火腿生意，程仁昌旅店就是一例。据《永康名店名厂》记载，每年当秋天的香汛过后，店里就开始准备腌制火腿。生意好的时候，每年可以腌制4000只。火腿的招牌为"雪舫仁昌隆记"，并按"天地玄黄，宇宙洪荒"八个字，编号并运往杭州销售。还有一些中小型的店面，例如程振昌，为了能在和大店的竞争中生存下来，主人不但要苦心经营，还要做到面面俱到。它们不但做火腿生意，还利用沿街的房屋开店。一边卖方岩货，还有从青田贩来的石雕，另一边卖自家做的火腿。
sections.content_en:
Indispensable to the tourism economy are distinctive tourist souvenirs. According to the Yongkang County Gazetteer from the Republican period: "Yanxia Street has over 100 shops, and atop Fangyan Mountain there are over 20 shops, mostly selling Beijing goods and general merchandise." After Reform and Opening Up, Fangyan Town had over 280 retail shops and more than 70 stalls. Most of these sold traditional tourist handicrafts made locally, commonly known as Fangyan goods, including various children's toys, paper flowers, and umbrellas.

Paper Flowers

The most distinctive Fangyan goods are Fangyan paper flowers. It is impossible to verify when paper flower making began, but according to the Yongkang County Gazetteer compiled in 1991, it was "already flourishing during the Qianlong period of the Qing Dynasty." Paper used for making paper flowers usually comes in several colors: bright red, light red, pink, yellow, and blue. But with different styles of cutting, layering, or color overlaying, one can make varieties such as camellia, peony, chrysanthemum, Chinese rose, rose, azalea, hibiscus, and violet, all brilliantly colorful.

On the street at the foot of Fangyan Mountain, once known as the "Flower Corridor," there is now only one paper flower stall. Its owner is Bai Linglong, an elderly woman nearly seventy years old. Elder Bai Linglong is not a local; before liberation she moved with her father from Lechang County in Guangdong to Yongkang to make a living, later married into the Cheng family, and now lives in Yanshang Village at the foot of Fangyan Mountain. According to her recollection, when she was around thirty, she and many other women in the village began making paper flowers. The craft of making paper flowers was learned from a wanderer who called himself "Old Yang," claiming to be from Jinyun County in Lishui, who was then living in Luohan Cave halfway up Fangyan Mountain. Like other women in the village, she exchanged meals for "Old Yang" to teach her how to make peonies. On this basis they made slight variations, eventually forming so many varieties today.

Paper flower making is divided into three processes: "chisel," "dye," and "assemble." The first step is to use a small chisel with a blade shaped like a crescent moon to outline the contours of flowers or leaves on stacks of colored paper. "Dyeing" means using colors coordinated with the colored paper to add a little color overlay and gradient at the tips of the "petals." This is like the finishing touch that brings a painting to life; if done just right, it not only increases the three-dimensional effect of the paper flower but also makes the colors more vivid. Elder Bai Linglong says "dyeing" is the most critical step and also the most time-consuming. She usually puts stacks of dyed colored paper in shoebox-sized boxes, brings them up the mountain together with wire and paste, and can make a lifelike paper flower in just a few minutes on the mountain.

According to the old woman's recollection, after the end of the Cultural Revolution, as the number of people worshipping Hugong gradually increased, the paper flower business grew better and better. At that time, on this street less than one hundred meters long, there were seventy to eighty small stalls, with fifty to sixty people selling only paper flowers, and people coming to worship Hugong simply called them "Hugong flowers." During the off-season for Hugong worship, she would, like other women, take several boxes of dyed colored paper to other provinces to sell. She herself went to Fujian, Jiangxi, Hunan, and other places, with the best business in Hubei and Guangdong. Each trip lasted about a month, and she returned only after using up all the materials she brought. Since paper flowers then sold for only five fen a bunch, when train tickets became more expensive later, she stopped going. In the past one or two decades, due to the gradual increase in Fangyan Mountain ticket prices and the prevalence of plastic substitutes, fewer and fewer people sell paper flowers. But the women in the village, including the old woman's daughter and daughter-in-law, all know how to make paper flowers. They make a few during festivals or喜庆 days to add festivity; some insert paper flowers on dragon lanterns, and some take them out to sell.

Toys

Fangyan has a long history of making toys, with a great variety and exquisite workmanship. Among them are not only cute and lovely ones, but also ones that can move and make sounds. For example, there are bamboo xiao flutes and jointed dragons made of bamboo, clay little roosters that crow, wooden carved chicks pecking at rice and small swords, as well as metal-cast bells and cymbals. The most famous among them are whistles made of various materials. The most common are white iron whistles cast in metal, with a loud and clear sound. Wooden-bamboo whistles, also called horn whistles, are about the size of a thumb, with a rough sound. Inside is a bamboo mouthpiece, and outside is covered with a wooden small cylinder painted bright red. Clay whistles are made of clay shaped into small animals such as little fish and chicks; when blown, one aims at the animal's mouth, and the hollow interior vibrates to produce a crisp sound. The most distinctive must be the clay-made leather tiger. It has a clay round plate at each end, with the tiger's head and tail painted on the outer sides respectively, connected in the middle by pleated paper, producing sound by the hands squeezing and releasing the round plates on both sides. Today, however, traditional toys face challenges from plastic toys and electric toys.

Umbrellas

Fangyan's oiled paper flower umbrellas are also famous far and near. Umbrella styles are mainly divided into three types: umbrellas sold to the elderly are relatively large; those sold to adults are mostly painted with patterns, and there are also beautiful flower umbrellas specially prepared for young women; umbrellas sold to children are not only small, but the handle is also made into a whistle that can be blown.

The making of oiled paper flower umbrellas involves dozens of processes, with great attention paid from material selection to workmanship. The moso bamboo used for umbrella frames is generally bought in Zhiying, because the moso bamboo produced there has thicker walls. The moso bamboo must first be soaked, dried in the sun, then cut into sections, threaded with hairline to make umbrella ribs, and its edges must also be wrapped with cotton yarn several times to ensure sturdiness and durability. The cotton paper used for the umbrella surface must be purchased in Zhuji and Yiwu; the cotton paper is cut into triangles, then dipped in persimmon oil for sizing. The selection of persimmons is also particular: in May and June, one goes to Xinlou to buy unripe persimmons, brings them back, crushes them, removes the seeds, and puts them in large water-filled jars for later use. The sized cotton paper is then pasted one by one onto the umbrella ribs; after drying, patterns such as flowers, birds, mountains, and water can be painted on it. Elder Cheng Zhenfeng (born 1939, Chong generation, 21st generation of the Cheng family) says the hardest part of making umbrellas is "applying oil"; the oil is a mixture of tung oil and green oil, and only after oiling can the paper umbrella be waterproof. While "applying oil," it must be dried over an open flame, so "heat control" is most important—oil that is too old is easily damaged, while oil that is too tender is difficult to open.

At the southern end of the old street, near Huilong Bridge, there were originally several umbrella shops that made and sold their own products. Elder Cheng Shouyue, who lives at the bridgehead, says his family before liberation always made a living by making and selling umbrellas. He also proudly says that during peak seasons, the umbrellas his family made were in short supply, so they had to buy some umbrellas from Wenzhou and resell them to Wenzhou people coming up Fangyan. After he grew up, steel-ribbed cloth umbrellas and plastic umbrellas gradually replaced paper umbrellas, so he had to switch to being a lacquerer. Elder Cheng Zhenfeng's grandfather and father both did paper umbrella business at the end of the old street; according to him, one year on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month, over 1,900 paper umbrellas were sold in a single day.

Jinhua Ham

On the old street, there is also a highly renowned specialty: Jinhua ham. Historically, present-day Yongkang, Yiwu, Dongyang, Pujiang, Jinhua, and other places were all under the jurisdiction of Jinhua Prefecture, so ham produced in these areas is collectively called "Jinhua ham," and Yongkang is one of the main production areas of Jinhua ham. In the Jinhua region, folk ham curing began in the Tang Dynasty. During the Kaiyuan period of the Tang Dynasty (713-742), Chen Cangqi wrote in "Supplement to Materia Medica": "Ham, those produced in Jinhua are excellent." By the Southern Song Dynasty, Jinhua ham had already been listed as a tribute.

In the past, every family on Yanxia Old Street raised pigs, and pigs ready for market were slaughtered after the fifteenth day of the twelfth lunar month. Ordinary families would sell the pig legs to people in the village who did ham business, keeping only the pig's head and internal organs for New Year. Only wealthy families would cure pig legs to keep for their own consumption, and use pig intestines to make sausages. This kind of ham cured in winter is called "winter leg"; compared with spring leg, winter leg tastes more delicious and can be stored for a longer time. The ham made on the old street is basically "winter leg" made from hind legs; front legs, due to too much fat and inferior taste, are not the first choice. The first step in making ham is to stir-fry the pig leg with salt, then put it in a large jar to cure, each time for over ten days, curing three times in total. After curing, it must first be steamed for one night, then taken out to sun for three days, and finally hung under the corridor for over half a month. Ham made this way can be guaranteed not to spoil for two years.

On Yanxia Old Street there are several shops specializing in ham business, among which Cheng Zhengwei Ham Shop, located at the mouth of Shanghu Keng, is the most famous. Elder Cheng Shengyan (born 1935, Sheng generation, 22nd generation of the Cheng family), over seventy years old, is a descendant of this family. According to him, his great-grandfather Cheng Zhengwei started the ham business and, in the mid-nineteenth century, built an east-west two-courtyard compound immediately west of the old street, with the front courtyard floor paved with cobblestones in a Bagua pattern. Later, the business was taken over and continuously expanded by his grandfather Cheng Xuanyao, who built another north-south two-courtyard compound against the west wall of the old house. The old house, due to its exquisite carvings, was once a cultural relic protection unit, but unfortunately was destroyed by fire. Before liberation, the ham shop closed following Cheng Xuanyao's death, but this building remains a witness to the thriving business of those years. The beams and rafters under the corridor and hall roofs of this building are not only exceptionally thick and sturdy, but also denser than usual. On the sides of the beams, about every four inches, a wooden wedge protrudes. Elder Cheng Shengyan says these were for hanging ham; in the past, under the corridors, in the halls, and in both front and rear courtyards, ham hung everywhere, totaling over a thousand.

Because ham business, like inn business, is seasonal, several large inns on the old street also did ham business during the off-season for lodging, and Cheng Renchang Inn is one example. According to "Famous Stores and Factories of Yongkang," every year after the autumn incense season, the shop begins preparing to cure ham. In good business years, up to 4,000 hams could be cured annually. The ham's brand was "Xuefang Renchang Longji," numbered according to the eight characters "Heaven, Earth, Dark, Yellow, Universe, Vast, Flood, Wilderness," and shipped to Hangzhou for sale. There were also some small and medium-sized shops, such as Cheng Zhenchang; to survive in competition with large shops, the owners not only had to manage painstakingly but also be comprehensive in every aspect. They not only did ham business but also used street-facing houses to open shops. On one side they sold Fangyan goods and stone carvings brought from Qingtian, and on the other side they sold homemade ham.
