chapters.name: 第五章 方岩山与广慈寺

sections.name: 一、方岩山
sections.content_zh:
方岩山坐落在永康县城东五十里，海拔高度约350米。它位于岩下村的西侧，和东面的狮子山、蜥蜴山和蜈蚣山等一起界定了岩下村的空间范围。清康熙《永康县志》里有一段对方岩山精辟而生动的描写：

高二百丈，周六里，平地拔起，四面如削，惟南通一道，至山腰而绝，叠石为磴，阶级而升，曰百步峻。磴上沿岩架石为栈道，曰飞桥。将至顶，有两石对竖，屋之，曰透关，俗呼曰峰门。下有飞虹亭，寺僧慧韬新筑也。入关，地更平旷，约数百亩，有井，曰砚井，有池，可亩余。

方岩山

对于上方岩的香客，当老街走到底之后，就会向西拐进方岩山脚下的一个山坳里，再顺着"南通一道"上山。所谓的"南通一道"其实就是夹在方岩和南岩之间的一条登山小路。进山后，沿着这条路走不远就是因下马泉而得名的下马泉长廊。这里因为以前曾经挤满卖方岩纸花的摊位，所以又被称为"花廊"。下马泉顾名思义标志着这"南通一道"的终点，从这里开始人们就可以体会到北宋永康进士应材所描写的那番景色：

石磴巍峨促膝行，行时不觉看时惊。纵教良匠描难就，自是天工造化成。

罗汉洞

过下马泉不远，就是坐落在南岩岩腰的罗汉洞。罗汉洞也是当年大悲寺的肇基祖师，正德禅师的栖息之所。相传正德禅师借化缘得来的资助，塑了十八尊罗汉置于洞中，并希望借助罗汉的法力在方岩山顶修建大悲寺，罗汉洞便由此得名。在大悲寺建好之后，罗汉洞便不再被寺院使用。不知从什么时候开始，便有尼姑在这里安家，并一直持续到"文革"。最后一位尼姑叫应绍为，她在这里不但给人看病，而且还收留流浪的乞丐，所以广受大家尊敬。她去世之后，就被埋葬在罗汉洞对面方岩山腰的山洞里。

在罗汉洞的西南角，有一口名为"蛟龙泉"的古井。其"水甘美如饴，性沉厚，尝置铜钱数枚于杯水中，而水不外溢"。在《蛟龙泉记》里，还记载着关于这口井的一个美丽传说。据说曾经有一个姓应的尼姑居住在罗汉洞里，夏天，她每天都要翻山越岭到五峰下的龙湫泉取水，供香客饮用。她的举动感动了龙王，于是龙王就变成鲤鱼托梦于她，指出可以打井的地点。经过了数年的努力，她终于打井成功并找到了泉水，因此取名为"蛟龙泉"。

百步峻与步云亭

过了罗汉洞就是"叠石为磴"的"百步峻"。由于这段台阶坡度较大，人们在上行的时候，会不由自主地看到每一块条石的侧面和石栏杆上都刻着捐献者的姓名和籍贯，就好像在读一本用石头写的书。这个过程既让人忘却了攀登的辛劳与枯燥，又不禁油然升起一番敬意。百步峻的尽端就是横跨在路中，飞檐翘角的步云亭。步云亭的位置恰到好处，人们可以在这里稍事休息，凭栏远眺。正如挂在上面的对联所说，"憩步邀群仙，随云来半山"。依清康熙县志的描述，透关"下有飞虹亭，寺僧慧韬新筑也"，但是这段话在清光绪县志中却被删掉了；再加上朱谨的诗句"飞虹亭畔息，贾勇入峰关"，这里的"峰关"应该就是县志里所提的"峰门"。可以推断飞虹亭可能就是现在的步云亭的前身。这也符合广慈寺前住持允明禅师所说，即步云亭是寺里的和尚建造的。

飞桥

步云亭再往上就是长一百多米，"沿岩架石"的栈道，又称"飞桥"。这段栈道架设在悬崖峭壁之间，曲折有致，在清晨和雨后，就会呈现永康十景之一的"飞桥锁雾"。现在的飞桥是1962年夏天用钢筋混凝土重建的，宽度近2.5米。已经比当年少了些险峻。据允明禅师讲，飞桥始建于开山祖师时期，它以前的状况可以从题刻在旁边的《重建飞桥记略》中略知一二，"原砌以石，宽仅尺许，几经改造，增至五尺"。当地人对飞桥的改造还可以从其他文献中找到一些印记，例如在《程公孟举墓表》中有记载程氏四世祖程鹏在明永乐乙酉年（1405年）曾"造飞桥，设义浆"。

透关

走到飞桥头有两巨石对峙，最窄处仅相隔一米多。从现存最早的明正德《永康县志》，到清光绪《永康县志》里都有同样的记载，即两块巨石之上曾建有题额为透关的亭子。透关亭如今已不复存在，取而代之的是题额为"天门"，材料采用石材加钢筋混凝土的重檐八角亭。据允明禅师讲，"天门"下面的部分，是开山祖师最先建的，虽屡经重修，但是一直都有。目前上面的亭子是民国37年（1948年）造的。

天王殿

正如县志所述，过了天门地势就变得较为平缓空旷，而首先看到的便是天王殿。天王殿的出现预示着佛家圣地近在咫尺，但是它的位置和格局却十分独特。天王殿通常是中国寺院建筑群中轴线上的第一进殿。殿内中间通常供奉弥勒菩萨，并在其后供奉面向北方的韦驮菩萨，东西两旁则供奉四大天王。在广慈寺，天王殿没有和其他的大殿一起位于中轴线上，而是位于寺院主体建筑之前一里多远的位置。这座天王殿骑跨于路中，中间开敞以便走人，仿佛一座城门。不仅如此，殿内只有四大天王在两侧，并没有依常规供奉弥勒和韦驮菩萨。有学者认为，在历史上天王殿最初多见于净土宗的寺院，在两宋以后才开始出现在大部分其他宗派的寺院里。广慈寺是天台宗下的寺院并始建于唐代，这可能就是为什么寺院主体建筑群内并没有天王殿的位置。这一点还可以和从广慈寺关系密切的天台山国清寺得到旁证。广慈寺的肇基祖师正德禅师来自于天台山国清寺，国清寺在那个年代的平面布局已无从考究。目前寺院中轴线上的三幢建筑，即弥勒殿、雨花殿和大雄宝殿都是雍正十一年（1733年）重建的。但是殿内的塑像却是在"文革"末期，为了迎接日本天台宗佛教徒参拜祖庙而从其他地方调来的，或是以后重塑的。即便当时调来的塑像是以原有塑像为依据，国清寺的四大天王并没有与弥勒和韦驮菩萨坐落在同一间殿堂内，而是被单独供奉在雨花殿内。

天门头空基

天王殿后面这块稍为平坦的范围以前称作"天门头空基"，每年香汛期间这里都会散落一些卖小吃的摊位，以方便香客歇歇脚，填饱肚子以继续赶路。目前，路旁这些小吃摊位除了经营诸如馄饨、面条、豆干之类的食品外，最有特色的要算是被外地人称为"永康食果"的肉麦饼了。肉麦饼是用肥多瘦少的猪肉丁拌梅干菜作馅，包法类似于北方的馅饼，只是厚一点儿，最后用又浅又平的大锅烤熟。制作过程中的诀窍是，在捏摺的时候要稍向上提，使空气进入后再封口，这样烤出来的饼里面充满空气，从外面看起来非常饱满，而且还能保证皮又焦又脆。最重要的是，肉麦饼可以事先做好，叠落在一起放在锅边又不致变凉。若有客人来了，可以随来随买，随走随吃，不妨碍香客们赶路。

天街

从小吃街转过一个弯就到了"天街"，天街全长约半里，目前两端各矗立着一个石牌坊作为标志。天街以前称为"前街路"，路两边多是两层高的店面，大一点的还有三层高。这其中包括近十家小规模的旅店和以经营包括《方岩指南》等各类图书为主的"日新书社"。每年从阴历八月到三月之间还会有十余家临时小店开张，它们不但出售京广杂货、铁器、木器、儿童玩具、木梳等，还经营牛肉、油条、肉麦饼、馄饨、豆腐花、豆腐圆和茶水等当地小吃。

天街现在只在南侧有一两层高的店面，这些建筑都是在1988年重建的。店面多经营祭祀用品，例如蜡烛、香纸和佛像等，并兼营方岩货。经营类似商品的店面以前多位于寺院殿堂前后，1925年版的《方岩指南》中就列有杂货店十一家、玩具店一家，以及经营香纸烛锭摊位十余个。

天街的北侧是长生塘，传说是仙女的眼泪变成的，饮用塘中水后可以长生不老，并由此得名。塘边有井，叫砚井，是寺里和尚赖以生存的饮用水源。在天街中段南侧，有一棵据说是和广慈寺同龄的古樟树，因其旁边生长着许多小樟树，所以叫母子樟。母子樟旁边曾经有明万历年间（1573—1620年）建造的程方峰（1498—1585年）祠堂。现在取而代之的是"方岩仙人洞"，以借助现代化的手段来制造"会说话活菩萨"、"土地公公破土而出"、"猪八戒大闹盘丝洞"等视听效果来吸引香客。从仙人洞旁散落的巨大的柱基石和洞里依稀可见的方砖铺地，可以推测出程方峰祠堂当年的规模。据允明禅师讲，祠堂里面原有程方峰的塑像，祠堂大门从来都是关着的，只有在清明期间会开，那时候会有五六百人来这里祭祖。程方峰和其夫人孙氏的墓建在祠堂后面。现存的墓碑是1990年清明重立的，旁边刻有"千古英灵安在，万代浩气永存"的对联。

千人坑和听泉楼

在天街尽端的东北角是千人坑。在那里，方岩山被劈成一南一北两段，中间的山谷深数百米，且宽不到一米。关于千人坑，县志里还记载着这样的传说："相传昔乡人避寇岩上，寇至援藤升，顿见有蛇，刃挥之，藤断寇坠，死者若干人，遂溃去，此坑所由名也。"这里的"寇"指的是在北宋宣和二年（1120年），永康人陈十四和他率领的农民起义军。陈十四的起义军是永康方岩地区响应方腊起义的一支队伍。当年他们攻破县城，迫使知县赵琪退据方岩山，县志里描述的就是发生在这之后的故事。陈十四的起义虽然在次年就被镇压了，但是人们却借此来纪念当时牺牲的起义军战士。

千人坑西边曾有"听泉楼"，如今楼去泉干，只能借县志中的记载来想象那清脆的泉水声：

坑上西行百步许，下有石谷，泉出谷间，如环佩声。旧有楼，曰听泉，里人胡济源作。大夫士赋诗成集，曰听泉楼集。不传，惟吕双泉潆序，见双泉集中。

听泉楼：在方岩千人坑，元邑人胡济源筑，邑大夫士多为之赋诗，集录成编，郎中吕双泉序之，李草阁有诗。

并庙有寺

在方岩山顶上，目前并排坐落着一座不大为人知的千年名刹广慈寺和常年香火旺盛的胡公庙。虽然在历史上的很长一段时间里，广慈寺和胡公庙都同时矗立在这里，但是它们的关系却和现在大不相同。现在的胡公庙用地原属广慈寺，而胡公庙曾经位于广慈寺左面，临近长生塘的位置。这一点可以从历年的县志里找到证明，例如明嘉靖《永康县志》里讲，"有祠，曰佑顺侯祠。右有佛庐，曰广慈寺"；而清道光《永康县志》中却写道，"临池有庙，曰赫灵。……并庙有寺，曰广慈"。这一寺一庙之间相互关系的变化，要从了解广慈寺的历史开始。
sections.content_en:
Fangyan Mountain is located fifty li east of Yongkang county seat, with an elevation of about 350 meters. It lies west of Yanxia Village, and together with Lion Mountain, Lizard Mountain, and Centipede Mountain to the east, defines the spatial scope of Yanxia Village. The Qing Kangxi "Yongkang County Gazetteer" contains a concise and vivid description of Fangyan Mountain:

Two hundred zhang high, six li in circumference, rising abruptly from the plain, sheer on all four sides, with only a passage to the south that ends at the mountainside; stones stacked as steps, ascending by degrees, called Hundred-Steep Steps. Above the steps, a stone plank road built along the cliff, called Flying Bridge. Near the summit, two stones stand opposite each other, with a structure atop them, called Transparent Pass, commonly known as Peak Gate. Below is Flying Rainbow Pavilion, newly built by monk Huitao. Beyond the pass, the land is more level and open, about several hundred mu, with a well called Inkstone Well and a pond of over one mu.

Fangyan Mountain

For pilgrims going up Fangyan, after walking to the end of the old street, they turn west into a ravine at the foot of Fangyan Mountain, then ascend along the "Southern Passage." The so-called "Southern Passage" is actually a mountain path between Fangyan and Nanyan. After entering the mountain, walking not far along this path is the Xiamquan (Dismounting Horse Spring) Corridor, named after the spring. Because it was once crowded with stalls selling Fangyan paper flowers, it is also called "Flower Corridor." Xiamquan, as its name implies, marks the end of the "Southern Passage"; from here, people can begin to experience the scenery described by Northern Song Yongkang jinshi Ying Cai:

Stone steps towering, walking knee-to-knee; while walking one feels nothing, but looking is startling. Even a skilled craftsman could hardly depict it; it is naturally formed by heaven's work.

Luohan Cave

Not far past Xiamquan is Luohan (Arhat) Cave, located on the mountainside of Nanyan. Luohan Cave was also the dwelling place of Zhengde Chan Master, the founding patriarch of Dabei Temple. It is said that Zhengde Chan Master, using funds obtained through alms-gathering, molded eighteen Arhat statues and placed them in the cave, hoping to借助 the Arhats' spiritual power to build Dabei Temple on the summit of Fangyan Mountain—hence the name Luohan Cave. After Dabei Temple was built, Luohan Cave was no longer used by the temple. It is unknown when nuns began settling here, but this continued until the Cultural Revolution. The last nun was Ying Shaowei, who not only treated people's illnesses but also took in wandering beggars, so she was widely respected. After her death, she was buried in a cave on the mountainside of Fangyan opposite Luohan Cave.

In the southwest corner of Luohan Cave is an ancient well called "Jiaolong Spring" (Flood Dragon Spring). Its water "is as sweet as malt syrup, thick in nature; once several copper coins were placed in a cup of the water, and it did not overflow." In the "Record of Jiaolong Spring," a beautiful legend about this well is also recorded. It is said that once a nun surnamed Ying lived in Luohan Cave; in summer, she had to cross mountains every day to fetch water from Longqiu Spring below the Five Peaks for pilgrims to drink. Her actions moved the Dragon King, so the Dragon King transformed into a carp and appeared to her in a dream, pointing out a location where a well could be dug. After several years of effort, she finally succeeded in digging the well and finding spring water, hence named "Jiaolong Spring."

Hundred-Steep Steps and Buyun Pavilion

Past Luohan Cave is the "Hundred-Steep Steps" of "stones stacked as steps." Because this section of steps has a steep gradient, while ascending people cannot help but notice that the sides of every stone slab and the stone railings are carved with donors' names and native places, as if reading a book written in stone. This process both makes people forget the toil and tedium of climbing and spontaneously raises a sense of reverence. At the end of the Hundred-Steep Steps is Buyun (Step into Clouds) Pavilion, spanning the road with upturned eaves. The pavilion's location is just right, where people can rest briefly and lean on the railing to gaze into the distance. As the couplet hanging above says, "Resting steps invite all immortals; following clouds comes to the half-mountain." According to the Qing Kangxi gazetteer, below Transparent Pass "there is Feihong Pavilion, newly built by monk Huitao," but this passage was deleted in the Qing Guangxu gazetteer; plus Zhu Jin's poem "Resting by Feihong Pavilion, summoning courage to enter Peak Pass," the "Peak Pass" here should be the "Peak Gate" mentioned in the gazetteer. It can be inferred that Feihong Pavilion may be the predecessor of today's Buyun Pavilion. This also aligns with what Yunming Chan Master, former abbot of Guangci Temple, said—that Buyun Pavilion was built by the temple's monks.

Flying Bridge

Above Buyun Pavilion is the over-hundred-meter-long plank road "built along the cliff with stones," also called "Flying Bridge." This plank road is set between sheer cliffs, winding gracefully; in early morning and after rain, it presents one of Yongkang's Ten Scenes, "Flying Bridge Locked in Mist." Today's Flying Bridge was rebuilt in reinforced concrete in the summer of 1962, nearly 2.5 meters wide—already less precipitous than in former times. According to Yunming Chan Master, Flying Bridge was first built in the founding patriarch's era; its former condition can be glimpsed from the "Brief Record of Rebuilding Flying Bridge" inscribed beside it: "Originally paved with stone, only about a chi wide; after several renovations, increased to five chi." Local renovations of Flying Bridge can also find traces in other documents—for example, the "Epitaph of Cheng Gong Mengju" records that the fourth-generation Cheng ancestor Cheng Peng in the Ming Yongle Yiyou year (1405) once "built Flying Bridge and provided free gruel."

Transparent Pass

At the head of Flying Bridge, two giant stones face each other, with the narrowest point only just over a meter apart. From the earliest surviving Ming Zhengde "Yongkang County Gazetteer" to the Qing Guangxu "Yongkang County Gazetteer," there is the same record: above the two giant stones once stood a pavilion inscribed "Transparent Pass." The Transparent Pass Pavilion no longer exists today, replaced by a double-eave octagonal pavilion inscribed "Heavenly Gate," built of stone and reinforced concrete. According to Yunming Chan Master, the part below "Heavenly Gate" was first built by the founding patriarch; though repeatedly renovated, it has always existed. The current upper pavilion was built in the 37th year of the Republic (1948).

Heavenly King Hall

As the gazetteer states, past Heavenly Gate the terrain becomes relatively level and open, and the first thing seen is the Heavenly King Hall. The appearance of the Heavenly King Hall预示 that the Buddhist holy land is near at hand, but its location and layout are quite unique. The Heavenly King Hall is usually the first hall on the central axis of Chinese temple complexes. Inside, the center usually enshrines Maitreya Bodhisattva, with Skanda Bodhisattva facing north behind him, and the Four Heavenly Kings on the east and west sides. At Guangci Temple, the Heavenly King Hall is not located on the central axis with other main halls, but rather over a li away in front of the temple's main buildings. This Heavenly King Hall straddles the road, with an open center for passage, like a city gate. Moreover, inside only the Four Heavenly Kings stand on both sides, without the conventional Maitreya and Skanda Bodhisattvas. Some scholars believe that historically, Heavenly King Halls were initially most common in Pure Land temples, only appearing in most other sect temples after the Northern and Southern Song dynasties. Guangci Temple is a Tiantai sect temple founded in the Tang Dynasty, which may explain why there is no Heavenly King Hall within the temple's main building complex. This can also be corroborated by Guoqing Temple on Tiantai Mountain, which has close ties with Guangci Temple. Guangci Temple's founding patriarch Zhengde Chan Master came from Guoqing Temple on Tiantai Mountain; the planar layout of Guoqing Temple in that era can no longer be researched. Currently, the three buildings on the temple's central axis—Maitreya Hall, Yuhua Hall, and Mahavira Hall—were all rebuilt in the eleventh year of Yongzheng (1733). But the statues inside were either transferred from elsewhere or later recast in the late Cultural Revolution period, to welcome Japanese Tiantai sect Buddhists visiting the ancestral temple. Even if the transferred statues were based on original statues, Guoqing Temple's Four Heavenly Kings were not housed in the same hall as Maitreya and Skanda Bodhisattvas, but were separately enshrined in the Yuhua Hall.

Tianmentou Kongji (Heavenly Gate Head Empty Foundation)

The relatively level area behind the Heavenly King Hall was formerly called "Tianmentou Kongji." Every year during incense season, snack stalls scatter here,方便 pilgrims to rest, fill their stomachs, and continue on their way. Currently, besides foods like wontons, noodles, and dried tofu, the most distinctive snack at these roadside stalls is the rou mai bing (meat wheat cake), called "Yongkang fruit" by outsiders. Rou mai bing uses diced pork with more fat than lean mixed with dried preserved vegetables as filling; the wrapping method is similar to northern pies, only thicker, finally baked in a shallow flat pan. The trick in making it is to lift slightly while pinching the folds, allowing air to enter before sealing—so the baked cake is full of air inside, looks very plump from outside, and ensures the crust is both焦 and crisp. Most importantly, rou mai bing can be made in advance, stacked by the pan without getting cold. When customers come, they can buy and eat as they go, without hindering pilgrims' journey.

Tianjie (Heavenly Street)

Turning a corner from the snack street brings one to "Tianjie" (Heavenly Street), about half a li long, currently marked by a stone paifang standing at each end. Tianjie was formerly called "Qianjie Road" (Front Street Road), with mostly two-story shops on both sides, and larger ones three stories high. These include nearly ten small-scale inns and the "Rixin Book Society," mainly selling various books including "Fangyan Guide." Every year from the eighth lunar month to the third month, over a dozen temporary shops open, selling not only Jingguang (Beijing-Guangzhou) general goods, ironware, woodenware, children's toys, and wooden combs, but also local snacks such as beef, fried dough sticks, rou mai bing, wontons, tofu pudding, tofu balls, and tea.

Tianjie now only has one- to two-story shops on the south side, all rebuilt in 1988. The shops mostly sell sacrificial supplies such as candles, incense paper, and Buddha statues, and also deal in Fangyan goods. Shops selling similar goods were formerly mostly located in front of and behind temple halls; the 1925 edition of "Fangyan Guide" lists eleven general stores, one toy store, and over a dozen stalls selling incense, paper, candles, and ingots.

North of Tianjie is Changsheng Pond (Long Life Pond), legendarily formed from a fairy's tears; drinking the pond water can grant eternal youth, hence the name. Beside the pond is a well called Yanjing (Inkstone Well), the drinking water source on which the temple monks relied for survival. South of the middle section of Tianjie stands an ancient camphor tree said to be the same age as Guangci Temple; because many small camphor trees grow beside it, it is called Mother-and-Child Camphor. Beside the Mother-and-Child Camphor once stood the Cheng Fangfeng (1498-1585) Ancestral Hall, built during the Ming Wanli period (1573-1620). Now replaced by "Fangyan Immortal Cave," which uses modern means to create audio-visual effects like "Talking Living Bodhisattva," "Earth God Bursting Forth," and "Zhu Bajie's Great Disturbance in the Spider Silk Cave" to attract pilgrims. From the giant pillar foundation stones scattered beside the Immortal Cave and the faintly visible square brick paving inside, the scale of the former Cheng Fangfeng Ancestral Hall can be inferred. According to Yunming Chan Master, the hall originally contained a statue of Cheng Fangfeng; the hall gate was always closed, only opening during Qingming, when five to six hundred people would come to worship ancestors. The tombs of Cheng Fangfeng and his wife Lady Sun were built behind the hall. The existing tombstone was re-erected at Qingming in 1990, with the couplet "Eternal heroic spirit abides; myriad generations of noble spirit endure" carved beside it.

Thousand-Man Pit and Tingquan Tower

At the northeast corner of Tianjie's end is the Thousand-Man Pit. There, Fangyan Mountain is split into north and south sections, with the valley between them hundreds of meters deep and less than a meter wide. About the Thousand-Man Pit, the gazetteer records this legend: "It is said that in ancient times, villagers took refuge from bandits on the mountain; when bandits came and grabbed vines to climb, they suddenly saw snakes; they struck with blades, the vines broke, the bandits fell, and many died, then they retreated in disarray—hence the name of this pit." The "bandits" here refer to Chen Shisi of Yongkang and his peasant rebel army in the second year of Northern Song Xuanhe (1120). Chen Shisi's rebel army was a unit in the Yongkang-Fangyan area responding to Fang La's rebellion. That year they captured the county seat, forcing County Magistrate Zhao Qi to retreat to Fangyan Mountain; what the gazetteer describes is the story that followed. Although Chen Shisi's rebellion was suppressed the following year, people used it to commemorate the rebel soldiers who died then.

West of the Thousand-Man Pit once stood "Tingquan Tower" (Listening to Spring Tower); now the tower is gone and the spring dry, and one can only imagine the clear spring sound through gazetteer records:

Westward from the pit, about a hundred paces, below is a stone valley; spring emerges from the valley, sounding like jade pendants. Formerly there was a tower called Tingquan, built by local Hu Jiyuan. Scholars and officials composed poems into a collection called Tingquan Tower Collection. Not transmitted, only preface by Lü Shuangquan (Ying), seen in Shuangquan Collection.

Tingquan Tower: at Fangyan Thousand-Man Pit, built by Yuan dynasty local Hu Jiyuan; county officials and scholars mostly composed poems for it, collected into a volume, preface by Director Lü Shuangquan, with poems by Li Caoge.

Temple Beside Temple

On the summit of Fangyan Mountain, currently stand side by side the little-known thousand-year-old famous temple Guangci Temple and the perpetually incense-prosperous Hugong Temple. Although for a long period in history both Guangci Temple and Hugong Temple stood here simultaneously, their relationship was very different from today. The current Huguang Temple site originally belonged to Guangci Temple, while Hugong Temple was once located to the left of Guangci Temple, near Changsheng Pond. This can be proven by gazetteers over the years—for example, the Ming Jiajing "Yongkang County Gazetteer" states, "There is a shrine called Youshun Marquis Shrine. To the right is a Buddhist dwelling called Guangci Temple"; while the Qing Daoguang "Yongkang County Gazetteer" writes, "By the pond there is a temple called Heling. ... Beside the temple there is a temple called Guangci." The change in the relationship between this one temple and one shrine begins with understanding the history of Guangci Temple.
key_terms: 方岩山坐落在永康县城东五十里海拔高度约350米
方岩山位于岩下村西侧和东面狮子山蜥蜴山蜈蚣山等一起界定岩下村空间范围
清康熙永康县志对方岩山描写高二百丈周六里平地拔起四面如削惟南通一道至山腰而绝叠石为磴阶级而升曰百步峻
磴上沿岩架石为栈道曰飞桥将至顶有两石对竖屋之曰透关俗呼曰峰门下有飞虹亭寺僧慧韬新筑也入关地更平旷约数百亩有井曰砚井有池可亩余
对于上方岩的香客当老街走到底之后就会向西拐进方岩山脚下的一个山坳里再顺着南通一道上山
南通一道其实就是夹在方岩和南岩之间的一条登山小路
进山后沿着这条路走不远就是因下马泉而得名的下马泉长廊
下马泉长廊因为以前曾经挤满卖方岩纸花的摊位所以又被称为花廊
下马泉顾名思义标志着南通一道的终点从这里开始人们就可以体会到北宋永康进士应材所描写的那番景色石磴巍峨促膝行行时不觉看时惊纵教良匠描难就自是天工造化成
罗汉洞坐落在南岩岩腰过下马泉不远
罗汉洞也是当年大悲寺的肇基祖师正德禅师的栖息之所
相传正德禅师借化缘得来的资助塑了十八尊罗汉置于洞中并希望借助罗汉的法力在方岩山顶修建大悲寺罗汉洞便由此得名
大悲寺建好之后罗汉洞便不再被寺院使用
不知从什么时候开始便有尼姑在这里安家并一直持续到文革
最后一位尼姑叫应绍为她在这里不但给人看病而且还收留流浪的乞丐所以广受大家尊敬
应绍为去世之后就被埋葬在罗汉洞对面方岩山腰的山洞里
罗汉洞西南角有一口名为蛟龙泉的古井其水甘美如饴性沉厚尝置铜钱数枚于杯水中而水不外溢
蛟龙泉记里记载着关于这口井的一个美丽传说
据说曾经有一个姓应的尼姑居住在罗汉洞里夏天她每天都要翻山越岭到五峰下的龙湫泉取水供香客饮用
她的举动感动了龙王于是龙王就变成鲤鱼托梦于她指出可以打井的地点
经过了数年的努力她终于打井成功并找到了泉水因此取名为蛟龙泉
过了罗汉洞就是叠石为磴的百步峻
百步峻这段台阶坡度较大人们在上行的时候会不由自主地看到每一块条石的侧面和石栏杆上都刻着捐献者的姓名和籍贯就好像在读一本用石头写的书
这个过程既让人忘却了攀登的辛劳与枯燥又不禁油然升起一番敬意
百步峻的尽端就是横跨在路中飞檐翘角的步云亭
步云亭的位置恰到好处人们可以在这里稍事休息凭栏远眺
步云亭对联憩步邀群仙随云来半山
依清康熙县志描述透关下有飞虹亭寺僧慧韬新筑也但是这段话在清光绪县志中却被删掉了
朱谨诗句飞虹亭畔息贾勇入峰关这里的峰关应该就是县志里所提的峰门
可以推断飞虹亭可能就是现在的步云亭的前身
广慈寺前住持允明禅师说步云亭是寺里的和尚建造的
步云亭再往上就是长一百多米沿岩架石的栈道又称飞桥
飞桥这段栈道架设在悬崖峭壁之间曲折有致在清晨和雨后就会呈现永康十景之一的飞桥锁雾
现在的飞桥是1962年夏天用钢筋混凝土重建的宽度近2.5米已经比当年少了些险峻
据允明禅师讲飞桥始建于开山祖师时期它以前的状况可以从题刻在旁边的重建飞桥记略中略知一二原砌以石宽仅尺许几经改造增至五尺
程氏四世祖程鹏在明永乐乙酉年1405年曾造飞桥设义浆
走到飞桥头有两巨石对峙最窄处仅相隔一米多
从现存最早的明正德永康县志到清光绪永康县志里都有同样的记载即两块巨石之上曾建有题额为透关的亭子
透关亭如今已不复存在取而代之的是题额为天门材料采用石材加钢筋混凝土的重檐八角亭
据允明禅师讲天门下面的部分是开山祖师最先建的虽屡经重修但是一直都有
目前上面的亭子是民国37年1948年造的
过了天门地势就变得较为平缓空旷而首先看到的便是天王殿
天王殿的出现预示着佛家圣地近在咫尺但是它的位置和格局却十分独特
天王殿通常是中国寺院建筑群中轴线上的第一进殿
殿内中间通常供奉弥勒菩萨并在其后供奉面向北方的韦驮菩萨东西两旁则供奉四大天王
在广慈寺天王殿没有和其他的大殿一起位于中轴线上而是位于寺院主体建筑之前一里多远的位置
这座天王殿骑跨于路中中间开敞以便走人仿佛一座城门
殿内只有四大天王在两侧并没有依常规供奉弥勒和韦驮菩萨
有学者认为在历史上天王殿最初多见于净土宗的寺院在两宋以后才开始出现在大部分其他宗派的寺院里
广慈寺是天台宗下的寺院并始建于唐代这可能就是为什么寺院主体建筑群内并没有天王殿的位置
广慈寺的肇基祖师正德禅师来自于天台山国清寺
目前寺院中轴线上的三幢建筑即弥勒殿雨花殿和大雄宝殿都是雍正十一年1733年重建的
殿内的塑像是在文革末期为了迎接日本天台宗佛教徒参拜祖庙而从其他地方调来的或是以后重塑的
国清寺的四大天王并没有与弥勒和韦驮菩萨坐落在同一间殿堂内而是被单独供奉在雨花殿内
天王殿后面这块稍为平坦的范围以前称作天门头空基
每年香汛期间这里都会散落一些卖小吃的摊位以方便香客歇歇脚填饱肚子以继续赶路
路旁这些小吃摊位除了经营诸如馄饨面条豆干之类的食品外最有特色的要算是被外地人称为永康食果的肉麦饼了
肉麦饼是用肥多瘦少的猪肉丁拌梅干菜作馅包法类似于北方的馅饼只是厚一点儿最后用又浅又平的大锅烤熟
制作肉麦饼的诀窍是在捏摺的时候要稍向上提使空气进入后再封口这样烤出来的饼里面充满空气从外面看起来非常饱满而且还能保证皮又焦又脆
肉麦饼可以事先做好叠落在一起放在锅边又不致变凉若有客人来了可以随来随买随走随吃不妨碍香客们赶路
从小吃街转过一个弯就到了天街天街全长约半里目前两端各矗立着一个石牌坊作为标志
天街以前称为前街路路两边多是两层高的店面大一点的还有三层高
天街包括近十家小规模的旅店和以经营包括方岩指南等各类图书为主的日新书社
每年从阴历八月到三月之间还会有十余家临时小店开张它们不但出售京广杂货铁器木器儿童玩具木梳等还经营牛肉油条肉麦饼馄饨豆腐花豆腐圆和茶水等当地小吃
天街现在只在南侧有一两层高的店面这些建筑都是在1988年重建的
天街店面多经营祭祀用品例如蜡烛香纸和佛像等并兼营方岩货
1925年版的方岩指南中就列有杂货店十一家玩具店一家以及经营香纸烛锭摊位十余个
天街北侧是长生塘传说是仙女的眼泪变成的饮用塘中水后可以长生不老并由此得名
塘边有井叫砚井是寺里和尚赖以生存的饮用水源
天街中段南侧有一棵据说是和广慈寺同龄的古樟树因其旁边生长着许多小樟树所以叫母子樟
母子樟旁边曾经有明万历年间1573-1620建造的程方峰1498-1585祠堂
现在取而代之的是方岩仙人洞以借助现代化的手段来制造会说话活菩萨土地公公破土而出猪八戒大闹盘丝洞等视听效果来吸引香客
从仙人洞旁散落的巨大的柱基石和洞里依稀可见的方砖铺地可以推测出程方峰祠堂当年的规模
据允明禅师讲祠堂里面原有程方峰的塑像祠堂大门从来都是关着的只有在清明期间会开那时候会有五六百人来这里祭祖
程方峰和其夫人孙氏的墓建在祠堂后面现存的墓碑是1990年清明重立的旁边刻有千古英灵安在万代浩气永存的对联
在天街尽端的东北角是千人坑
千人坑那里方岩山被劈成一南一北两段中间的山谷深数百米且宽不到一米
关于千人坑县志里记载着这样的传说相传昔乡人避寇岩上寇至援藤升顿见有蛇刃挥之藤断寇坠死者若干人遂溃去此坑所由名也
这里的寇指的是在北宋宣和二年1120年永康人陈十四和他率领的农民起义军
陈十四的起义军是永康方岩地区响应方腊起义的一支队伍
当年他们攻破县城迫使知县赵琪退据方岩山县志里描述的就是发生在这之后的故事
陈十四的起义虽然在次年就被镇压了但是人们却借此来纪念当时牺牲的起义军战士
千人坑西边曾有听泉楼如今楼去泉干只能借县志中的记载来想象那清脆的泉水声
听泉楼记载坑上西行百步许下有石谷泉出谷间如环佩声旧有楼曰听泉里人胡济源作大夫士赋诗成集曰听泉楼集不传惟吕双泉潆序见双泉集中
听泉楼在方岩千人坑元邑人胡济源筑邑大夫士多为之赋诗集录成编郎中吕双泉序之李草阁有诗
在方岩山顶上目前并排坐落着一座不大为人知的千年名刹广慈寺和常年香火旺盛的胡公庙
虽然在历史上的很长一段时间里广慈寺和胡公庙都同时矗立在这里但是它们的关系却和现在大不相同
现在的胡公庙用地原属广慈寺而胡公庙曾经位于广慈寺左面临近长生塘的位置
明嘉靖永康县志里讲有祠曰佑顺侯祠右有佛庐曰广慈寺
清道光永康县志中却写道临池有庙曰赫灵并庙有寺曰广慈
这一寺一庙之间相互关系的变化要从了解广慈寺的历史开始

sections.name: 二、广慈寺历史
sections.content_zh:
创建初期

广慈寺原名大悲寺，是一座有上千年历史的天台宗名刹。它始建于唐宣宗大中四年（850年），也就是"会昌法难"结束后，恢复佛教的第四年。佛教自西汉传入中国以来，到隋唐时期已发展到鼎盛。在唐朝建立之初的二百年里，历任皇帝都大力提倡佛教并给予极高的礼遇。到唐朝后期，随着佛教影响力的不断扩大和经济势力的日益膨胀，作为一种宗教信仰，它便逐渐威胁到了唐朝的中央统治。不仅如此，唐武宗（840—846年）本人信仰道教，因此在他即位后，便推行了一系列的"灭佛"政策，包括下令拆毁寺宇，勒令僧尼还俗等。广慈寺的肇基祖师正德禅师在那个时候也被迫离开了天台山国清寺。正德禅师，原为寺里的一个火头和尚，即负责烧饭的和尚。离开国清寺之前，他曾在国清寺第十二世祖师物外禅师门下修习止观（即是禅定、智慧二学，是修学一切佛法的根本）。

公元847年，崇信佛教的唐宣宗即位，改国号为大中元年，并立即下令恢复所有在会昌年间被废的佛寺。由于天台山国清寺没有能被马上恢复，正德禅师可能因此便来到不远的方岩山来修头陀行，即佛教苦行之一，并居住在现方岩山腰罗汉洞内。他见方岩山"仍属混沌绝境，遂访山农指点，缘藤而上，匍匐跻攀，透洞始见山巅古树参天，槁木横卧，荆棘遍地，万般寂寥。探至凹处见上中下三潭水清澈见底，涧水淙淙不绝"。于是，正德禅师在上、中潭畔先建茅棚以弘扬佛法，并于大中四年（850年）在原地创建了大悲寺。在这之后的一百多年间，方岩山清清静静，只听得到寺院里回荡的晨钟暮鼓和木鱼罄声。

胡则借读

在北宋端拱元年（988年）的春天，永康胡库人胡则来到寺院里借住，专心读书以准备赴考。作为回报，他在读书堂里教授寺院里的小和尚们读书写字，正因为如此，他广受寺院里和尚们的尊敬。据广慈寺前任住持允明禅师讲，胡则走的时候，当时的住持资助了胡则上京赶考的路费，并叮嘱他，如果考不上，就一定要回来；如果考上了，也一定要回来报喜。胡则就这样带着老和尚的嘱托和小和尚们的希望走了，他在这里读书的故事也从此被老和尚传小和尚这样一代一代地流传了下来。胡则在离别之前的阴历八月初一，"率为五言十二韵，书于屋壁下"，题名为《别方岩》，以抒发他临行前的依依不舍之情：

寓居峰顶寺，不觉度炎天。山叟频为约，林僧每出禅。
虚怀思往事，宴坐息诸缘。照像龛镫暗，通宵磬韵传。
宴心资寂寞，琢句极幽玄。拾菌寒云外，烹茶翠竹前。
远阴临岳树，清响落岩泉。僻道无来客，深秋足乱蝉。
松风生井浪，溪雨长苔钱。自省浮尘世，终难驻永年。
遍游曾宛转，欲别重留连。明日东西路，依依独黯然。

胡则于北宋端拱二年（989年）进士及第，并随即开始了他的为官生涯。他辗转睦州、温州、信州、福州、杭州、池州等地，但是却再也没有回到方岩山大悲寺来看看。胡则于北宋宝元二年（1039年）病死他乡，葬于杭州钱塘县南山履泰乡龙井源。当消息传到大悲寺，当年受胡则教诲的小和尚都已经成了老和尚，出于对老师的怀念，他们便给胡则立了一个牌位，供奉在读书堂里。关于胡则读书堂的位置，在明嘉靖《永康县志》里，还有这样一段描写，在广慈寺东边的千人坑"之侧有小径，缘崖而登，行二百余步，有石穴，曰读书堂。俗传胡侯弦诵之地"。在清光绪《永康县志》里则把读书堂列入了地理志，古迹篇，"读书堂：去听泉楼百许步，岩腰有小石洞即胡侍郎读书处。好事者架飞甍为游人临眺之所"。但是广慈寺前住持允明禅师却说，读书堂位于长生塘的西侧，又由于"宋高宗敕赐赫灵庙额诰"中提到"遂就旧读书处永康方岩寺池边立祠"，可以认为在山腰上的小石穴可能只是胡则的"弦诵之地"，而在长生塘西侧的读书堂则是他读书及教书的地方，也是后来被改称为佑顺侯祠和赫灵庙的建筑。

胡则从"人"到"神"的转变

在胡则去世后的八十多年里，他可能只有一个排位被寺里的和尚供奉在当年的读书堂，并享用一些来自里人的香火；读书堂也可能依然被用作小和尚的读书处。在这期间，大悲寺于北宋治平二年（1065年）失火，同年重建后易名为广慈寺。据广慈寺前住持允明禅师讲，从那时起胡则的牌位和一尊小的塑像就被放在了如来佛的前面。在近六十年后，方岩山广慈寺在北宋宣和二年（1120年）爆发的方腊起义中，曾作为永康知县的赵琪退守并最终击败起义军的地方。这件貌似偶然且毫无关系的事件却成为胡则从"人"变成"神"的关键第一步，其实这两件事之间暗含着深刻的历史原因。

自汉朝以来，中国历代的皇帝都独尊儒术，不但封其为官教，而且把它作为维护统治阶级的一种精神工具。但是儒家学说中教化的理念占到主要成分，它对生命的体会却十分肤浅，甚至不能回答一些有关生、死、祸、福等从皇帝到老百姓都关心的人生根本问题。所以历代皇帝在独尊儒术的同时，又利用佛教或道教来满足这些世俗的需求，同时进一步巩固其统治地位。换句话说，"原始宗教的天命观、鬼神观、巫术等，在皇权的暗中保护下，大量地保存下来，并在人民中找到适宜的生存空间。封建皇帝对民间信仰中的神灵也从不一概排斥，甚至对许多地方涌现出的神予以册封。"与胡则生活在同一时代，家喻户晓的"妈祖"（960—987年）就是一个有力的证明。"妈祖"真名为林默，由于她生前和死后的众多传说，宋、元、明、清的历代帝王都对她有多次的册封，封号也从"夫人"、"天妃"、"天后"到"天上圣母"，并列入国家祀典。历代帝王们不但通过对神祇的册封来确立神的地位，从而巩固自己的统治，更重要的是借此来证明一种远远比"君权神授"更高的权力地位，即"神权君授"。

宋代政权建立之后的前几代皇帝都推崇佛教，但是宋徽宗（在位1100—1125年），却尊信道教，他曾一度命令佛教和道教合流，改寺院为道观，并使佛号、僧尼的名称都道教化。在历史上，每当新任皇帝弃佛从道的时期，起源于异国的佛教为了生存，都不得不对土生土长在中国大地上的道教进行妥协，把一些属于道教的，或者是民间的神祇请入佛堂共享香火。在这一点上，广慈寺也不例外，这也是它能历经千年依然香火旺盛的原因之一。在宋徽宗当政时期发生的一件事，恰好让广慈寺顺理成章地把一位民间神祇纳入了自己的领地。

宣和二年（1120年）十月初九，歙州农民方腊由于不满北宋腐朽统治，借摩尼教的旗号在睦州青溪爆发起义。摩尼教又称明教，在唐会昌年间被禁，随后转入民间秘密流行，历经五代至宋朝仍在闽浙一带有广泛的信徒，因此这次起义迅速得到了广大农民的热烈拥护和响应。北宋王朝的统治者在镇压这次带有宗教色彩的农民起义的时候，也充分利用了地方神祇的力量，宣传神人相助的神话。由于这次起义在短短一年半的时间就被全部镇压，所以在这其中的所有战斗都能最终以正派神祇的胜利作为结束，从而一箭双雕地打击"邪教"和"寇匪"。在此期间，北宋王朝大力褒奖地方神祇，因此"在方腊起义中显灵庇护官军而报至朝廷请求嘉奖的祠庙不在少数"，如"上虞遗德庙、嵊县显应庙等"。有些即使是未受"寇匪"侵扰的地方，地方统治者也会宣称是因为有神人暗中相助的结果。

在方腊起义中，永康方岩陈十四也揭竿而起。他们攻破永康县城，迫使知县赵琪退据方岩山。虽然赵琪最终是仓皇逃离了方岩山，但是因为陈十四的起义军不久后就被镇压了，可以推测知县赵琪也顺势迎合皇帝的意愿，杜撰了在方岩山有神人助王师灭寇的神话。而曾经"逮事三朝，十握州符，六持使节"，并且已经被当地人所熟悉和爱戴的永康人胡则，也顺理成章地成了神人助王师神话的主角。况且当时胡则在广慈寺读书堂里已立有牌位，把他神化成方岩山神便再合适不过了。这些神话故事有许多版本，它们的真实性和逻辑性并不是本文所讨论的重点，所以不妨就引用"宋高宗敕赐赫灵庙额诰"中所记述的官方版本，"民以重罹兵革为患，神独感梦于主将，显灵而阴助之。又贼魁梦一巨人，衣白衣跨白马饮池，黎明视水涸，其徒惊骇，遂至大败"。在宋徽宗宣和四年（1122年），也就是方腊起义被全面镇压后的这年，胡则被封为"佑顺侯"，这也是他去世后得到的第一次封赏。或许因为在同时有众多的地方神祇都因为类似的原因而得到了封赏，以至于"王廉访当时奏请失于勘斟，遂致所封敕中不言姓名"，而"止用方岩神奏"。

或许是这次册封的确不重要，以至于没能引起胡氏后人的重视，因为这次册封的诰书并没有收录进《库川胡氏宗谱》。广慈寺在当时并没有推崇道教的大背景下，倒是可能利用了这次册封，把胡则称为"方岩神佑顺侯"而纳入佛家圣地，并"香火供养甚谨"。而同时，方岩附近的一些地区也开始供奉胡则。作为一方神祇，胡则是"若水若旱若疫若疠，有求无不应，有祷无不答"。随着他在当地的名气越来越大，胡氏后人可能不满足于这次未言姓名的封赏，于是"阖邑之士状于有司"。在绍兴二十一年（1151年），作为建安县丞，也是胡则重孙的胡廷直向当时的宋高宗"详述始末，力求正名"。在核实了衢州委司户参军赵善和绍兴府诸暨县主簿赵彦伦之后，礼部依建炎三年（1129年）颁布的"挥神祠遇有灵应即先赐额"的圣旨，向皇帝建议赐"赫灵庙"为胡则祠的匾额。绍兴二十二年（1152年）二月，宋高宗降旨"敕赐赫灵庙"。

胡则的这次被册封，只是他日后一系列册封的开始。在宋代，册封制度已经逐步完善，规定对于有灵应的神祠要"无爵号者赐以额，已赐额者加封爵。初封侯，再封公，次封王"。而对于同一级别内封号的字数也有限制，开始为两个字，可逐步增加最多到八个字。关于册封制度的这些具体要求，从胡则的历次册封就可以看出来。在宋绍熙三年（1192年），胡则被宋光宗赐为"佑顺嘉应侯"；随后在嘉泰三年（1203年）和嘉定三年（1210年），被宋宁宗分两次册封至"佑顺嘉应福泽显灵侯"。从这些封号用词的选择中，可以看出在表彰胡则时间中态度的变化。"佑顺"是从皇帝角度上一种客观的认可；"嘉应"代表了一种赞许和肯定；"福泽"则是站在人民的立场上一种不遗余力的褒扬；最终到"显灵"，即一种超客观的神化。与此同时，胡则被"庙祀于衢、婺之间，无虑数十"。到淳祐六年（1246年），宋理宗封胡则"显应公"，随后"加正惠，宝祐初再加忠祐"。

在胡则被一次一次加封的同时，方岩山上供奉胡则的读书堂却"岁久事殊，址存堂废"。宋景定三年（1262年），里人王氏"不忍其坏，举而新之夫"。在这篇吴邃写的《方岩读书堂记》中还提到了作者本人在读书堂重修之后，"谨即斯堂拜公遗像"。由此可见，位于读书堂内的胡则塑像，最迟在重修后就已经存在了。据广慈寺前住持允明禅师讲，胡公庙以前就位于读书堂的位置。如此看来，有了胡则塑像的读书堂，日后就逐渐演化成了明嘉靖《永康县志》中提到的"佑顺侯祠"和清道光《永康县志》里所指的"赫灵祠"。近一百年后，写于元至正九年（1349年）的《胡侍郎庙碑阴记》中再次提到地方的胡则庙"布满于郡境，不啻数十百区"，胡则更是被演化成了一位"能出云为风雨"的万能神。

明清两代的继续发展

在经历了崇奉喇嘛教的元代，明代是佛教各个宗派逐步恢复和发展的时期。在这个时期里，广慈寺的香火也逐步趋于鼎盛。值得一提的是在明万历年间（1589—1619年）任住持的聿孤禅师，以及在他任职期间发生的两件事。据说聿孤禅师买了八个小孩当徒弟，改革创寺之始就实行的"子孙派"，将其分为乾、天、承、地、人、才、宝、智八房，轮流管理寺院香火和常务工作。"子孙派"规定只接收不超过五岁的幼儿皈依，小沙弥自幼与师父同起居、同饮食，形同父子，并死后合葬。聿孤禅师的改革既保持了"子孙派"极具亲和力的特点，又使寺院管理可以互相监督，并在此基础上发展了众多"下属寺院"。这也是广慈寺能历经多种磨难而成为千年古刹矗立在此的主要原因。

另一件事对广慈寺则是一个"重创"。据允明禅师讲，在明隆庆五年（1571年），附近的文楼村出了一个榜眼叫程正谊，后任四川左布政。程正谊的父亲叫程方峰（1498—1585年），他看上了方岩山这块宝地，便让儿子向当时的住持聿孤禅师借地做坟。聿孤禅师开始并不愿意，但念在自己是程方峰的孙子辈，便写了"卖地十丈"的地契。若干年后，聿孤禅师圆寂了，程方峰也过世了，程氏子孙把"卖地十丈"改成了"卖地千丈"，并在前街路边上的母子樟旁开始建造程方峰祠堂，一场官司便由此而生。寺里的和尚以整个方岩山也没有千丈为据来证明"卖地千丈"不实。审判结果是"卖地是真，千丈是假"，并判以千人坑和长生塘为界，南边归程氏，北侧归广慈寺。而这个审判结果在清光绪《永康县志》中也有明确记载，"程方峰先生梓墓：方岩上自千人坑流水为界，至峰门悬崖峭壁俱属墓地。万历（1573—1620年）年间奉勘合给。"这件事不知过了多久以后，文楼村的程氏看出了方岩山上的商机，开始在天街上做起了香烛、供品等生意。

一半的方岩山归了别人，广慈寺的香火和收入多少都会受到影响。清顺治十一年（1654年），赫灵庙就在胡氏后人的帮助下历经了一次修葺。可是几十年后，清康熙《永康县志》中就已经记载赫灵祠因年久失修，几近坍塌，寺里的僧人便把胡则的塑像搬到了广慈寺内。同时搬过去的应该还有胡则的牌位和那块敕赐的"赫灵庙"匾，它们一起被供奉在当时广慈寺的前殿内，从而真正意义上做到了寺庙合一。在这以后，从雍正七年（1729年）到道光二十七年（1847年）的一百多年里，奉胡则为伯祖的库川胡氏后人，先后多次出资帮助广慈寺修理或重建前厅和大殿，仅有记载的就有六次。其中嘉庆二十四年（1819年）对前厅的重建和扩建，基本上奠定了广慈寺中轴线最终的平面格局。

据允明禅师回忆，广慈寺中轴线上有四进殿堂，各殿堂之间有廊相连。第一进为广慈寺前厅，挂"广慈寺"匾；第二进为前殿，挂"赫灵庙"匾，中间供吃荤的"行公"胡则，背面为韦驮，两旁供胡则十弟兄；第三进为大雄宝殿，中间供如来佛，前面是乾隆三年（1738年）重塑的胡则像，旁边是文殊和普贤菩萨，殿堂两侧为十八罗汉；第四进是屏风阁，主供玉皇大帝；在大雄宝殿的东侧还建有观音阁。八房僧人的僧房则位于这些殿堂的外围，在平面上形成一个"八卦"图案。在宣统二年（1910年），出于对"人神共庙"批判的回应，寺里的僧人把玉皇大帝请到了位于西侧的地藏殿，把如来佛前的胡则像单独供奉于屏风阁，为吃素的"坐公"胡则。胡公虽然从大雄宝殿里被请了出来，但是据允明禅师说，即使现在胡公像后面依旧有如来、文殊和普贤菩萨的小塑像。

走向衰落

不幸的是，道光二十九年（1849年）九月初四的一场大火烧毁了整个祠庙及僧房。虽然在一年多以后，广慈寺得以重建，但是这已经成为它走向衰落的第一步。据允明禅师讲，清朝末年，当地老百姓的生活十分穷苦。再加上鸦片的泛滥，所以时常有人上山拿走庙里的东西，甚至是拆掉殿宇靠卖木头的钱为生。僧人也因此越来越少，八房僧人也只剩下了四房。《方岩指南》中也提到"清光绪年间（1875—1908年），寺僧相率而去"。在民国20和21两年，广慈寺还被后钱村来的一个道士霸占，寺内的僧人还被迫流落到附近的下属寺院。

在接下来几十年里一系列的人为灾害中，文化大革命无疑带给了广慈寺前所未有的重创。广慈寺几乎所有的建筑均在1966年8月下旬被拆除，仅有屏风阁和一幢僧房幸免于难。屏风阁原归方岩公社拆除，但是由于近千年对胡则的尊重，老街上的人拒绝这样做。于是，屏风阁被留了下来，并先后被用作大队开会的地方，林场仓库、邮电学校和602工厂。不仅如此，广慈寺内的字画和书籍从山上往下挑了十担，整整烧了一天。虽然《广慈寺寺志》在允明禅师的保护下逃过了这场浩劫，但却不明不白地遗失在永康市宗教科的各种卷宗之间。

"文革"后的复苏

文化大革命结束两年后，在1978年八月初一的凌晨，由岩下村村民黄埔林的母亲发起，她和另外三个妇女把一尊新塑的小胡公像抬上了山。"文革"后的第一任住持允明禅师于1979年十月初三上山，并凭记忆重塑了胡则像和屏风阁里其他的塑像，包括文曲星、财神、龙王和关公等。由于屏风阁还在，所以就有香客慕名来拜胡则。允明禅师用募捐来的香火钱，在1980年到1984年的五年间，买了四座祠堂，用以恢复广慈寺的建筑。第一个是在1980年用3000多元买的古竹畈村的一个厅，用来重建屏风阁前的大雄宝殿。紧接着用比较便宜的价格买下了因建杨汘水库而被迫拆除的汘下周村的周氏祠堂。随后用4000多元买了龙油县山買村的牛王殿，用来恢复天王殿、步云亭、后山的亭子和做一些修修补补的工作。最后买了永康市里的徐氏祠堂，在观音阁原址上重建了现在的广慈寺观音殿。
sections.content_en:
Early Founding Period

Guangci Temple, originally named Dabei Temple, is a famous Tiantai sect temple with over a thousand years of history. It was founded in the fourth year of Tang Xuanzong's Dazhong era (850), the fourth year after the "Huichang Persecution" ended and Buddhism was restored. Since Buddhism was introduced to China in the Western Han Dynasty, it had developed to its peak by the Sui and Tang dynasties. In the first two hundred years after the Tang Dynasty was established, successive emperors vigorously promoted Buddhism and gave it extremely high treatment. By the late Tang Dynasty, as Buddhism's influence and economic power continued to expand, as a religious belief it gradually threatened the central rule of the Tang Dynasty. Moreover, Tang Wuzong (840-846) himself believed in Daoism, so after ascending the throne he implemented a series of "Buddha-destroying" policies, including ordering the demolition of temples and forcing monks and nuns to return to lay life. Guangci Temple's founding patriarch Zhengde Chan Master was also forced to leave Guoqing Temple on Tiantai Mountain at that time. Zhengde Chan Master was originally a fire-head monk in the temple, i.e., the monk responsible for cooking. Before leaving Guoqing Temple, he had studied Zhiguan (both samadhi and prajna, the foundation of all Buddhist practice) under the twelfth patriarch Wuwai Chan Master of Guoqing Temple.

In 847, Tang Xuanzong, who believed in Buddhism, ascended the throne, changed the era name to the first year of Dazhong, and immediately ordered the restoration of all Buddhist temples abolished during the Huichang period. Since Guoqing Temple on Tiantai Mountain could not be restored immediately, Zhengde Chan Master may have come to nearby Fangyan Mountain to practice dhuta practices, one of the Buddhist ascetic practices, and lived in what is now Luohan Cave on the mountainside of Fangyan. He saw that Fangyan Mountain was "still a chaotic and desolate place, so he sought guidance from mountain farmers, climbed up by vines, crawled and scrambled, and only after penetrating the cave did he see ancient trees towering to the sky on the summit, withered trees lying horizontally, thorns everywhere, and utter desolation. Exploring to the depression, he saw the upper, middle, and lower pools with crystal-clear water, and the stream gurgling endlessly." Thus, Zhengde Chan Master first built thatched huts by the upper and middle pools to propagate Buddhism, and founded Dabei Temple on the original site in the fourth year of Dazhong (850). For over a hundred years after that, Fangyan Mountain was quiet and peaceful, with only the morning bells and evening drums and wooden fish and chime sounds echoing in the temple.

Hu Ze's Study at the Temple

In the spring of the first year of Northern Song Duangong (988), Hu Ze from Huku, Yongkang, came to stay at the temple, focusing on his studies in preparation for the imperial examination. In return, he taught the young monks in the study hall to read and write, and for this reason he was widely respected by the monks. According to Yunming Chan Master, former abbot of Guangci Temple, when Hu Ze left, the then-abbot funded his travel expenses to the capital for the examination, and urged him: if he failed, he must return; if he passed, he must also return to report the good news. Hu Ze left with the old monk's exhortations and the young monks' hopes, and the story of his studying here has been passed down generation after generation from old monks to young monks. On the first day of the eighth lunar month before his departure, Hu Ze "composed a twelve-rhyme five-character poem, written on the wall," titled "Farewell to Fangyan," to express his reluctance to leave:

Dwelling at the summit temple, unknowingly passing the hot summer. Mountain elders often made appointments, forest monks frequently emerged from meditation.
Empty mind recalling past events, seated in stillness ceasing all conditions. Image-reflecting niche lamp dim, all night chime tones transmitted.
Calm mind nourished by solitude, crafting phrases reaching profound mystery. Gathering mushrooms beyond cold clouds, brewing tea before green bamboos.
Distant shade over mountain trees, clear sounds falling on rocky springs. Remote path with no visitors, late autumn full of restless cicadas.
Pine wind generating well waves, stream rain growing moss coins. Self-reflecting in the floating world, ultimately hard to halt eternal years.
Wandering everywhere once winding, wanting to leave again lingering. Tomorrow east-west roads, reluctantly alone in gloom.

Hu Ze passed the jinshi examination in the second year of Duangong (989), and immediately began his official career. He served in Muzhou, Wenzhou, Xinzhou, Fuzhou, Hangzhou, Chizhou and other places, but never returned to Dabei Temple on Fangyan Mountain to visit. Hu Ze died of illness in a foreign land in the second year of Northern Song Baoyuan (1039), and was buried at Longjingyuan, Lütai Township, Nanshan, Qiantang County, Hangzhou. When the news reached Dabei Temple, the young monks who had been taught by Hu Ze had all become old monks; out of nostalgia for their teacher, they erected a memorial tablet for Hu Ze, enshrined in the study hall. Regarding the location of Hu Ze's study hall, the Ming Jiajing "Yongkang County Gazetteer" contains this description: east of Guangci Temple, beside the Thousand-Man Pit, "there is a small path, climbing along the cliff, walking over two hundred paces, there is a stone cave called Study Hall. Commonly said to be the place where Marquis Hu recited." In the Qing Guangxu "Yongkang County Gazetteer," the study hall is listed in the geography chapter, historic sites section: "Study Hall: about a hundred paces from Tingquan Tower, there is a small stone cave on the mountainside where Vice Minister Hu studied. Enthusiasts built flying eaves as a place for tourists to view." But Yunming Chan Master, former abbot of Guangci Temple, said the study hall was located west of Changsheng Pond; and since the "Song Gaozong Imperial Edict Granting Heling Temple Plaque" mentions "thus established a shrine by the pool at Yongkang Fangyan Temple at the old study place," it can be considered that the small stone cave on the mountainside may only have been Hu Ze's "recitation place," while the study hall west of Changsheng Pond was where he studied and taught, and also the building later renamed Youshun Marquis Shrine and Heling Temple.

Hu Ze's Transformation from "Man" to "God"

In the eighty-some years after Hu Ze's death, he may have had only a memorial tablet enshrined by the temple monks in the former study hall, enjoying some incense from local people; the study hall may also have continued to be used as a place for young monks to study. During this period, Dabei Temple caught fire in the second year of Northern Song Zhiping (1065), and after reconstruction in the same year was renamed Guangci Temple. According to Yunming Chan Master, from that time Hu Ze's memorial tablet and a small statue were placed in front of the Buddha. Nearly sixty years later, during the Fang La Rebellion that broke out in the second year of Northern Song Xuanhe (1120), Guangci Temple on Fangyan Mountain served as the place where Zhao Qi, magistrate of Yongkang, retreated and ultimately defeated the rebel army. This seemingly accidental and unrelated event became the key first step in Hu Ze's transformation from "man" to "god"; in fact, profound historical reasons lie between these two events.

Since the Han Dynasty, Chinese emperors of all dynasties exclusively honored Confucianism, not only establishing it as the state religion but also using it as a spiritual tool to maintain the ruling class. However, the concept of moral education dominated Confucian doctrine, while its understanding of life was quite superficial, unable even to answer fundamental questions of life and death, fortune and misfortune that concerned everyone from emperor to commoner. Therefore, while exclusively honoring Confucianism, successive emperors also used Buddhism or Daoism to satisfy these worldly needs, further consolidating their rule. In other words, "the primitive religious concepts of heavenly mandate, ghosts and spirits, and sorcery, under the covert protection of imperial power, were largely preserved and found suitable living space among the people. Feudal emperors never uniformly rejected deities in folk beliefs, even enfeoffing many local deities that emerged." The well-known "Mazu" (960-987), who lived in the same era as Hu Ze, is a powerful proof. "Mazu's" real name was Lin Mo; due to numerous legends about her life and after death, emperors of the Song, Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties enfeoffed her multiple times, with titles from "Lady," "Heavenly Consort," "Empress of Heaven" to "Heavenly Holy Mother," and she was included in the national sacrificial canon. Emperors not only established the status of deities through enfeoffment to consolidate their rule, but more importantly used it to prove a power status far higher than "royal authority granted by god," namely "divine authority granted by emperor."

The first few emperors after the Song Dynasty was established all promoted Buddhism, but Song Huizong (reigned 1100-1125) believed in Daoism; he once ordered Buddhism and Daoism to merge, converting temples to Daoist temples, and making Buddhist titles and monk/nun names Daoist. Historically, whenever a new emperor abandoned Buddhism for Daoism, Buddhism—originating in a foreign land—for survival had to compromise with Daoism native to China, inviting some Daoist or folk deities into Buddhist halls to share incense. In this respect, Guangci Temple was no exception, which is one reason it has maintained prosperous incense for a thousand years. An event during Song Huizong's reign恰好 allowed Guangci Temple to naturally incorporate a folk deity into its domain.

On the ninth day of the tenth month in the second year of Xuanhe (1120), Fang La, a farmer from Shezhou, dissatisfied with the corrupt Northern Song rule, launched an uprising in Qingxi, Muzhou, under the banner of Manichaeism. Manichaeism, also called Mingjiao, was banned during the Tang Huichang period, then转入 secret folk circulation, and through the Five Dynasties to the Song Dynasty still had wide followers in the Fujian-Zhejiang region, so this uprising quickly received enthusiastic support and response from the broad peasantry. The Northern Song rulers, in suppressing this religiously-colored peasant uprising, also充分 utilized the power of local deities, propagating myths of divine-human assistance. Because this uprising was completely suppressed in just one and a half years, all battles in it could ultimately end with the victory of orthodox deities, thus killing two birds with one stone by打击 "heretical religion" and "bandits." During this period, the Northern Song Dynasty vigorously rewarded local deities, so "there were not a few shrines that manifested spirits to protect official troops during the Fang La Rebellion and were reported to the court requesting commendation," such as "Shangyu Yide Temple, Shengxian Xianying Temple, etc." Even in places not harassed by "bandits," local rulers would claim it was the result of divine暗中 assistance.

During the Fang La Rebellion, Chen Shisi of Yongkang Fangyan also rose up. They captured Yongkang county seat, forcing Magistrate Zhao Qi to retreat to Fangyan Mountain. Although Zhao Qi ultimately fled Fangyan Mountain in panic, because Chen Shisi's rebel army was suppressed shortly after, it can be inferred that Magistrate Zhao Qi also followed the emperor's wishes and fabricated a myth of divine assistance to the royal army in destroying bandits on Fangyan Mountain. And Hu Ze, a Yongkang native who had "served three dynasties, held ten prefectural seals, and six envoy credentials," and was already familiar and beloved by locals, naturally became the protagonist of the divine-assistance myth. Moreover, Hu Ze already had a memorial tablet in the Guangci Temple study hall, so deifying him as the Fangyan Mountain god was most appropriate. These myths have many versions; their authenticity and logic are not the focus of this discussion, so we may cite the official version recorded in the "Song Gaozong Imperial Edict Granting Heling Temple Plaque": "The people suffered greatly from warfare; the god alone appeared in dreams to the commander, manifesting spirit and secretly assisting. Moreover, the bandit leader dreamed of a giant in white clothes riding a white horse drinking from the pool; at dawn the water was seen dry, his followers terrified, and they suffered a great defeat." In the fourth year of Xuanhe (1122), the year after the Fang La Rebellion was fully suppressed, Hu Ze was enfeoffed as "Youshun Marquis," his first posthumous title. Perhaps because many local deities received enfeoffment for similar reasons at the same time, "Royal Inspector Wang's memorial was insufficiently investigated, resulting in the enfeoffment edict not mentioning the name," and "only memorialized as Fangyan God."

Perhaps this enfeoffment was indeed unimportant, failing to attract the attention of Hu's descendants, because the edict was not included in the "Kuchuan Hu Family Genealogy." Guangci Temple, without the broader context of promoting Daoism at the time, may have used this enfeoffment to call Hu Ze "Fangyan God Youshun Marquis" and incorporate him into the Buddhist holy land, with "incense offerings very diligent." Meanwhile, some areas near Fangyan also began to worship Hu Ze. As a local deity, Hu Ze was "whether flood or drought or plague or epidemic, every request answered, every prayer responded." As his fame grew locally, Hu's descendants may have been dissatisfied with this unnamed enfeoffment, so "the gentlemen of the entire county petitioned the authorities." In the twenty-first year of Shaoxing (1151), Hu Tingzhi, Hu Ze's great-grandson and then magistrate of Jian'an County, "detailed the entire story to Song Gaozong, striving to correct the name." After verifying with Zhao Shan, registrar of Quzhou, and Zhao Yanlun, registrar of Zhuji County, Shaoxing Prefecture, the Ministry of Rites, following the imperial decree issued in the third year of Jianyan (1129) that "divine shrines with spiritual responses should first be granted plaques," recommended to the emperor granting "Heling Temple" as the plaque for Hu Ze's shrine. In the second month of the twenty-second year of Shaoxing (1152), Song Gaozong issued the edict "Imperially Granting Heling Temple."

This enfeoffment of Hu Ze was only the beginning of a series of future enfeoffments. In the Song Dynasty, the enfeoffment system was gradually perfected, stipulating that for spiritually responsive shrines, "those without titles should be granted plaques; those already granted plaques should receive additional noble titles. First enfeoffed as marquis, then as duke, then as king." There were also limits on the number of characters in titles within the same rank, starting with two characters, gradually increasing to a maximum of eight. These specific requirements of the enfeoffment system can be seen from Hu Ze's successive enfeoffments. In the third year of Shaoxi (1192), Hu Ze was granted "Youshun Jiaying Marquis" by Song Guangzong; subsequently in the third year of Jiatai (1203) and the third year of Jiading (1210), he was enfeoffed in two stages by Song Ningzong to "Youshun Jiaying Fuze Xianling Marquis." From the choice of words in these titles, one can see the change in attitude toward commending Hu Ze over time. "Youshun" was an objective recognition from the emperor's perspective; "Jiaying" represented approval and affirmation; "Fuze" was a wholehearted praise from the people's standpoint; finally "Xianling" was a super-objective deification. Meanwhile, Hu Ze was "worshipped in temples between Quzhou and Wuzhou, no fewer than several dozen." By the sixth year of Chunyou (1246), Song Lizong enfeoffed Hu Ze as "Xianying Duke," subsequently "adding Zhenghui, and in the early Baoyou period adding Zhongyou."

While Hu Ze was repeatedly enfeoffed, the study hall on Fangyan Mountain enshrining Hu Ze was "as years passed and things changed, the site remained but the hall was ruined." In the third year of Jingding (1262), a local surnamed Wang "could not bear its ruin, and renovated it." In the "Record of Fangyan Study Hall" written by Wu Sui, the author mentions that after the study hall was renovated, he "reverently bowed to the duke's portrait in this hall." This shows that the statue of Hu Ze in the study hall existed no later than after the renovation. According to Yunming Chan Master, Hugong Temple was formerly located at the study hall site. Thus, the study hall with Hu Ze's statue gradually evolved into the "Youshun Marquis Shrine" mentioned in the Ming Jiajing "Yongkang County Gazetteer" and the "Heling Shrine" referred to in the Qing Daoguang "Yongkang County Gazetteer." Nearly a hundred years later, the "Record on the Back of the Hu Shilang Temple Stele" written in the ninth year of Yuan Zhizheng (1349) again mentions that local Hu Ze temples "filled the prefecture, no fewer than several dozen to a hundred districts," and Hu Ze had evolved into an omnipotent god who "can summon clouds and bring rain."

Continued Development in the Ming and Qing Dynasties

After the Yuan Dynasty, which revered Lamaism, the Ming Dynasty was a period when various Buddhist sects gradually recovered and developed. During this period, Guangci Temple's incense also gradually reached its peak. Worth mentioning is the abbot Yugu Chan Master who served during the Ming Wanli period (1589-1619), and two events that occurred during his tenure. It is said that Yugu Chan Master bought eight children as disciples, reforming the "descendant school" implemented since the temple's founding, dividing it into eight houses: Qian, Tian, Cheng, Di, Ren, Cai, Bao, Zhi, taking turns managing temple incense and daily affairs. The "descendant school" stipulated only accepting children under five years old for conversion; young novices lived and ate with their masters from childhood, like father and son, and were buried together after death. Yugu Chan Master's reform both maintained the "descendant school's" highly approachable characteristics and enabled temple management to mutually supervise, and on this basis developed numerous "subsidiary temples." This is also the main reason Guangci Temple could survive various tribulations and stand here as a thousand-year-old ancient temple.

Another event was a "heavy blow" to Guangci Temple. According to Yunming Chan Master, in the fifth year of Ming Longqing (1571), a bangyan (second-place jinshi) named Cheng Zhengyi emerged from nearby Wenlou Village, later serving as Sichuan Left Administrative Commissioner. Cheng Zhengyi's father was Cheng Fangfeng (1498-1585), who took a fancy to the precious land of Fangyan Mountain and had his son borrow land from the then-abbot Yugu Chan Master for a tomb. Yugu Chan Master was initially unwilling, but considering himself a grandson-generation of Cheng Fangfeng, wrote a land deed of "selling ten zhang of land." Several years later, Yugu Chan Master passed away, and Cheng Fangfeng also died; Cheng's descendants changed "selling ten zhang" to "selling a thousand zhang," and began building the Cheng Fangfeng Ancestral Hall beside the Mother-and-Child Camphor by the front street road—a lawsuit thus arose. The temple monks used the fact that even the entire Fangyan Mountain did not have a thousand zhang as evidence to prove "selling a thousand zhang" was false. The trial result was "the sale was real, the thousand zhang was false," and it was ruled that with the Thousand-Man Pit and Changsheng Pond as the boundary, the south belonged to the Cheng family, and the north to Guangci Temple. This trial result is also clearly recorded in the Qing Guangxu "Yongkang County Gazetteer": "Cheng Fangfeng先生's tomb: on Fangyan, bounded by the flowing water of the Thousand-Man Pit, to the Peak Gate cliffs all belong to the cemetery. Granted during the Wanli period (1573-1620)." Sometime after this event, the Cheng family of Wenlou Village saw business opportunities on Fangyan Mountain and began selling incense, candles, and offerings on Tianjie.

With half of Fangyan Mountain归 to others, Guangci Temple's incense and income were inevitably affected. In the eleventh year of Qing Shunzhi (1654), Heling Temple underwent a renovation with the help of Hu's descendants. But decades later, the Qing Kangxi "Yongkang County Gazetteer" already recorded that Heling Shrine, due to long neglect, was nearly collapsed, so the temple monks moved Hu Ze's statue into Guangci Temple. Also moved should have been Hu Ze's memorial tablet and the imperially-granted "Heling Temple" plaque, which were together enshrined in the then-front hall of Guangci Temple, thus truly achieving temple-shrine unity. After this, from the seventh year of Yongzheng (1729) to the twenty-seventh year of Daoguang (1847), over more than a hundred years, the Kuchuan Hu descendants, who revered Hu Ze as their grand-uncle, repeatedly funded the repair or reconstruction of Guangci Temple's front hall and main hall, with six recorded instances. Among them, the reconstruction and expansion of the front hall in the twenty-fourth year of Jiaqing (1819) basically established the final planar layout of Guangci Temple's central axis.

According to Yunming Chan Master's recollection, Guangci Temple's central axis had four halls, connected by corridors. The first was the Guangci Temple front hall, with the "Guangci Temple" plaque; the second was the front hall, with the "Heling Temple" plaque, in the center enshrining the meat-eating "Xinggong" (Walking Duke) Hu Ze, with Skanda behind him, and Hu Ze's ten brothers on both sides; the third was the Mahavira Hall, in the center enshrining the Buddha, with the Hu Ze statue recast in the third year of Qianlong (1738) in front, Manjushri and Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas beside him, and the Eighteen Arhats on both sides of the hall; the fourth was the Screen Pavilion, mainly enshrining the Jade Emperor; east of the Mahavira Hall was also built the Guanyin Pavilion. The eight houses' monk quarters were located around these halls, forming a "bagua" (eight trigrams) pattern on the plane. In the second year of Xuantong (1910), in response to criticism of "humans and gods sharing a temple," the temple monks moved the Jade Emperor to the Ksitigarbha Hall on the west side, and separately enshrined the Hu Ze statue from before the Buddha in the Screen Pavilion as the vegetarian "Zuogong" (Sitting Duke) Hu Ze. Although Hu Gong was moved out of the Mahavira Hall, according to Yunming Chan Master, even now behind the Hu Gong statue there are still small statues of the Buddha, Manjushri, and Samantabhadra.

Decline

Unfortunately, a great fire on the fourth day of the ninth month in the twenty-ninth year of Daoguang (1849) destroyed the entire shrine and monk quarters. Although Guangci Temple was rebuilt over a year later, this had already become its first step toward decline. According to Yunming Chan Master, in the late Qing Dynasty, local people's lives were very poor. Coupled with the spread of opium, people often went up the mountain to take things from the temple, even demolishing halls to sell wood for a living. Monks thus became fewer and fewer, and the eight houses were reduced to four. The "Fangyan Guide" also mentions "during the Qing Guangxu period (1875-1908), temple monks left one after another." In the 20th and 21st years of the Republic, Guangci Temple was even occupied by a Daoist from Houqian Village, and the temple monks were forced to wander to nearby subsidiary temples.

Among a series of man-made disasters in the following decades, the Cultural Revolution undoubtedly dealt Guangci Temple an unprecedented heavy blow. Almost all of Guangci Temple's buildings were demolished in late August 1966, with only the Screen Pavilion and one monk quarter surviving. The Screen Pavilion was originally scheduled for demolition by the Fangyan Commune, but due to nearly a thousand years of respect for Hu Ze, the old street people refused to do so. Thus, the Screen Pavilion was retained, and was successively used as a brigade meeting place, forest farm warehouse, post and telecommunications school, and 602 Factory. Moreover, the calligraphy, paintings, and books in Guangci Temple were carried down the mountain in ten担 and burned for a whole day. Although the "Guangci Temple Gazetteer" escaped this catastrophe under Yunming Chan Master's protection, it was inexplicably lost among various files of the Yongkang Municipal Religious Affairs Section.

Recovery After the Cultural Revolution

Two years after the Cultural Revolution ended, in the early morning of the first day of the eighth lunar month in 1978, initiated by the mother of Yanxia Village villager Huang Pulin, she and three other women carried a newly molded small Hu Gong statue up the mountain. Yunming Chan Master, the first post-Cultural Revolution abbot, went up the mountain on the third day of the tenth lunar month in 1979, and from memory recast the Hu Ze statue and other statues in the Screen Pavilion, including the Wenqu Star, God of Wealth, Dragon King, and Guan Gong. Because the Screen Pavilion still stood, pilgrims came to worship Hu Ze. Using donated incense money, Yunming Chan Master bought four ancestral halls over the five years from 1980 to 1984 to restore Guangci Temple's buildings. The first was a hall from Guzhufan Village bought for over 3,000 yuan in 1980, used to rebuild the Mahavira Hall in front of the Screen Pavilion.紧接着, at a relatively cheap price, he bought the Zhou Clan Ancestral Hall of Hanxia Zhou Village, which had been forced to demolish due to the construction of the Hanqian Reservoir. Subsequently, he bought the Niuwang Hall of Shanmai Village, Longyou County, for over 4,000 yuan, used to restore the Heavenly King Hall, Buyun Pavilion, back-mountain pavilions, and do some repair work. Finally, he bought the Xu Clan Ancestral Hall in Yongkang city, rebuilding the current Guangci Temple Guanyin Hall on the original site of the Guanyin Pavilion.

王廉访当时奏请失于勘斟遂致所封敕中不言姓名而止用方岩神奏
广慈寺利用了这次册封把胡则称为方岩神佑顺侯而纳入佛家圣地并香火供养甚谨

胡则被庙祀于衢婺之间无虑数十
淳祐六年1246年宋理宗封胡则显应公随后加正惠宝祐初再加忠祐
