屏风阁被留了下来并先后被用作大队开会的地方林场仓库邮电学校和602工厂
广慈寺内的字画和书籍从山上往下挑了十担整整烧了一天
广慈寺寺志在允明禅师的保护下逃过了这场浩劫但却不明不白地遗失在永康市宗教科的各种卷宗之间
1978年八月初一的凌晨由岩下村村民黄埔林的母亲发起她和另外三个妇女把一尊新塑的小胡公像抬上了山
文革后的第一任住持允明禅师于1979年十月初三上山并凭记忆重塑了胡则像和屏风阁里其他的塑像包括文曲星财神龙王和关公等
允明禅师用募捐来的香火钱在1980年到1984年的五年间买了四座祠堂用以恢复广慈寺的建筑
1980年用3000多元买的古竹畈村的一个厅用来重建屏风阁前的大雄宝殿
买下了因建杨汘水库而被迫拆除的汘下周村的周氏祠堂
用4000多元买了龙油县山買村的牛王殿用来恢复天王殿步云亭后山的亭子和做一些修修补补的工作
买了永康市里的徐氏祠堂在观音阁原址上重建了现在的广慈寺观音殿

sections.name: 三、广慈寺和胡公庙现状
sections.content_zh:
在二十世纪八十年代中叶，以发展旅游业为目的，胡公庙从广慈寺中被分离出来，作为一个独立的寺院，再次和广慈寺肩并肩地坐落在方岩山顶上。胡公庙在西侧，占据了广慈寺原有中轴线的位置，即以屏风阁为最后一进大殿。在屏风阁前刚刚建好没几年的大雄宝殿再次被拆除，取而代之的是两幢新建的胡公庙前殿和大殿。广慈寺则被迫向东平移，改以重建的观音殿为中轴线，并在后面补建了大雄宝殿。

广慈寺

这里的老人们都说，广慈寺以前的各个殿堂之间也都是有围廊相连的，下雨都不会湿鞋。不仅如此，允明禅师讲，以前从山脚到山顶都是有长廊的，是太平村的一个村民每年来修，用了很多年才建成。现任住持释明修也说，在他去"应聘"广慈寺住持的时候，也曾经见过一张广慈寺的图，上面画着从山下到寺院都有走廊相连。

如今的广慈寺有三进殿堂。一进前厅和二进观音殿为允明禅师于1984年复建；第三进殿堂是在寺、庙分离之后补建的大雄宝殿。观音殿与前厅有侧廊相连，中间围合成一个小的院落。由于是利用祠堂建筑的木料重建，所以无论从大木构件或小木雕饰中都可以看到世俗建筑的影子。一进前厅会让人不禁想起祠堂里的戏台。前厅正中间的神龛里目前供奉着弥勒佛，神龛本身看上去很像戏台上使用的建筑道具。神龛正上方是一个通常只用于祠堂戏台顶上的精致藻井，藻井里的斗拱呈螺旋形层叠上升。边上两间各有一组九格天花，四周还有小斗拱做支撑，天花上绘制的都是《西游记》中的经典场面。壁画颜色以黄、绿色为底，线条精美，退晕渲染也十分讲究。观音殿和两侧围廊中祠堂建筑的痕迹就更加明显。这其中的大木构件不仅用神牛、寿桃、喜鹊做雕饰主题，还可以看到富有张力的月梁，极富装饰效果的"蠖梁"以及活灵活现的狮子舞球。广慈寺的这座建筑是中国建筑构造特点和设计理念的最好体现：一幢建筑不仅能拆了异地重建，而且还能把所有构建重新排列组合，建造成平面和功能都不尽相同的新建筑。

方岩山上另外一幢没有在文化大革命期间被拆毁的建筑就是位于现广慈寺东南角的僧房。这幢仅存的僧房是在清道光二十九年（1849年）的那场大火后重建的。僧房高三层，坡屋顶，平面为异形，中间却围合了一个四四方方的小院，院内正中是一个巨大的"放生池"，池上有小拱桥。说是放生池，其实其主要目的是预防火灾。最值得一提的是，僧房的外立面明显受到西方古典主义建筑的影响：通高的壁柱，三角形山墙，以及山墙中圆形的装饰母题。

胡公庙前殿和大殿

胡公庙的第一进殿是一个三开间的一层木建筑，挂"胡公祠"横匾。虽然我们无法区分建筑的哪些构建来自于拆掉的大雄宝殿，哪些来自于其他建筑，而哪些又是后来新做的，更不用说被允明禅师重建的大雄宝殿本身就是利用拆除后的一幢民居为建筑原料，但是这些都并不重要。乡土建筑的一大魅力就在于它创作中的自由性和追求物尽其用的特点，这种"重新组装"的做法不但延续了原有建筑物的生命，而且这种"再创造"本身就具有非常的意义。

前殿大木雕饰所采用的题材，都明显带有当地祠堂建筑的痕迹。例如，两个中榀檐柱的牛腿上就雕有当地祠堂建筑中通常采用的狮子戏球；牛腿上向各个方向飞扬伸展的叠拱和插叶所采用的卷草图案也和世远公祠里的非常相似。不过，前殿里最有特点的部分还要算天花。这里建筑的梁架通常是露明的，但是前殿的中榀的两个金柱中间却有天花，天花中间还形成一个八面锥体的藻井。藻井正中绘有盘龙，八个面上不但绘有如来佛、弥勒佛、观音、太上老君，还有《西游记》里的四个主要人物；四周的天花上则画满《西游记》中的一些主要故事情节。可以说，在这几米见方的二维画板上，已经完全看不到佛教、道教与世俗尘世之间的任何界限。前殿的屋面应该是新的，但在这里人、神之间的界限也是模糊的。垂脊的末端各有一尊小的雕像，前面分别是哪吒、托塔李天王，后面则是两名天兵天将。

胡公庙大殿是一个用钢筋混凝土做支撑结构的两层高建筑，坐落在一个半米多高的基础上，俨然一副官式建筑的气派。大殿正中有一个两米多高、玉皇大帝扮相的胡公正襟端坐在一个一米多高的须弥座上，他略微低头，审视着跪倒在他面前的虔诚香客。依照惯例，这尊胡公是"吃荤"的，也就是说，三牲之类的供品都会摆放在须弥座前面的香案上。胡公的头顶上也有一个半球形的藻井，上面绘着龙和凤。硕大的一个殿堂，只有一尊塑像在中间，平时显得空荡荡的，但是在庙会期间，据说就会挤得水泄不通。

屏风阁

最后一进殿是屏风阁，现存建筑基本上是清道光二十九年（1849年）那场大火之后重建的。允明禅师说，重建的时候，一些主要构件改用石材以防火灾。可是到清朝末年，寺院变得十分不景气，原本的八房僧人也只剩下了四房，每房的人数也少了许多。于是就有人说是因为"狮子（石子的谐音）吃人"，所以在宣统年间（1909—1911年），屏风阁又改回了木构。

屏风阁也是利用天然岩洞建造的，但是它和罗汉洞或五峰书院有着根本的不同。屏风阁的建筑空间不但延伸到了石洞以外，而且还利用石洞上的巨石作为"楼板"，在上面加建了二层。允明禅师说，二层以前供的是玉皇大帝，直到宣统二年（1910年），才把玉皇大帝移到了现在的地藏殿。屏风阁一、二层之间没有任何垂直的联系，像搬佛像这样大的变故，可能只有在重建或大修的时候才可以进行。把这种可望而不可即的位置留给玉皇大帝本是无可厚非，但是在佛家圣地的正殿里高高供奉道教的"众神之皇"，这不得不归功于中国式"宗教"无与伦比的博大和宽容。

屏风阁和它前面殿堂之间的空间比较小，再加上这里总是烟雾缭绕，所以很难看清它的全貌。屏风阁正面原本有墙，香客通过左右两侧的拱形门洞进出。院墙和凹字形的建筑围合了一个小院，院内靠墙的一侧有香炉。后来因为香客太多，香炉离建筑太近，有火灾隐患，所以拆除了围墙。现在从屏风阁前面的铺地上还可以清楚地看到墙基和门的位置。

屏风阁的大木雕饰奢华精美到了极点。由于一层屋檐有两根挑檐枋承托，所以又多了许多可以用以雕饰的叠斗、穿子、雀替、垂花等构件。抬头审视檐下、柱头的这一圈，眼睛找不到可以小憩的地方：凤凰、牡丹、仙鹤、神仙……又一只凤凰。鎏了金的木雕，在经历了几十年，甚至上百年的烟熏之后，没有了最初的那种浮华亮丽，多了些凝重和斑驳。木雕中最抢眼的就是在两个中榀檐柱上的龙形"牛腿"。一条金龙盘旋在五彩的云海里，头上顶着蜀柱，龙身"穿过"檐柱，又变成一条短梁用以连接后面的蜀柱，短梁和两个梁托也都雕有云海的图案。

屏风阁里面，沿石洞内壁一共排列着大大小小的塑像二十三尊。正中间的一个当然是红面长须、笑容可掬的胡公大帝，他的两个儿子陪坐在两边，后面是他的三个夫人。据说胡则原本只有两个夫人，第三位只是猝死在胡公大帝面前的一位女香客，人们见她如此虔诚，便封她为胡公的第三任夫人。在胡公的右侧依次是关公、龙王和平安菩萨；左边则是文曲星、婚姻美满神和财神。除了婚姻美满神是一对夫妻塑像以外，其他每一个神仙和菩萨两边还配有侍从两人。基本说来，这里可以满足人们生活中的一切所求，不论是求财还是求雨，求前程似锦还是求出入平安，抑或是求家庭美满还是求功名利禄。就算是各路神仙都帮不了忙，还可以求无所不能的胡公大帝。在每组神像前都有一个巨大的蜡烛台，上面插满了高高低低的蜡烛，胡公大帝面前的蜡烛更是多到看不见他的脸。在这黑黢黢的山洞里，扑朔迷离的光影变化加上烟雾缭绕的视觉效果，给诸神平添了些神秘的色彩。

据允明禅师说，自从把胡公从大雄宝殿请到屏风阁之后，他的后面一直有如来、文殊和普贤菩萨的三尊小塑像。如此说来，人们在祭拜胡公大帝的同时，其实是在求助如来佛祖的保佑。在香客眼里，胡公大帝是无所不能的一方神祇；在广慈寺眼里，无所不能的仍旧是胡则后面的如来佛祖，胡则只是能带给寺院旺盛人间香火的护法神。

胡公签诗

胡公庙里最抢人眼球的要算是在屏风阁前，沿大殿后墙一字排开的十几名"解签人"。他们都是六七十岁的老人，一个个面露慈祥，穿着也很干净体面。解签人每两个人用一张桌子，桌子前面有一条长板凳留给香客坐。桌面正中中有一个细长的缝，后面还立着一个"付费自愿"的小牌。偶尔香客少的时候，解签人要么就一遍一遍地翻看着不知是哪天的报纸；看完了，还会在报纸的空白处，用那种平头艺术钢笔认认真真、一笔一顿地练字。想想原因很简单：中国人普遍认为字写得好的人一定有学问，显然有学问的人解签准错不了。其实解签人给每个香客写的字不过十几个，所以他们便更要精益求精、一丝不苟。还好需要写的字总数不过几百个，所以每一个解签人都能写一手好字。

胡公签诗一共有一百签，解签人讲上、中、下签各有三分之一。每一签都是一首七言绝句，其中涉及的典故在时间上最迟到元末明初。据允明禅师讲，签诗的创作者是文楼村程方峰的子孙兆亨公，而《文楼村程氏家谱》中则记载为程兆选（1724—1786年）。这兄弟两人皆为进士，又生活在同一个年代，所以推测胡公签诗的形成时间可能是在清朝初年。

签诗形成之初，解签人基本上都是文楼村的程氏后人，他们还不能进入广慈寺解签，只能搬个小桌子，在天街上等候香客。允明禅师回忆，广慈寺虽然对此很不满意，但是由于天街在明万历年间（1573—1620年）就判归文楼村程氏，所以他们对此也没有办法。这种情况最迟到民国初年已经有所改变："解签诗摊：二十余摊。在后殿及观音堂。每张铜元二枚。"现在的解签人基本上都是老街上的程氏后人，由于这份工作相对轻松，收入又不错，所以是人人都想做的美差。现在如果要做解签人，不但要考试选拔，还要根据"水平"定级。不禁试想如果兆亨公、兆选公知道这些，是会哭还是会笑。
sections.content_en:
In the mid-1980s, for the purpose of developing tourism, Hugong Temple was separated from Guangci Temple as an independent temple, once again standing side by side with Guangci Temple on the summit of Fangyan Mountain. Hugong Temple is on the west side, occupying Guangci Temple's original central axis position, with the Screen Pavilion as the last hall. The Mahavira Hall that had just been built in front of the Screen Pavilion a few years earlier was again demolished, replaced by two newly built Hugong Temple front hall and main hall. Guangci Temple was forced to shift eastward, changing to the rebuilt Guanyin Hall as its central axis, and adding a Mahavira Hall behind it.

Guangci Temple

The elderly here all say that in the past, the various halls of Guangci Temple were connected by surrounding corridors, so one's shoes would not get wet in the rain. Moreover, Yunming Chan Master said that in the past there were long corridors from the foot of the mountain to the summit, built by a villager from Taiping Village who came to repair every year, taking many years to complete. The current abbot Shi Mingxiu also said that when he went to "apply" for the position of Guangci Temple abbot, he once saw a map of Guangci Temple showing corridors connecting from below the mountain to the temple.

Today's Guangci Temple has three halls. The first front hall and second Guanyin Hall were rebuilt by Yunming Chan Master in 1984; the third hall is the Mahavira Hall added after the temple-shrine separation. The Guanyin Hall and front hall are connected by side corridors, enclosing a small courtyard in the middle. Because they were rebuilt using timber from ancestral hall buildings, traces of secular architecture can be seen in both large timber components and small wood carvings. The first front hall inevitably reminds one of the stage in an ancestral hall. In the central shrine of the front hall, Maitreya Buddha is currently enshrined, and the shrine itself looks much like a stage prop used in theatrical performances. Directly above the shrine is an exquisite caisson ceiling usually only used on ancestral hall stage roofs, with the bracket sets in the caisson spiraling upward in layers. The two side rooms each have a group of nine-grid ceilings, supported by small bracket sets around the perimeter, with classic scenes from "Journey to the West" painted on the ceilings. The mural colors are based on yellow and green, with exquisite lines and meticulous gradation rendering. Traces of ancestral hall architecture are even more evident in the Guanyin Hall and surrounding corridors. Among them, the large timber components not only use divine oxen, longevity peaches, and magpies as carving themes, but also show tension-filled moon beams, highly decorative "huo beams," and vivid lions playing with balls. This building of Guangci Temple is the best embodiment of Chinese architectural construction characteristics and design concepts: a building can not only be dismantled and rebuilt in a different location, but also all its components can be rearranged and combined into new buildings with different planes and functions.

Another building on Fangyan Mountain that was not demolished during the Cultural Revolution is the monk quarters located at the southeast corner of the current Guangci Temple. This only surviving monk quarters was rebuilt after the great fire in the twenty-ninth year of Qing Daoguang (1849). The monk quarters are three stories high with a pitched roof and an irregular plane, enclosing a square courtyard in the middle, with a huge "free-life pond" at the center of the courtyard and a small arched bridge over it. Called a free-life pond, its main purpose is actually fire prevention. Most notably, the exterior facade of the monk quarters was clearly influenced by Western classical architecture: full-height pilasters, triangular gables, and circular decorative motifs in the gables.

Hugong Temple Front Hall and Main Hall

The first hall of Hugong Temple is a three-bay single-story wooden building, with a horizontal plaque reading "Hugong Shrine" (Hu Gong Ancestral Hall). Although we cannot distinguish which components of the building came from the demolished Mahavira Hall, which from other buildings, and which were newly made later—not to mention that the Mahavira Hall rebuilt by Yunming Chan Master itself used a demolished residence as building material—none of this is important. A major charm of vernacular architecture lies in the freedom of its creation and the pursuit of making the best use of everything; this "reassembly" approach not only extends the life of original buildings, but the "re-creation" itself is of great significance.

The themes used in the large wood carvings of the front hall clearly bear traces of local ancestral hall architecture. For example, the ox-legs on the two middle-bay eave columns are carved with lions playing with balls, commonly used in local ancestral hall architecture; the scrolling grass patterns used in the bracket sets and inserted leaves extending in all directions on the ox-legs are also very similar to those in Shiyuan Gong Hall. However, the most distinctive part of the front hall must be the ceiling. The building's beam frame here is usually exposed, but between the two gold columns of the middle bay in the front hall there is a ceiling, with an eight-sided pyramidal caisson formed in the center of the ceiling. A coiling dragon is painted in the center of the caisson; on the eight faces are painted not only the Buddha, Maitreya Buddha, Guanyin, and the Supreme Lord Lao Zi, but also the four main characters from "Journey to the West"; the surrounding ceilings are filled with major story plots from "Journey to the West." It can be said that on this few-meter-square two-dimensional panel, any boundary between Buddhism, Daoism, and the secular world has completely disappeared. The roof of the front hall should be new, but here the boundary between humans and gods is also blurred. At the ends of the vertical ridges are small statues, with Nezha and the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King Li in front, and two heavenly soldiers and generals behind.

The Hugong Temple main hall is a two-story building with reinforced concrete as the supporting structure, sitting on a foundation over half a meter high, with the imposing air of an official-style building. In the center of the hall, a Hu Gong statue over two meters tall, dressed as the Jade Emperor, sits solemnly on a sumeru pedestal over one meter high, slightly bowing his head to examine the devout pilgrims kneeling before him. As is customary, this Hu Gong "eats meat"—that is, offerings such as the three sacrificial animals are placed on the incense table in front of the sumeru pedestal. Above Hu Gong's head is also a hemispherical caisson, painted with dragons and phoenixes. This huge hall has only one statue in the center, appearing empty on ordinary days, but during temple festivals it is said to be packed so tightly that not even water can leak through.

Screen Pavilion

The last hall is the Screen Pavilion; the existing building was basically rebuilt after the great fire in the twenty-ninth year of Qing Daoguang (1849). Yunming Chan Master said that during reconstruction, some main components were changed to stone to prevent fire. But by the late Qing Dynasty, the temple became very depressed, and the original eight houses of monks were reduced to four, with far fewer people in each house. So some people said it was because "lions (homophone for stone) eat people," so during the Xuantong period (1909-1911), the Screen Pavilion was changed back to wooden construction.

The Screen Pavilion was also built using a natural rock cave, but it is fundamentally different from Luohan Cave or Wufeng Academy. The architectural space of the Screen Pavilion not only extends beyond the cave, but also uses the giant rock above the cave as a "floor slab," adding a second story above it. Yunming Chan Master said that the second story formerly enshrined the Jade Emperor, and it was not until the second year of Xuantong (1910) that the Jade Emperor was moved to the current Ksitigarbha Hall. There is no vertical connection between the first and second stories of the Screen Pavilion; a major change like moving a Buddha statue could probably only be carried out during reconstruction or major repairs. Leaving this unattainable position for the Jade Emperor is understandable, but enshrining the Daoist "Emperor of All Gods" high in the main hall of a Buddhist holy site must be attributed to the unparalleled broadness and tolerance of Chinese-style "religion."

The space between the Screen Pavilion and the hall in front of it is relatively small, and with smoke always curling here, it is difficult to see its full appearance. The front of the Screen Pavilion originally had walls, with pilgrims entering and exiting through arched doorways on the left and right sides. The courtyard wall and the concave-shaped building enclosed a small courtyard, with an incense burner on the side against the wall inside. Later, because there were too many pilgrims and the incense burner was too close to the building, posing a fire hazard, the courtyard wall was demolished. Now the wall foundations and door positions can still be clearly seen on the paving in front of the Screen Pavilion.

The large wood carvings of the Screen Pavilion are extravagantly exquisite to the extreme. Because the first-story eaves are supported by two eave-purlin brackets, there are many more components available for carving, such as stacked brackets, through-pieces, spandrel brackets, and pendant flowers. Looking up at the circle under the eaves and at the column heads, the eyes find no place to rest: phoenixes, peonies, cranes, immortals... another phoenix. The gilded wood carvings, after decades or even over a hundred years of smoke, have lost their original flashy brilliance and gained more gravitas and mottling. The most eye-catching wood carvings are the dragon-shaped "ox-legs" on the two middle-bay eave columns. A golden dragon coils in a sea of five-colored clouds, with a shu column on its head; the dragon body "passes through" the eave column and becomes a short beam connecting to the shu column behind, and the short beam and two beam brackets are also carved with cloud-sea patterns.

Inside the Screen Pavilion, along the inner wall of the rock cave, a total of twenty-three statues of various sizes are arranged. The one in the exact center is of course the red-faced, long-bearded, smiling Hu Gong Emperor, with his two sons sitting in attendance on both sides and his three wives behind him. It is said that Hu Ze originally had only two wives; the third was merely a female pilgrim who died suddenly in front of Hu Gong Emperor, and seeing her such devotion, people enfeoffed her as Hu Gong's third wife. To Hu Gong's right are依次 Guan Gong, the Dragon King, and the Peace Bodhisattva; to his left are the Wenqu Star, the Marriage-Fulfillment God, and the God of Wealth. Except for the Marriage-Fulfillment God, which is a pair of husband-and-wife statues, each other god and bodhisattva has two attendants on both sides. Basically speaking, here can satisfy all requests in people's lives—whether seeking wealth or rain, seeking a bright future or safe travels, or seeking family happiness or fame and fortune. Even if all the various gods cannot help, one can still seek the omnipotent Hu Gong Emperor. In front of each group of statues is a huge candlestick filled with candles of various heights, and the candles in front of Hu Gong Emperor are so numerous that his face cannot be seen. In this dark cave, the confusing changes of light and shadow coupled with the visual effect of curling smoke add a mysterious color to the various gods.

According to Yunming Chan Master, since Hu Gong was moved from the Mahavira Hall to the Screen Pavilion, there have always been three small statues of the Buddha, Manjushri, and Samantabhadra behind him. Thus, while people worship Hu Gong Emperor, they are actually seeking the Buddha's protection. In the eyes of pilgrims, Hu Gong Emperor is an omnipotent local deity; in the eyes of Guangci Temple, the omnipotent one remains the Buddha behind Hu Ze, and Hu Ze is merely a Dharma-protecting god who can bring the temple prosperous worldly incense.

Hu Gong Fortune Poems

The most eye-catching thing in Hugong Temple is the dozen or so "fortune-tellers" lined up in a row along the back wall of the main hall in front of the Screen Pavilion. They are all elderly people in their sixties and seventies, each with a kind face and clean, decent clothing. Two fortune-tellers share one table, with a long bench in front of the table for pilgrims to sit on. In the center of the tabletop is a narrow slit, with a small sign reading "Payment Voluntary" standing behind it. Occasionally when there are few pilgrims, the fortune-tellers either flip through newspapers of unknown date over and over; after reading, they also practice calligraphy seriously and stroke by stroke in the blank spaces of the newspapers with that kind of flat-tip artistic fountain pen. The reason is simple: Chinese people generally believe that those who write well must be learned, and obviously learned people cannot be wrong in interpreting fortunes. In fact, the fortune-tellers write no more than a dozen characters for each pilgrim, so they must be even more精益求精 and meticulous. Fortunately, the total number of characters to write is only a few hundred, so every fortune-teller can write good calligraphy.

There are one hundred fortune poems in total, and the fortune-tellers say that upper, middle, and lower fortunes each account for one-third. Each fortune is a seven-character quatrain, with the allusions involved dating as late as the late Yuan and early Ming dynasties. According to Yunming Chan Master, the creator of the fortune poems was Zhaheng Gong, a descendant of Cheng Fangfeng of Wenlou Village, while the "Wenlou Village Cheng Family Genealogy" records it as Cheng Zhaoxuan (1724-1786). These two brothers were both jinshi and lived in the same era, so it is推测 that the formation time of the Hu Gong fortune poems may be in the early Qing Dynasty.

At the beginning of the fortune poems' formation, the fortune-tellers were basically Cheng descendants of Wenlou Village, who could not yet enter Guangci Temple to interpret fortunes and could only move a small table to wait for pilgrims on Tianjie. Yunming Chan Master recalled that although Guangci Temple was very dissatisfied with this, because Tianjie had been awarded to the Cheng family of Wenlou Village during the Ming Wanli period (1573-1620), they had no way to deal with it. This situation had changed by the early Republic of China at the latest: "Fortune poem interpretation stalls: over twenty stalls. In the rear hall and Guanyin Hall. Two copper coins each." The current fortune-tellers are basically Cheng descendants of the old street; because this job is relatively easy and the income is good, it is a coveted position that everyone wants. Now to become a fortune-teller, one must not only pass an examination selection but also be graded according to "level." One cannot help but wonder if Zhaheng Gong and Zhaoxuan Gong knew this, would they cry or laugh.
key_terms: 二十世纪八十年代中叶以发展旅游业为目的胡公庙从广慈寺中被分离出来作为一个独立的寺院再次和广慈寺肩并肩地坐落在方岩山顶上
胡公庙在西侧占据了广慈寺原有中轴线的位置即以屏风阁为最后一进大殿
在屏风阁前刚刚建好没几年的大雄宝殿再次被拆除取而代之的是两幢新建的胡公庙前殿和大殿
广慈寺则被迫向东平移改以重建的观音殿为中轴线并在后面补建了大雄宝殿
广慈寺以前的各个殿堂之间也都是有围廊相连的下雨都不会湿鞋
以前从山脚到山顶都是有长廊的是太平村的一个村民每年来修用了很多年才建成
现任住持释明修说在他去应聘广慈寺住持的时候也曾经见过一张广慈寺的图上面画着从山下到寺院都有走廊相连
如今的广慈寺有三进殿堂一进前厅和二进观音殿为允明禅师于1984年复建第三进殿堂是在寺庙分离之后补建的大雄宝殿
观音殿与前厅有侧廊相连中间围合成一个小的院落
由于是利用祠堂建筑的木料重建所以无论从大木构件或小木雕饰中都可以看到世俗建筑的影子
一进前厅会让人不禁想起祠堂里的戏台
前厅正中间的神龛里目前供奉着弥勒佛神龛本身看上去很像戏台上使用的建筑道具
神龛正上方是一个通常只用于祠堂戏台顶上的精致藻井藻井里的斗拱呈螺旋形层叠上升
边上两间各有一组九格天花四周还有小斗拱做支撑天花上绘制的都是西游记中的经典场面
壁画颜色以黄绿色为底线条精美退晕渲染也十分讲究
观音殿和两侧围廊中祠堂建筑的痕迹就更加明显
大木构件不仅用神牛寿桃喜鹊做雕饰主题还可以看到富有张力的月梁极富装饰效果的蠖梁以及活灵活现的狮子舞球
广慈寺的这座建筑是中国建筑构造特点和设计理念的最好体现一幢建筑不仅能拆了异地重建而且还能把所有构建重新排列组合建造成平面和功能都不尽相同的新建筑
方岩山上另外一幢没有在文化大革命期间被拆毁的建筑就是位于现广慈寺东南角的僧房
这幢仅存的僧房是在清道光二十九年1849年的那场大火后重建的
僧房高三层坡屋顶平面为异形中间却围合了一个四四方方的小院院内正中是一个巨大的放生池池上有小拱桥
说是放生池其实其主要目的是预防火灾
僧房的外立面明显受到西方古典主义建筑的影响通高的壁柱三角形山墙以及山墙中圆形的装饰母题
胡公庙的第一进殿是一个三开间的一层木建筑挂胡公祠横匾
无法区分建筑的哪些构建来自于拆掉的大雄宝殿哪些来自于其他建筑而哪些又是后来新做的更不用说被允明禅师重建的大雄宝殿本身就是利用拆除后的一幢民居为建筑原料
乡土建筑的一大魅力就在于它创作中的自由性和追求物尽其用的特点这种重新组装的做法不但延续了原有建筑物的生命而且这种再创造本身就具有非常的意义
前殿大木雕饰所采用的题材都明显带有当地祠堂建筑的痕迹
两个中榀檐柱的牛腿上就雕有当地祠堂建筑中通常采用的狮子戏球
牛腿上向各个方向飞扬伸展的叠拱和插叶所采用的卷草图案也和世远公祠里的非常相似
前殿里最有特点的部分还要算天花
这里建筑的梁架通常是露明的但是前殿的中榀的两个金柱中间却有天花天花中间还形成一个八面锥体的藻井
藻井正中绘有盘龙八个面上不但绘有如来佛弥勒佛观音太上老君还有西游记里的四个主要人物
四周的天花上则画满西游记中的一些主要故事情节
在这几米见方的二维画板上已经完全看不到佛教道教与世俗尘世之间的任何界限
前殿的屋面应该是新的但在这里人神之间的界限也是模糊的
垂脊的末端各有一尊小的雕像前面分别是哪吒托塔李天王后面则是两名天兵天将
胡公庙大殿是一个用钢筋混凝土做支撑结构的两层高建筑坐落在一个半米多高的基础上俨然一副官式建筑的气派
大殿正中有一个两米多高玉皇大帝扮相的胡公正襟端坐在一个一米多高的须弥座上他略微低头审视着跪倒在他面前的虔诚香客
依照惯例这尊胡公是吃荤的也就是说三牲之类的供品都会摆放在须弥座前面的香案上
胡公的头顶上也有一个半球形的藻井上面绘着龙和凤
硕大的一个殿堂只有一尊塑像在中间平时显得空荡荡的但是在庙会期间据说就会挤得水泄不通
最后一进殿是屏风阁现存建筑基本上是清道光二十九年1849年那场大火之后重建的
允明禅师说重建的时候一些主要构件改用石材以防火灾
到清朝末年寺院变得十分不景气原本的八房僧人也只剩下了四房每房的人数也少了许多
有人说是因为狮子石子的谐音吃人所以在宣统年间1909-1911屏风阁又改回了木构
屏风阁也是利用天然岩洞建造的但是它和罗汉洞或五峰书院有着根本的不同
屏风阁的建筑空间不但延伸到了石洞以外而且还利用石洞上的巨石作为楼板在上面加建了二层
允明禅师说二层以前供的是玉皇大帝直到宣统二年1910年才把玉皇大帝移到了现在的地藏殿
屏风阁一二层之间没有任何垂直的联系像搬佛像这样大的变故可能只有在重建或大修的时候才可以进行
把这种可望而不可即的位置留给玉皇大帝本是无可厚非但是在佛家圣地的正殿里高高供奉道教的众神之皇这不得不归功于中国式宗教无与伦比的博大和宽容
屏风阁和它前面殿堂之间的空间比较小再加上这里总是烟雾缭绕所以很难看清它的全貌
屏风阁正面原本有墙香客通过左右两侧的拱形门洞进出
院墙和凹字形的建筑围合了一个小院院内靠墙的一侧有香炉
后来因为香客太多香炉离建筑太近有火灾隐患所以拆除了围墙
现在从屏风阁前面的铺地上还可以清楚地看到墙基和门的位置
屏风阁的大木雕饰奢华精美到了极点
由于一层屋檐有两根挑檐枋承托所以又多了许多可以用以雕饰的叠斗穿子雀替垂花等构件
抬头审视檐下柱头的这一圈眼睛找不到可以小憩的地方凤凰牡丹仙鹤神仙又一只凤凰
鎏了金的木雕在经历了几十年甚至上百年的烟熏之后没有了最初的那种浮华亮丽多了些凝重和斑驳
木雕中最抢眼的就是在两个中榀檐柱上的龙形牛腿
一条金龙盘旋在五彩的云海里头上顶着蜀柱龙身穿过檐柱又变成一条短梁用以连接后面的蜀柱短梁和两个梁托也都雕有云海的图案
屏风阁里面沿石洞内壁一共排列着大大小小的塑像二十三尊
正中间的一个当然是红面长须笑容可掬的胡公大帝他的两个儿子陪坐在两边后面是他的三个夫人
胡则原本只有两个夫人第三位只是猝死在胡公大帝面前的一位女香客人们见她如此虔诚便封她为胡公的第三任夫人
在胡公的右侧依次是关公龙王和平安菩萨左边则是文曲星婚姻美满神和财神
除了婚姻美满神是一对夫妻塑像以外其他每一个神仙和菩萨两边还配有侍从两人
这里可以满足人们生活中的一切所求不论是求财还是求雨求前程似锦还是求出入平安抑或是求家庭美满还是求功名利禄
就算是各路神仙都帮不了忙还可以求无所不能的胡公大帝
在每组神像前都有一个巨大的蜡烛台上面插满了高高低低的蜡烛胡公大帝面前的蜡烛更是多到看不见他的脸
在这黑黢黢的山洞里扑朔迷离的光影变化加上烟雾缭绕的视觉效果给诸神平添了些神秘的色彩
据允明禅师说自从把胡公从大雄宝殿请到屏风阁之后他的后面一直有如来文殊和普贤菩萨的三尊小塑像
人们在祭拜胡公大帝的同时其实是在求助如来佛祖的保佑
在香客眼里胡公大帝是无所不能的一方神祇在广慈寺眼里无所不能的仍旧是胡则后面的如来佛祖胡则只是能带给寺院旺盛人间香火的护法神
胡公庙里最抢人眼球的要算是在屏风阁前沿大殿后墙一字排开的十几名解签人
解签人都是六七十岁的老人一个个面露慈祥穿着也很干净体面
解签人每两个人用一张桌子桌子前面有一条长板凳留给香客坐
桌面正中中有一个细长的缝后面还立着一个付费自愿的小牌
偶尔香客少的时候解签人要么就一遍一遍地翻看着不知是哪天的报纸看完了还会在报纸的空白处用那种平头艺术钢笔认认真真一笔一顿地练字
中国人普遍认为字写得好的人一定有学问显然有学问的人解签准错不了
解签人给每个香客写的字不过十几个所以他们便更要精益求精一丝不苟
需要写的字总数不过几百个所以每一个解签人都能写一手好字
胡公签诗一共有一百签解签人讲上中下签各有三分之一
每一签都是一首七言绝句其中涉及的典故在时间上最迟到元末明初
据允明禅师讲签诗的创作者是文楼村程方峰的子孙兆亨公而文楼村程氏家谱中则记载为程兆选1724-1786
兆亨公和兆选公兄弟两人皆为进士又生活在同一个年代所以推测胡公签诗的形成时间可能是在清朝初年
签诗形成之初解签人基本上都是文楼村的程氏后人他们还不能进入广慈寺解签只能搬个小桌子在天街上等候香客
广慈寺虽然对此很不满意但是由于天街在明万历年间1573-1620就判归文楼村程氏所以他们对此也没有办法
民国初年解签诗摊二十余摊在后殿及观音堂每张铜元二枚
现在的解签人基本上都是老街上的程氏后人由于这份工作相对轻松收入又不错所以是人人都想做的美差
现在如果要做解签人不但要考试选拔还要根据水平定级

chapters.name: 第六章 五峰坳里的书院

sections.name: 一、寿山往事
sections.content_zh:
书院作为文教建筑的一种，是中国实行科举制度后的产物。科举制度开始于隋大业元年（605年），到清朝光绪三十一年（1905年）举行最后一科进士考试为止，是中国历代皇朝采用的取士制度。尽管科举制度有许多弊端和局限性，但是其最大意义就在于它给广大平民百姓提供了改变自己以至整个家族社会地位的唯一途径。于是乎，在科举制度实行的一千三百年里，中华大地上就出现了无以计数的学子，不计十年寒窗，孜孜苦读。相伴而来的，就是私塾、书院、书斋、文馆、文庙、文昌阁等文教建筑的广泛普及。

唐末至五代期间，战乱频繁导致官学衰败，所以许多读书人就避居山林，以模仿佛教、禅林的讲经制度创立书院。浙江境内始建于唐朝的书院，现知有五处，分别是象山蓬莱书院、诸暨溪山书院、龙游九峰书院、建德青山书院和绍兴丽正书院。这些书院通常是住宅的一部分，建筑形式也十分简朴。

宋代是书院林立的时代。在北宋期间书院多以讲学为主，而随着理学的发展，南宋的书院逐渐成为各学派活动的场所。书院作为一种正式的教育制度，几乎取代官学而成为当时主要的教育机关。浙江地区当时有书院三十余家，数量仅次于江西，居全国第二。

书院制度以及书院建筑在明、清两代又有了进一步的发展，但是已经逐渐从学者云集、自由讲学的私立书院，发展到受统治阶级控制的官学化书院。直至光绪二十七年（1901年），皇帝诏令各省的书院改为大学堂，各府、厅、直隶州的书院改为中学堂，各州县的书院改为小学堂，书院这种教育制度便退出了历史舞台。

寿山往事

在和尚、陈亮、县令、胡氏后人、国民党政府、还有我们这一行人进入寿山坑之前，坑里这五座山峰就已经屹立在那里了。有了这五座山峰，才有了美丽的传说和故事；再然后，才有了接下来所有的事情……

寿山在方岩北三里，有五峰皆石壁平地拔起，周围如城郭，曰固厚、曰瀑布、曰桃花、曰覆釜、曰鸡鸣。固厚之下有大石洞，高敞轩豁，可容千人……

瀑布之上有龙湫，水四时不竭，直下数十丈如练，及霁水杀，飘飘飏之，溅洒四出若雾雨然，可望而不可即，亦奇观也。

固厚峰，主峰也。悬崖千仞，峭壁如削，较诸峰为淳固深厚，故其名。其下石洞在焉。

瀑布峰，在固厚之右，上有飞泉下注……

覆釜峰，在瀑布之下，巅广而圆，如大釜覆其上。

桃花峰，与覆釜峰相连，专专耸妙，其岩色赤白相间，状类桃花……

鸡鸣峰，……午风微过，嘐然一声，彼唱此应，遂神其说耳……

天蜜，……悬崖直下，天风偶吹，大者如珠，细者如雾，其味甘美故名。

位于五峰之间、石洞之中、瀑布之下的这块世外桃源，终于在南北朝时期的梁普通元年（520年）迎来了它的第一位主人，即吃素念经的和尚们。固厚峰下有两个大石洞，上文中提到的是西边这个，靠东还有一个，叫外洞。这些出家人利用这两个天然的石洞创建了永康县境内的第一座寺院——桃岩寺，并于日后改名为寿山寺。关于寿山寺的具体情况已经无从查证，只知道固厚峰下的这个山洞里曾经有过一个罗汉堂，里面的罗汉还是在明朝为建造五峰书院时撤掉的；外洞"之前有台三层，甚壮伟"，猜想或许是大雄宝殿的位置。据《库川胡氏宗谱》中关于一场官司的记录，"寿山寺自正德以前无论已"，那三层的高台也在"明万历间始圮"。

到了南宋乾道八年（1172年），永康人陈亮（1143—1195年）开始在寿山坑里设帐授学，宣讲他的"商籍农而立，农赖商而行"、"义利双行"和"各务其实"等有悖于传统儒学和经学的新思想。在接下去的两三年中，陈亮的挚友吕祖谦（1137—1181年），即事功学派下金华学派的创始人，也曾来这里讲学。宋淳熙九年（1182年）秋，刚刚上任一年的浙东提举朱熹（1130—1200年）回访陈亮于五峰。这是朱熹与陈亮的第二次会面，第一次是在这年正月，朱熹来婺州赈灾，陈亮赶去相见，并与朱熹畅谈十日。第二次会面的盛况在《五峰书院志》中略有记载，陈亮"请晦翁主讲席，从游者数百人"。相传固厚峰下外洞岩壁上的"兜率台"三个朱砂大字就是朱熹当时题写的。这里的"兜率"二字同"兜率天"，为梵语音译，代表佛教中的第四层天，这层天的内院是弥勒菩萨的净土，外院是天上众生所居之处；"台"应该指的是当时在这里的三层高台。宋绍熙四年（1193年），年已五十一岁的陈亮金榜题名中了状元，却不幸在一年多后死在赴任的途中。在这以后，我们无从查证寿山坑里是否依然回荡有士大夫高亢的辩论；或是仅留下与晨钟暮鼓相伴的木鱼声；还是一切都静了下来，只听得见水激顽石和风吹树叶的声音。
sections.content_en:
Academies, as a type of cultural-educational architecture, were a product of China after the implementation of the imperial examination system. The imperial examination system began in the first year of Sui Daye (605) and lasted until the last jinshi examination was held in the thirty-first year of Qing Guangxu (1905), serving as the scholar-selection system adopted by successive Chinese dynasties. Although the imperial examination system had many drawbacks and limitations, its greatest significance was that it provided the broad common people with the only path to change their own and even their entire family's social status. Thus, during the thirteen hundred years the imperial examination system was in practice, countless scholars appeared on the land of China, studying diligently regardless of ten years of cold window hardship. Accompanying this was the widespread普及 of cultural-educational architecture such as private schools, academies, study studios, literary halls, Confucian temples, and Wenchang pavilions.

During the late Tang to Five Dynasties period, frequent warfare led to the decline of official schools, so many scholars retreated to mountain forests and established academies by imitating the Buddhist and Chan forest scripture-lecturing systems. There are currently five known academies in Zhejiang that were first built in the Tang Dynasty: Xiangshan Penglai Academy, Zhuji Xishan Academy, Longyou Jiufeng Academy, Jiande Qingshan Academy, and Shaoxing Lizheng Academy. These academies were usually part of residences, with very simple architectural forms.

The Song Dynasty was an era of numerous academies. During the Northern Song, academies were mainly for lecturing; with the development of Neo-Confucianism, Southern Song academies gradually became venues for various schools of thought. As a formal educational system, academies almost replaced official schools as the main educational institutions of the time. There were over thirty academies in the Zhejiang region at that time, second only to Jiangxi in number, ranking second nationwide.

The academy system and academy architecture further developed in the Ming and Qing dynasties, but gradually evolved from private academies with gathered scholars and free lecturing into official-style academies controlled by the ruling class. It was not until the twenty-seventh year of Guangxu (1901) that the emperor ordered provincial academies to be changed to university halls, prefectural, sub-prefectural, and directly-administered department academies to middle school halls, and county academies to primary school halls, at which point the academy as an educational system exited the historical stage.

Shoushan Past Events

Before monks, Chen Liang, county magistrates, Hu descendants, the Nationalist government, and our group entered Shoushan Ravine, the five peaks in the ravine had already stood there. With these five peaks came beautiful legends and stories; and then came everything that followed...

Shoushan is three li north of Fangyan, with five peaks all of stone cliffs rising abruptly from the plain, surrounding like city walls: called Guhou (Solid-Thick), Pubu (Waterfall), Taohua (Peach Blossom), Fufu (Covered-Cauldron), and Jiming (Rooster-Crowing). Below Guhou is a large stone cave, high and spacious, capable of holding a thousand people...

Above the waterfall is Longqiu (Dragon Pool), with water never exhausted in all four seasons, plunging straight down several dozen zhang like white silk; when the water lessens after rain, it flutters and sprinkles in all directions like mist and rain, visible but unreachable—also a marvelous sight.

Guhou Peak is the main peak. With thousand-ren cliffs and sheer walls like cut, it is more solid and thick than the other peaks, hence its name. The stone cave is below it.

Pubu Peak, to the right of Guhou, has a flying spring pouring down from above...

Fufu Peak, below the waterfall, has a broad and round summit like a large cauldron overturned above it.

Taohua Peak, connected to Fufu Peak, stands uniquely graceful, with its rock colors alternating red and white, resembling peach blossoms...

Jiming Peak... when the noon wind passes gently, with a crowing sound, one calls and another responds, thus the legend was deified...

Tianmi (Heavenly Honey)... from the cliff it falls straight down, blown occasionally by the heavenly wind, large as pearls, fine as mist, sweet and delicious in taste, hence the name.

This paradise located between the five peaks, within the stone caves, and below the waterfall finally welcomed its first masters in the first year of Liang Putong (520) during the Northern and Southern Dynasties: vegetarian, scripture-reciting monks. Below Guhou Peak are two large stone caves; the one mentioned above is the western one, and there is another to the east called the Outer Cave. These monastics used these two natural stone caves to establish the first Buddhist temple in Yongkang County—Taoyan Temple, later renamed Shoushan Temple. The specific circumstances of Shoushan Temple can no longer be verified; we only know that there was once an Arhat Hall in the cave below Guhou Peak, and the Arhats inside were removed when the Wufeng Academy was built in the Ming Dynasty; the Outer Cave "previously had a three-tier platform, very grand and magnificent," conjectured to perhaps be the location of the Mahavira Hall. According to a record of a lawsuit in the "Kuchuan Hu Family Genealogy," "Shoushan Temple before Zhengde is no longer discussed," and that three-tier high platform also "began to collapse during the Ming Wanli period."

In the eighth year of Southern Song Qiandao (1172), Chen Liang (1143-1195), a native of Yongkang, began setting up tents to teach in Shoushan Ravine, propagating his new ideas such as "commerce stands on agriculture, agriculture relies on commerce," "righteousness and profit go together," and "each attends to reality," which contradicted traditional Confucianism and classical studies. In the following two or three years, Chen Liang's close friend Lü Zuqian (1137-1181), founder of the Jinhua School under the School of Statecraft, also came here to lecture. In the autumn of the ninth year of Chunxi (1182), Zhu Xi (1130-1200), who had just taken office as Eastern Zhejiang Commissioner one year earlier, visited Chen Liang at Wufeng. This was the second meeting between Zhu Xi and Chen Liang; the first was in the first month of that year, when Zhu Xi came to Wuzhou for disaster relief and Chen Liang rushed to meet him, talking with Zhu Xi for ten days. The grand occasion of the second meeting is briefly recorded in the "Wufeng Academy Gazetteer": Chen Liang "invited Huiweng (Zhu Xi) to lecture, with several hundred followers." It is said that the three cinnabar characters "Doushuai Terrace" on the rock wall of the Outer Cave below Guhou Peak were written by Zhu Xi at that time. The word "Doushuai" here is the same as "Tusita Heaven," a Sanskrit transliteration representing the fourth heaven in Buddhism; the inner court of this heaven is the pure land of Maitreya Bodhisattva, and the outer court is where heavenly beings dwell; "Terrace" should refer to the three-tier high platform that was here at that time. In the fourth year of Shaoxi (1193), Chen Liang, already fifty-one years old, passed the examination as zhuangyuan (first-place jinshi), but unfortunately died over a year later on his way to take office. After this, we cannot verify whether the ravine still echoed with the heated debates of scholar-officials; or only left the sound of wooden fish accompanying morning bells and evening drums; or whether everything fell silent, with only the sound of water striking stubborn stones and wind blowing leaves audible.
key_terms: 书院作为文教建筑的一种是中国实行科举制度后的产物
科举制度开始于隋大业元年605年到清朝光绪三十一年1905年举行最后一科进士考试为止是中国历代皇朝采用的取士制度
科举制度最大意义就在于它给广大平民百姓提供了改变自己以至整个家族社会地位的唯一途径
在科举制度实行的一千三百年里中华大地上就出现了无以计数的学子不计十年寒窗孜孜苦读
相伴而来的就是私塾书院书斋文馆文庙文昌阁等文教建筑的广泛普及
唐末至五代期间战乱频繁导致官学衰败所以许多读书人就避居山林以模仿佛教禅林的讲经制度创立书院
浙江境内始建于唐朝的书院现知有五处分别是象山蓬莱书院诸暨溪山书院龙游九峰书院建德青山书院和绍兴丽正书院
这些书院通常是住宅的一部分建筑形式也十分简朴
宋代是书院林立的时代
北宋期间书院多以讲学为主而随着理学的发展南宋的书院逐渐成为各学派活动的场所
书院作为一种正式的教育制度几乎取代官学而成为当时主要的教育机关
浙江地区当时有书院三十余家数量仅次于江西居全国第二
书院制度以及书院建筑在明清两代又有了进一步的发展但是已经逐渐从学者云集自由讲学的私立书院发展到受统治阶级控制的官学化书院
光绪二十七年1901年皇帝诏令各省的书院改为大学堂各府厅直隶州的书院改为中学堂各州县的书院改为小学堂书院这种教育制度便退出了历史舞台
在和尚陈亮县令胡氏后人国民党政府还有我们这一行人进入寿山坑之前坑里这五座山峰就已经屹立在那里了
有了这五座山峰才有了美丽的传说和故事再然后才有了接下来所有的事情
寿山在方岩北三里有五峰皆石壁平地拔起周围如城郭曰固厚曰瀑布曰桃花曰覆釜曰鸡鸣
固厚之下有大石洞高敞轩豁可容千人
瀑布之上有龙湫水四时不竭直下数十丈如练及霁水杀飘飘飏之溅洒四出若雾雨然可望而不可即亦奇观也
固厚峰主峰也悬崖千仞峭壁如削较诸峰为淳固深厚故其名其下石洞在焉
瀑布峰在固厚之右上有飞泉下注
覆釜峰在瀑布之下巅广而圆如大釜覆其上
桃花峰与覆釜峰相连专专耸妙其岩色赤白相间状类桃花
鸡鸣峰午风微过嘐然一声彼唱此应遂神其说耳
天蜜悬崖直下天风偶吹大者如珠细者如雾其味甘美故名
位于五峰之间石洞之中瀑布之下的这块世外桃源终于在南北朝时期的梁普通元年520年迎来了它的第一位主人即吃素念经的和尚们
固厚峰下有两个大石洞上文中提到的是西边这个靠东还有一个叫外洞
这些出家人利用这两个天然的石洞创建了永康县境内的第一座寺院桃岩寺并于日后改名为寿山寺
固厚峰下的这个山洞里曾经有过一个罗汉堂里面的罗汉还是在明朝为建造五峰书院时撤掉的
外洞之前有台三层甚壮伟猜想或许是大雄宝殿的位置
据库川胡氏宗谱中关于一场官司的记录寿山寺自正德以前无论已那三层的高台也在明万历间始圮
南宋乾道八年1172年永康人陈亮1143-1195开始在寿山坑里设帐授学宣讲他的商籍农而立农赖商而行义利双行和各务其实等有悖于传统儒学和经学的新思想
陈亮的挚友吕祖谦1137-1181即事功学派下金华学派的创始人也曾来这里讲学
宋淳熙九年1182年秋刚刚上任一年的浙东提举朱熹1130-1200回访陈亮于五峰
这是朱熹与陈亮的第二次会面第一次是在这年正月朱熹来婺州赈灾陈亮赶去相见并与朱熹畅谈十日
第二次会面的盛况在五峰书院志中略有记载陈亮请晦翁主讲席从游者数百人
相传固厚峰下外洞岩壁上的兜率台三个朱砂大字就是朱熹当时题写的
兜率二字同兜率天为梵语音译代表佛教中的第四层天这层天的内院是弥勒菩萨的净土外院是天上众生所居之处台应该指的是当时在这里的三层高台
宋绍熙四年1193年年已五十一岁的陈亮金榜题名中了状元却不幸在一年多后死在赴任的途中
在这以后无从查证寿山坑里是否依然回荡有士大夫高亢的辩论或是仅留下与晨钟暮鼓相伴的木鱼声还是一切都静了下来只听得见水激顽石和风吹树叶的声音

sections.name: 二、五峰书院
sections.content_zh:
书院历史

再次找到有关于寿山坑的文字记载，已经到明正德年间（1506—1521年）。

尚宝丞应典，周视壁上有龙川书（今遍观壁上，但有时少章记龙川书，或在兜率台上，然无登览矣），志晦翁、东莱行迹，乃即堂东偏之隙建祠，以祀朱、吕、及张南轩、陆象山，而龙川配焉，曰丽泽祠。

丽泽祠，正德间应石门先生建，太守张公钺题此额，嗣守姚公文炤记……

应典字天彝，号石门，浙江永康芝英人，明正德（1506—1521年）九年（1514年）进士，曾任丽泽书院和白鹿书院山长。这也就是说丽泽祠应该建于1514年到1521年之间。这里的朱、吕、张指的是朱熹、吕祖谦和张栻，在宋乾道、淳熙时期（1165—1189年），他们三人被并称为"东南三贤"。除了这三个人之外，还以陆九渊和陈亮配祭。

"丽泽"这个名字，可能取自于位于金华明招山的丽泽书院。丽泽书院原名丽泽堂，为吕祖谦在宋乾道初年（约1165—1166年）创建。书院前有两个湖泊，而"丽泽"的原意为两个沼泽相连，所以恰到好处。更重要的是，《易·兑》中写道，"丽泽，兑。君子以朋友讲习"。由此可见，"丽泽"之意深远，朱熹还曾经做过如下的评价，"两泽相丽，互相滋益，朋友讲习，其象如此"。

十几年之后，丽泽祠东侧又建造了一幢规模稍大的建筑，取名为"桃岩丽泽精舍"。当时的永康知县洪坦写道，"嘉靖癸巳秋，余偕虚谷姚公访石门子于岩，览遗迹名胜，作而叹曰：……朱子欲屋之而未成，盖有所待也，乃命耆老吕瑗购材兴工，因其中岩下为楼数间，以广来学者，犹欲知先人丽泽之义，即名桃岩丽泽精舍"。嘉靖十五年（1536年），桃岩丽泽精舍建成，并改名为"五峰书院"。"五峰书院，嘉靖丙申太守姚公命耆老吕瑗建，原名桃岩丽泽精舍。邑侯洪坦记，嗣守陈公京书。"相比丽泽祠要盖在"堂东偏之隙"，桃岩丽泽精舍的建造则是以"撤去阿罗汉象"为代价的。

明末，永康学者周佑德在丽泽祠西侧又建造了一幢与丽泽祠规模相当，也是三间两层的建筑，取名为"学易斋"。

书院活动

在明朝最后的一百年里，有许多著名的学者都曾在五峰书院讲学，其中包括尚宝丞应典、江西抚州教授周桐、著名学者卢可久、周莹、应玠等人。这其中还有与岩下程氏同祖的三位程氏后人，他们是吏部左侍郎程文德（1497—1559年）、四川左布政程正谊（1531—1610年）和他的父亲程梓（1498—1585年）。来讲学的人大都是王阳明的弟子，讲习内容以倡导"致良知"学说为主，同时也包括"正心诚意"和程朱理学的部分内容。五峰书院在这段时间培养了许多优秀的人才，其中包括三十多位进士。

五峰书院除了"广来学者"和提供讲学场所之外，祭祀活动也是很重要的一个功能。丽泽祠创建之初共祀五人，但是程文德、应延育、周桐以陆九渊和张栻从未到过五峰为缘由，改仅祀朱熹、吕祖谦和陈亮三人。五峰书院则主祀"阳明王文成公；配祀石门应先生，方峰程先生"。学易斋的建造原本就是以纪念婺州学者何基、王柏、金履祥、许谦和章懋为初衷的。除了这五人之外，学易斋里还先后共配祀二十三人，其中不仅包括曾来五峰书院讲学的周桐、周莹等著名学者，还有程銈等当地乡绅。

随着五峰书院的名气越来越大，来赐额题联的名人也越来越多。清康熙二十二年（1683年），永康知县姬肇燕赐额"阐明理学"。乾隆四十五年（1780年），永康太平吕大宗祠和程、应、卢三姓后裔共同出资，重修五峰书院的三幢建筑，并请提督学使彭元瑞赐匾。次年一月彭元瑞亲自书写"丽泽如新"匾额。文楼村的程氏进士们也先后多次题写对联，例如"五峰书院"这幢建筑中就挂有程兆选题写的"学则数言矩矱遥承鹿洞；心传一脉渊源近溯姚江"，还有《五峰书院志》的作者程尚斐题写的"学术启良知，恍示鸢飞鱼跃；讲堂开胜地，何殊鹿洞鹅湖"。

进入清代中后期，讲学的气氛日渐衰退，每年的春秋两会便成了五峰书院最隆重的事情。会期各三天，届时前来讲学、奉祀的地方官绅多达数百人，其盛况不亚于朱熹来这里讲学的日子。关于"春会"的时间，《五峰书院志》里并没有提到，依惯例或许是在清明；秋天则在阴历九月初九，"每岁重阳日，祀朱、吕、陈三子，次日祀阳明王子，三日祀何、王、金、许诸儒"。关于祭祀的费用，则来自于应典、程梓和卢可久三人创置的会田，并由应、程、卢的后人负责料理会田和组织祭祀活动。会田创立之后，陈亮、程文德、王柏和吕祖谦的后人也相继捐出了部分田地。但是由于会田的收入还要支付日常开销，以及建筑修缮的费用，所以依旧入不敷出。清康熙二十年（1681年），五峰书院不得不取消春会，并把秋会祭祀的时间改为阴历九月十二、十三两日。五峰书院"秋会"不仅包括启龛、迎神、读祝文、献礼、献饭等通常意义上的祭祀活动，更是各路学者交流和学习的绝好机会。为此会规里有明确的规定，"十二日早膳后各出质言以相参证，其式正楷大书，登名于尾。凡与会者各带纸笔，午后互相抄录完时，实粘壁上。十三日早膳后，老成者各拈书一章，性理一章。三日内余功，或质疑问难、或阐发格言，言具登载于簿"。五峰书院"秋会"基本每年举行，一直由应、程、卢的后人负责，直到民国时期停办。

书院建筑

五峰书院的三幢建筑均位于固厚峰下能容千人的大石洞内，面南自东向西一字排开，均为三开间两层楼宇。其建筑的最大特点就是"即洞支木为之，不施椽瓦而雨雪霜露自然莫及"。丽泽祠的建造者应典还给这个山洞起名为"朝阳洞"，因为"朝日初出，苍苍凉凉，光射户牖"。

最东边的是"五峰书院"，其平面接近方形，一层有廊，二层有栏以供凭眺。虽然屡经修缮，但是梁架结构并没有改变，所以仍然可以看到明代建筑的特点，例如梁架采用穿斗式，横梁不加装饰，梁下采用丁头拱，使用有覆盆的鼓形柱础等。建筑东墙外有一间小室，曾作为厨房。

丽泽祠和学易斋规模相当，都是进深较短的长方形平面，只是丽泽祠一层有廊。在门窗的处理上，学易斋和五峰书院较为类似，都是步步锦，丽泽祠则采用较为简单的"满天星"样式。
sections.content_en:
Academy History

The next written record about Shoushan Ravine dates to the Ming Zhengde period (1506-1521).

Shangbaocheng (Keeper of the Imperial Seal) Ying Dian, observing the Longchuan (Chen Liang) calligraphy on the walls (now observing all walls, but sometimes finding few records of Longchuan's calligraphy, or on the Doushuai Terrace, yet no place to climb and view), remembering the traces of Huiweng (Zhu Xi) and Donglai (Lü Zuqian), then built a shrine in the gap east of the hall to worship Zhu, Lü, Zhang Nanxuan (Zhang Shi), and Lu Xiangshan (Lu Jiuyuan), with Longchuan (Chen Liang) as a companion sacrifice, called Lize Shrine.

Lize Shrine was built by Mr. Ying Shimen during the Zhengde period; Prefect Zhang Yue inscribed this plaque, and subsequent Prefect Yao Wenzhao wrote a record...

Ying Dian, courtesy name Tianyi, art name Shimen, a native of Zhiying, Yongkang, Zhejiang, became a jinshi in the ninth year of Ming Zhengde (1514), and served as head of Lize Academy and White Deer Academy. This means Lize Shrine should have been built between 1514 and 1521. The Zhu, Lü, and Zhang here refer to Zhu Xi, Lü Zuqian, and Zhang Shi; during the Song Qiandao and Chunxi periods (1165-1189), these three were collectively called the "Three Sages of the Southeast." Besides these three, Lu Jiuyuan and Chen Liang were also worshipped as companion sacrifices.

The name "Lize" may have been taken from Lize Academy located at Mingzhao Mountain in Jinhua. Lize Academy was originally named Lize Hall, founded by Lü Zuqian in the early years of Song Qiandao (c. 1165-1166). In front of the academy were two lakes, and the original meaning of "Lize" is two marshes connected, hence perfectly appropriate. More importantly, the "I Ching · Dui" states, "Lize, Dui. The superior man uses it for friends to discuss and practice." This shows the profound meaning of "Lize"; Zhu Xi once made the following evaluation, "Two marshes adjoining, mutually nourishing and benefiting, friends discussing and practicing—such is its image."

Over a decade later, a slightly larger building was constructed east of Lize Shrine, named "Taoyan Lize Jingshe" (Taoyan Lize Retreat). The then Yongkang County Magistrate Hong Tan wrote, "In the autumn of Jiajing Guisi (1533), I accompanied Mr. Yao Xugu to visit Shimenzi at the rock, viewing relics and scenic spots, and sighed: ... Zhu Xi wanted to build a house but did not complete it, perhaps waiting for something; then ordered elder Lü Yuan to purchase materials and start construction, building several rooms under the middle rock to welcome scholars, still wishing people to know the meaning of their ancestors' Lize, hence named Taoyan Lize Jingshe." In the fifteenth year of Jiajing (1536), Taoyan Lize Jingshe was completed and renamed "Wufeng Academy." "Wufeng Academy, built by elder Lü Yuan under the order of Prefect Yao in Jiajing Bingshen (1536), originally named Taoyan Lize Jingshe. Recorded by County Magistrate Hong Tan, calligraphy by subsequent Prefect Chen Jing." Compared to Lize Shrine, which had to be built in the "gap east of the hall," the construction of Taoyan Lize Jingshe came at the cost of "removing the Arhat statues."

In the late Ming, Yongkang scholar Zhou Youde built another building west of Lize Shrine, comparable in scale to Lize Shrine and also three bays and two stories, named "Xueyi Zhai" (Study of the Changes).

Academy Activities

During the last hundred years of the Ming Dynasty, many famous scholars lectured at Wufeng Academy, including Shangbaocheng Ying Dian, Jiangxi Fuzhou Professor Zhou Tong, famous scholars Lu Kejiu, Zhou Ying, and Ying Jie. Among them were three Cheng descendants sharing the same ancestor as the Yanxia Cheng family:吏部 Left Vice Minister Cheng Wende (1497-1559), Sichuan Left Administrative Commissioner Cheng Zhengyi (1531-1610), and his father Cheng Zi (1498-1585). Those who came to lecture were mostly disciples of Wang Yangming, with lecture content primarily advocating the doctrine of "innate knowledge" (zhi liangzhi), while also including "making the mind sincere and thoughts correct" and parts of Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism. During this period, Wufeng Academy cultivated many outstanding talents, including over thirty jinshi.

Besides "welcoming scholars" and providing a venue for lectures, sacrificial activities were also a very important function of Wufeng Academy. At its founding, Lize Shrine worshipped five people, but Cheng Wende, Ying Yanyu, and Zhou Tong, citing that Lu Jiuyuan and Zhang Shi had never been to Wufeng, changed it to worship only Zhu Xi, Lü Zuqian, and Chen Liang. Wufeng Academy primarily worshipped "Yangming Wang Wencheng Gong (Wang Yangming); with companion sacrifices to Shimen Mr. Ying (Ying Dian) and Fangfeng Mr. Cheng (Cheng Fangfeng)." The construction of Xueyi Zhai was originally intended to commemorate Wuzhou scholars He Ji, Wang Bai, Jin Lüxiang, Xu Qian, and Zhang Mao. Besides these five, Xueyi Zhai also successively had twenty-three companion sacrifices, including not only famous scholars such as Zhou Tong and Zhou Ying who had lectured at Wufeng Academy, but also local gentry such as Cheng Ji.

As Wufeng Academy's fame grew, more and more famous people came to grant plaques and write couplets. In the twenty-second year of Qing Kangxi (1683), Yongkang County Magistrate Ji Zhaoyan granted the plaque "Elucidating Neo-Confucianism." In the forty-fifth year of Qianlong (1780), the Yongkang Taiping Lü Great Ancestral Hall and the descendants of the Cheng, Ying, and Lu families jointly funded the renovation of the three buildings of Wufeng Academy, and requested Education Commissioner Peng Yuanrui to grant a plaque. The following January, Peng Yuanrui personally wrote the plaque "Lize as New." The Cheng jinshi of Wenlou Village also successively wrote couplets multiple times; for example, the "Wufeng Academy" building hangs a couplet by Cheng Zhaoxuan: "Learning follows few words, standards remotely inherit Lu Dong; mind transmits one lineage, origins trace back to Yao Jiang." There is also a couplet by Cheng Shangfei, author of the "Wufeng Academy Gazetteer": "Learning initiates innate knowledge, vaguely showing kites flying and fish leaping; lecture hall opens on sacred ground, no different from Lu Dong and Ehu."

Entering the mid-to-late Qing Dynasty, the atmosphere of lecturing gradually declined, and the annual spring and autumn assemblies became the most solemn events at Wufeng Academy. Each assembly lasted three days, with hundreds of local officials and gentry coming to lecture and worship, its grandeur no less than the days when Zhu Xi came to lecture. Regarding the time of the "spring assembly," the "Wufeng Academy Gazetteer" does not mention it; by convention it may have been at Qingming. The autumn assembly was on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month: "Every year on Double Ninth, worship Zhu, Lü, and Chen; the next day worship Yangming Wang; the third day worship He, Wang, Jin, and Xu scholars." The cost of sacrifices came from the "assembly fields" established by Ying Dian, Cheng Zi, and Lu Kejiu, with the descendants of Ying, Cheng, and Lu responsible for managing the fields and organizing sacrificial activities. After the assembly fields were established, the descendants of Chen Liang, Cheng Wende, Wang Bai, and Lü Zuqian also successively donated some fields. However, because the income from the assembly fields also had to cover daily expenses and building renovation costs, it still fell short of expenditures. In the twentieth year of Kangxi (1681), Wufeng Academy had to cancel the spring assembly and change the autumn assembly sacrifice time to the twelfth and thirteenth days of the ninth lunar month. Wufeng Academy's "autumn assembly" included not only ordinary sacrificial activities such as opening shrines, welcoming deities, reading congratulatory texts, presenting gifts, and offering meals, but was also an excellent opportunity for scholars of all schools to exchange and learn. To this end, the assembly rules had clear provisions: "On the twelfth day after breakfast, each presents substantive remarks for mutual verification, in formal regular script, with name signed at the end. All participants bring paper and brush; after mutual copying in the afternoon, paste on the wall. On the thirteenth day after breakfast, elders each select a chapter of a book and a chapter of nature-principle. Within three days, remaining time may be for questioning difficulties or expounding maxims, all recorded in the register." Wufeng Academy's "autumn assembly" was basically held annually, always managed by the descendants of Ying, Cheng, and Lu, until it was discontinued during the Republic period.

Academy Architecture

The three buildings of Wufeng Academy are all located in the large stone cave below Guhou Peak that can hold a thousand people, facing south and lined up from east to west, all three-bay two-story buildings. The greatest feature of their architecture is that "wood is supported directly in the cave, without rafters or tiles, yet rain, snow, frost, and dew naturally cannot reach." Ying Dian, builder of Lize Shrine, also named this cave "Chaoyang Cave" (Morning Sun Cave), because "when the morning sun first emerges, cool and green, light shines through the windows."

The easternmost is "Wufeng Academy," with a nearly square plane, corridors on the first floor, and railings on the second floor for leaning and viewing. Although repeatedly renovated, the beam-frame structure has not changed, so Ming Dynasty architectural features can still be seen, such as the column-and-tie (chuandou) beam frame, unadorned cross beams, dingtou brackets under beams, and drum-shaped column bases with inverted basins. There is a small room outside the east wall of the building, once used as a kitchen.

Lize Shrine and Xueyi Zhai are comparable in scale, both rectangular planes with shorter depth, except Lize Shrine has corridors on the first floor. In door and window treatment, Xueyi Zhai and Wufeng Academy are similar, both using "step-by-step brocade" (bubujin) lattice, while Lize Shrine uses the simpler "sky full of stars" (mantianxing) pattern.

sections.name: 三、胡公家庙
sections.content_zh:
来龙去脉

五峰书院东边不远就是外洞，"此寿山寺旧刹也，今为胡公庙"。据《库川胡氏宗谱》记载，寿山寺在明正德（1506—1521年）以前就已经名存实亡，十多年后为了盖桃岩丽泽精舍又移走了洞里的罗汉像。

到了"嘉靖三十七年（1558年），奉例清查寿山废寺产业，买价入官"，一个叫徐一勤的人用五十一两白银买下了寿山坑里的五十七亩田、二十一亩多的地、十八亩多的山林和近九亩的塘。四年之后，胡氏的后人以寿山为"祖墓所在"，并且"寿山寺虽久废，所存田地山场等业系故祖胡士胜舍助，却被异姓官买"为由，开始了一场长达十八年之久的官司。这块田地山塘在这期间又被转手多次，从徐家转到程家，再从程家转到吕家，最终胡氏在万历八年（1580年）十一月，以一百九十两赎回。

万历三十六年（1608年），库川胡氏后人聚集在寿山坑里，决定利用洞口原有三层高台的基础建造一个"胡公家庙"。或许是广慈寺害怕这个"正宗"的胡公会抢了自己的香火，或许老街上的程氏也担心这个半路"杀"出来的胡公家庙会让老街从此变得萧条，于是一个叫如昌的僧人便把胡氏告上了公堂。从以程氏代管山林的"一审"结果来看，程氏应该也是这场官司的幕后支持或是怂恿者。胡氏当然不服，把官司告上了金华府，"二审"结果虽然保住了胡氏的田地山塘，但是建胡公家庙这件事，还是维持原判。原因是"方岩有像，四方香火供奉……寿山去彼一里许，又安得重建祠宇耶……惟将寿山新建未成者拆毁……"。

经过这次教训之后，远在胡库的胡氏似乎明白了要想在寿山坑站稳脚跟，就要讨好邻山广慈寺的道理，于是在清顺治十一年（1654年），胡氏慷慨资助广慈寺修理前厅。随后，在康熙二十二年（1683年），寿山坑里的胡公家庙就建成了。康熙四十一年（1702年），胡氏又捐田助寺。在这之后的一百多年里，胡氏不仅多次资助广慈寺翻修大殿，双方还协定"方岩祭礼约"。这种友好的关系一直延续到1840年，在程氏的介入下双方再次对簿公堂。虽然胡氏胜诉，但是广慈寺"于道光二十九年（1849年）九月初四合庙并僧房尽皆同禄"，胡氏认为这是天意，决定从此放弃方岩大殿，仅去寿山祭祀。

建筑

民国23年（1934年），胡氏在当时永康罗骏超的建议下开始筹划重建胡公家庙。重建工程自1935年始，至1937年完工，于是就有了今天矗立在固厚峰下的"重楼"。

新建成的胡公家庙坐落在一个用石材垒砌的高大基座上，基座东西两侧的地面高差有一层多高。它的一层有五间，二层、三层原本各三间。三层利用岩壁围合空间，岩壁上"兜率台"三个大字清晰可见。建筑一层和三层进深较浅，二层不但空间高，而且进深为前后二进，一直深入洞中。重楼在结构上采用砖木混合形式，外立面用砖墙做竖向承重结构，辅以木梁和木质门窗，内部做法比较传统，以木构为主。建筑式样上则明显受到"新时代"的影响，东侧入口处为砖砌发券，西洋式小门楼，二层三层栏杆的做法也显然是机器加工的产品。

民国27年（1938年），浙江省政府迁至方岩临时办公，其中财政厅进驻胡公家庙的二层和三层。例如因房间不够，二层两侧便被各增加一间；为解决采光的问题，所有的门窗还被装上了玻璃。国民政府进驻期间，胡公家庙还得匾"春帆楼"，省政府主席黄绍竑还亲自题联"庙貌壮灵岩，历宋元明清，史册相传，会栋宇更新，欣兹后起多才争辉谱谍；官廨邻胜境，仰聪明正直，风微若接，待湖山重整，好与斯邦父母共荐馨香"。
sections.content_en:
Origins and Development

Not far east of Wufeng Academy is the Outer Cave: "This was the old temple of Shoushan Temple, now Hugong Temple." According to the "Kuchuan Hu Family Genealogy," Shoushan Temple had already existed in name only before the Ming Zhengde period (1506-1521), and over a decade later, the Arhat statues in the cave were moved away to build Taoyan Lize Jingshe.

By "the thirty-seventh year of Jiajing (1558), following regulations to investigate the property of the abandoned Shoushan Temple, the purchase price was paid to the government," a man named Xu Yiqin bought fifty-seven mu of fields, over twenty-one mu of land, over eighteen mu of mountain forest, and nearly nine mu of ponds in Shoushan Ravine for fifty-one taels of silver. Four years later, the Hu descendants, citing that Shoushan was "where ancestral tombs are located" and that "although Shoushan Temple has long been abandoned, the remaining fields, land, and mountain properties were donated by their ancestor Hu Shisheng, yet were purchased by officials of other surnames," began a lawsuit that lasted eighteen years. During this period, the fields, land, mountains, and ponds changed hands multiple times—from the Xu family to the Cheng family, then from the Cheng family to the Lü family—until the Hu family finally redeemed them in the eleventh month of the eighth year of Wanli (1580) for one hundred ninety taels.

In the thirty-sixth year of Wanli (1608), the Kuchuan Hu descendants gathered in Shoushan Ravine and decided to build a "Hugong Family Temple" on the foundation of the original three-tier high platform at the cave entrance. Perhaps Guangci Temple feared this "authentic" Hu Gong would steal its incense, or perhaps the Cheng family of the old street worried that this Hugong Family Temple that suddenly appeared would cause the old street to decline, a monk named Ruchang brought the Hu family to court. From the "first instance" result, in which the Cheng family managed the mountain forest, it appears the Cheng family was also the behind-the-scenes supporter or instigator of this lawsuit. The Hu family, of course, refused to accept it and appealed the case to Jinhua Prefecture. The "second instance" result虽然 preserved the Hu family's fields, land, mountains, and ponds, but the matter of building the Hugong Family Temple still upheld the original verdict. The reason was: "Fangyan has the statue, with incense offerings from all directions... Shoushan is about one li from there, how could another shrine be rebuilt... only demolish the unfinished new building at Shoushan..."

After this lesson, the Hu family, far away in Huku, seemed to understand that to gain a firm foothold in Shoushan Ravine, they must please the neighboring Guangci Temple. Thus in the eleventh year of Qing Shunzhi (1654), the Hu family generously funded Guangci Temple to repair its front hall. Subsequently, in the twenty-second year of Kangxi (1683), the Hugong Family Temple in Shoushan Ravine was completed. In the forty-first year of Kangxi (1702), the Hu family again donated fields to aid the temple. Over the following hundred-plus years, the Hu family not only repeatedly funded Guangci Temple to renovate its main hall, but both sides also agreed on the "Fangyan Sacrificial Ritual Covenant." This friendly relationship continued until 1840, when with the intervention of the Cheng family, both sides again went to court. Although the Hu family won the lawsuit, Guangci Temple "on the fourth day of the ninth month of the twenty-ninth year of Daoguang (1849), the entire temple including monk quarters was consumed by fire." The Hu family considered this the will of heaven and decided to abandon Fangyan Main Hall from then on, only going to Shoushan for sacrifices.

Architecture

In the 23rd year of the Republic (1934), the Hu family began planning to rebuild the Hugong Family Temple under the suggestion of Luo Junchao of Yongkang at that time. The reconstruction project began in 1935 and was completed in 1937, resulting in the "Multi-Story Building" (Chonglou) that stands today below Guhou Peak.

The newly built Hugong Family Temple sits on a tall foundation constructed of stone masonry, with a ground height difference of over one story on the east and west sides of the foundation. Its first floor has five bays, while the second and third floors originally had three bays each. The third floor uses the rock wall to enclose space, with the three large characters "Doushuai Terrace" clearly visible on the rock wall. The first and third floors have relatively shallow depth, while the second floor not only has high space but also a depth of two front-and-back courtyards, extending deep into the cave. The Multi-Story Building adopts a mixed brick-wood structure, with brick walls on the exterior facade as vertical load-bearing structure, supplemented by wooden beams and wooden doors and windows; the interior construction is relatively traditional, dominated by wooden structure. The architectural style was clearly influenced by the "new era": the east entrance has brick arch vaults, a Western-style small gatehouse, and the railings on the second and third floors are also obviously machine-made products.

In the 27th year of the Republic (1938), the Zhejiang Provincial Government moved to Fangyan for temporary office, with the Finance Department stationed on the second and third floors of the Hugong Family Temple. For example, due to insufficient rooms, one bay was added to each side of the second floor; to solve the lighting problem, all doors and windows were fitted with glass. During the Nationalist government's occupation, the Hugong Family Temple also received the plaque "Chunfan Tower," and Provincial Government Chairman Huang Shaohong personally wrote a couplet: "The temple's appearance strengthens Lingyan, through Song, Yuan, Ming, and Qing, passed down in historical records; may the building be renewed, rejoicing that later talents rise to shine in genealogy; the government office neighbors this scenic spot, admiring intelligence and uprightness, the gentle influence as if continuing, awaiting the reorganization of lakes and mountains, to jointly offer fragrance with the parents of this land."

sections.name: 四、没有了进士的五峰书院
sections.content_zh:
没有了科举考试，没有了进士，书院曾经举办的各种活动在民国时期就全部停止了。与胡公家庙一起，五峰书院在民国27年（1938年）到31年（1942年），也曾作为省政府的临时办公场所。或许是因为近千年来，曾经在这里徘徊的进士和学者们都久久不愿离去，所以政府工作人员走后的第一年，五峰书院就作为永康师范学校的校舍，一直到1962年。

如今，学生们也走了。空荡荡的五峰书院变成了展览馆，设有书院历史、书院制度、书院功能、书院与文房四宝、书院与科举制度、五峰书院与永康学派等专题展览，甚至还有祭堂。瀑布下、山洞里、水塘边还设有茶室，倒也颇具些意境。但是不知怎的，没有了进士和学者们穿梭其间，没有了"晦翁主讲席，从游者数百人"的热闹场面，没有了"或质疑问难、或阐发格言"的高声论辩，五峰书院便寂静的可怕。静得连偶尔来参观的游客，都不愿意在这本应该是诗意盎然的茶室里小坐，便毅然转身离去，只留下他们匆匆的脚步声回荡在寿山坑里。
sections.content_en:
Without the imperial examination and without jinshi, the various activities once held by the academy all ceased during the Republic period. Together with the Hugong Family Temple, Wufeng Academy also served as a temporary office for the provincial government from the 27th year (1938) to the 31st year (1942) of the Republic. Perhaps because for nearly a thousand years, the jinshi and scholars who once wandered here were all reluctant to leave for a long time, in the first year after the government staff left, Wufeng Academy became the school building of Yongkang Normal School, remaining so until 1962.

Today, the students have also left. The empty Wufeng Academy has become an exhibition hall, with thematic exhibitions on academy history, academy system, academy functions, academy and the four treasures of the study, academy and the imperial examination system, Wufeng Academy and the Yongkang School, and even a sacrificial hall. Tea rooms are also set up under the waterfall, in the caves, and by the pond, which is quite evocative. But somehow, without jinshi and scholars穿梭其间, without the lively scene of "Huiweng lecturing, with several hundred followers," without the loud debates of "questioning difficulties or expounding maxims," Wufeng Academy becomes terrifyingly quiet. So quiet that even occasional visiting tourists are unwilling to sit for a while in this tea room that should be full of poetry, but resolutely turn and leave, leaving only their hurried footsteps echoing in Shoushan Ravine.
